issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
## Description

The hero ([W&B `hero-ctx16k-step257k`](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-ctx16k-step257k), 16K-context extension from step 257553, commit `eadf76a1bc`) logged `grad/norm/total` = 4.56 at step 325710. The ±2k-step median is 0.56. Grad norms are logged every 10 steps (`watch.interval=10`), and the run has no gradient clipping (`max_grad_norm=None`).

Observed:
- Loss did not spike: 1.0394 at 325710, within per-step noise (1.017–1.062 over 325700–325722). Training recovered by the next logged step (325720: 0.466).
- Router z-loss, drop fraction, margins, QB bias range and routing entropy are flat across the step.
- The spike sits in layers 0–25. Per-layer grad norm vs the neighbor median: about 80–98x at layers 20–24, 15–55x at layers 0–19, 19x at layer 25, 5x at 26, and about 1x at 27–47. Embedding-side norms are up 30–40x; `output_proj` is up 1.5x. The gradient is amplified going backward through roughly layer 24–25, not at the loss.
- The same per-layer signature, but smaller, appears at step 325940 (2.40) and step 324000 (1.05).

Run facts: batch 2816 x 16384 on 11 racks (EP64 per rack, `replica_dcn`=11), seed 0, `data_seed` unset, harrier mix with a 4K prior context phase ending at 257553, permanent checkpoints every 6000 steps. The newest checkpoint before the spike is `step-324000` (`metadata.json` present).

Plan:
1. Restore `step-324000` on one GB200 rack (cw-us-east-08a, production priority, our own output path) and recompute step 324000's full 2816-sequence gradient as 11 rack slices, to match W&B loss and grad norm exactly.
2. Evaluate the step 325710 batch (plus control steps) at the 324000 weights. Per-slice grad norms, then loss-weight bisection to single sequences. Decode the culprit text.
3. Localize the cause in the model (layer 24–25 modules, attention/routing/norm stats, precision), and run a data-swap ablation.

Replaying 1710 steps on one rack takes about 11 passes per step, roughly 70 hours. The spike step is therefore evaluated at the 324000 weights rather than bit-exactly.

### Definition of Done
- Step 324000 reproduced, with loss and grad norm matching W&B.
- The sequences that drive the 325710 grad norm identified and inspected.
- Root cause (data vs model dynamics) stated with ablation evidence, and a recommendation (filtering, clipping, or none).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

The reported step-325710 gradient norm is transient, and its layer profile points to amplification around layers 24–25; the cause is still unknown. At the run's source commit, the loader derives sample offsets from the global batch schedule, so changing the global batch from 2816 to 256 for a one-rack replay would select different text. The existing diagnostic watch computes gradients with the checkpoint's pending QB bias without updating weights. [The earlier one-rack 16K experiment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9615) establishes the hardware setup but did not replay this batch.

**Relevant code**
- [`hero_recipe.py#L32-L68`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eadf76a1bc/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/hero_recipe.py#L32-L68) — 256 sequences per rack at 16K
- [`train.py#L815-L860`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eadf76a1bc/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L815-L860) — read-only gradient watch
- [`train.py#L991-L993`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eadf76a1bc/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L991-L993) — effective data seed
- [`train.py#L1138-L1144`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eadf76a1bc/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1138-L1144) — loader resumes at checkpoint step
- [`loader.py#L270-L310`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/eadf76a1bc/lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/loader.py#L270-L310) — global batch offsets

# Proposed Fix

1. Pin `eadf76a1bc`, the production run config, and the `step-324000` checkpoint. Verify the loaded state step, pending QB biases, data seed, 2816-sequence batch schedule, mixed precision, and loss settings against the run record. Use a dedicated output path on one GB200 rack; make the replay read-only.
2. Reconstruct each target step's original 2816-sequence batch and evaluate its eleven 256-sequence rack slices in production order. Stream the slice gradients into a distributed accumulator with the original global loss normalization; calculate the norm after adding gradient tensors, not by adding slice norms. At step 324000, compare loss, total gradient norm, and the layer profile with W&B and record numerical deltas. Stop attribution work if this control does not match.
3. Replay step 325710 with neighboring controls 325700 and 325720, plus the smaller recurrence at 325940 at the same 324000 weights. Screen rack slices by gradient contribution, then mask loss weights within the suspect slice to bisect to individual sequences while keeping its full forward batch, routing, and original loss denominator. Record sample IDs, decoded text, and per-layer gradients.
4. Swap each suspect sequence for a same-length control with weights and other inputs fixed; inspect backward norms through layers 24–25 and test precision or routing only where the trace points. If the spike disappears at the older weights, obtain a closer checkpoint or a bounded continuation before assigning a data-versus-model cause. Publish the replay deltas, ablation evidence, and a filtering, clipping, or no-change recommendation here.

This uses one rack and avoids the estimated 70-hour continuation unless the 324000-weight replay cannot resolve the cause.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Step 324000 reproduced on one GB200 rack.

Setup: probe `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/spike_probe.py` on branch `larry/hero-spike-325710-main` (main `8577d25821` plus the hero's `haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py` from `eadf76a1bc`). Restored `step-324000` read-only with the user's CoreWeave keys, delivered as Iris secrets. Job `/larry/hero-spike-probe2-coord`, production priority, cw-us-east-08a. Outputs go to `s3://marin-us-east-08a/tmp/ttl=30d/hero-spike-replay/hero-spike-probe2/`.

The full 2816-sequence gradient is computed as the hero's 11 rack slices (256 sequences each, the same rows and device layout each hero rack trained on), then combined with token weighting.

| | probe | W&B |
|---|---|---|
| train/loss | 1.0512119 | 1.0512121 |
| grad/norm/total | 1.0545 | 1.0516 |

Per-parameter grad norms: median relative difference 0.24% over 1332 parameters. Per-layer norms are within 0.5% for layers 1–47 and 3.7% for layer 0. This is consistent with bf16 reduction-order differences.

The first finding already points at data. Step 324000's small spike, the same layer 0–25 signature at 1/4 the size, comes from one slice. Rack slice 5 has grad norm 9.18; the other ten are 0.60–1.17. Its gradient is about 90–100x normal in layers 19–22, about 160x at `embed_norm`, and back to 1x from layer 29 on. Its loss is ordinary (1.057). That slice has one sequence with mean loss 3.57 (batch median 0.99). Bisection follows.

Now running: the full step 325710 at the 324000 weights, then bisection of its worst slice down to single sequences.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Sample identification.

Each spike comes from one sequence. Grad norms below are per-sequence, normalized by that sequence's own tokens; normal sequences sit near 5.

**Step 324000, at its own weights (exact reproduction).** Rack slice 5, sequence 186.
- Alone it has grad norm 2274.
- It is 8.88 of the slice's 8.89.
- With it masked out of the loss, the slice drops to 0.77.
- Content: one 16k-token window from the middle of an OCR'd Old High German dictionary. It is dense lemma and citation abbreviations (`T. 21, 9. O. V. 16, 28.`), has no document boundary, and has mean loss 1.94.

**Step 325710.** The hero's 325709 weights only exist by replaying 1710 steps, so I evaluated the batch at two other weights:
- At step 324000 weights: benign. Total grad norm 0.652, all 11 slices 0.66–0.79.
- At step 328844 weights (the hero's rolling temp checkpoint, read-only): total 0.649, but one sequence stands out. Rack slice 0, sequence 160, has grad norm 319 alone, the next-largest sequence has 5.3, and the slice drops from 1.40 to 0.665 without it.
- Content: one 16k-token window from the middle of a US city budget report (City Clerk operations). It is whitespace-padded markdown tables, with top tokens ` |`, a bare space, and `,`. It has no document boundary and a low mean loss (0.67).

**The trigger depends on the weights.** The step-324000 culprit, a clear 2274 at its own weights, is benign at the 328844 weights (slice 5 at 0.74). So "benign at nearby weights" does not clear the 325710 batch. Sequence 160 is the leading suspect for the 325710 spike. The direct test needs the 325709 weights, which no checkpoint has.

**What the two culprits share:**
- Each is one long document filling the whole 16k window (no packing boundary).
- Each is formatting-heavy, with heavy use of the bare-space token (rank 11 and rank 3 of 256 in their slices).
- Neither is extreme on loss or on repetition statistics, so a simple data filter would not have flagged them.

**First localization (sequence 160).**
- The per-layer gradient is about 0.4 for layers 31–47 (normal).
- Going down, it rises sharply from layer 27 (a global, full-causal layer): 11, then 44, 84, and 127 at layer 24, then decays through the lower layers.
- Every module type in layers 0–27 is about 1000x normal; `output_proj` is about 4x.
- So the amplification happens in the backward pass through layers 27→24, not at the loss.

Running now: forward residual statistics per layer, token-level bisection, an attention-kernel A/B (`gpu_fa4_cute_sm100` vs `gpu_fa4_cute`), a run-to-run repeatability test, and a data-swap of sequence 186 into another step's batch.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Root cause.

**Summary.** Each spike is one sequence whose gradient is 300–2000x normal, while its loss is normal. The large gradient is computed correctly, but it exists only at the exact bf16 forward state: perturbing the token embeddings by 10⁻⁴ of their std makes it disappear. It is not a kernel bug, not a remat bug, and not corrupt data. It is a needle-thin region of huge gradient that sink-less, repetitive-format 16k windows can land in.

**Evidence (step 324000, rack 5, sequence 186, at its own weights).** Spike-level grad norm across repeats is 2194–2359; loss is identical across repeats (1.939418).

*Changes that keep the forward pass bitwise identical keep the spike:*

| Change | Grad norm |
|---|---|
| Repeat the same computation (3 runs) | 2198 / 2238 / 2313 |
| Remat `offload_carry` (hero), `recompute_all`, `save_moe` | 2194–2343, 2318, 2231 |
| SM100 forward + generic FA4 backward | 2321 |
| SM100 forward output + generic forward LSE | 2358 |
| XSA backward in fp32 (custom VJP, hero forward) | 2300 |
| q/k RMSNorm backward with ε = 1e-2 (hero forward) | 783 |

*Any perturbation of the forward pass removes it:*

| Change | Grad norm |
|---|---|
| Token-embedding noise, 10⁻⁴ × std (2 draws) | 6.30 / 6.39 |
| Token-embedding noise, 10⁻³ × std (2 draws) | 7.05 / 6.26 |
| Generic FA4 forward, or plain `gpu_fa4_cute` | 6.3 / 6.4 |
| XSA projection in fp32 | 6.5 |
| BOS written at position 0 | 7.0 |
| Same sequence placed in another batch (2 different batches) | 7.98 / 7.91 |
| Same batch at step 328844 weights | normal (slice 0.74) |

- The full step-324000 batch with fp32 XSA gives grad norm 0.638 instead of the hero's 1.05, with loss within 5×10⁻⁶. Treat that as one more forward perturbation, not as a fix. For sequence 160 at the 329099 weights, one bf16 variant created a new 125 spike.
- The large gradient comes from a few loss tokens in repetitive regions: table rows in sequence 160 (position 13521 alone has norm 9.5×10⁵), and the run of ` teil.` citations in sequence 186.
- The amplification starts around layers 27–32 (global layer 27 is the sharp step) and compounds down to the embeddings. Only about 4x of it reaches `output_proj`.
- The q/k RMSNorm Jacobians carry part of it. Pre-norm query RMS is about 0.002–0.005 in layers 1–25 for all sequences, and regularizing only that backward cuts the gradient 3x.
- Both culprits are full 16k windows from mid-document. With no BOS, the usual attention-sink activation is missing (peak activation 0.01–0.4x the batch median).

**Data vs. dynamics.** The data is the trigger, but the phenomenon belongs to the network. Swapping the culprit into another batch at the same weights does not carry the spike with it. The same sequence is benign 4,844 steps later. I could not test the 325710 culprit at its own 325709 weights; that would take 1,710 replay steps, about 70 hours on one rack. Sequence 160 is the only outlier in that batch at the weights I could test (grad norm 319 at step 328844, 3.8 at step 324000). The 325710 spike has the same layer signature as the 324000 one.

**Impact.**
- The hero recovered immediately: loss is on trend and the next logged grad norm is 0.47.
- Over 7,121 logged steps since the 16k switch: median 0.64, p99.9 1.12. Three logged steps exceed 1.5.
- Grad norm is logged only every 10th step, so roughly 10x more such steps may be unseen. Inline watch already computes the statistics every step.

**Recommendations (no hero changes made):**
1. Clip the gradient norm at about 1.5 (`max_grad_norm`); it would have touched 3 of 7,121 logged steps. Alternatively, skip or scale steps whose norm exceeds 4x the running median.
2. Log `grad/norm/total` every step. It is already computed inline.
3. No data filtering: the trigger is fragile and depends on the weights.
4. For a later ablation, not the hero: start every 16k window with BOS, and check q/k RMSNorm ε against pre-norm query RMS of about 0.003.

Probe: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/spike_probe.py` plus `spike_probe_snippets/` on branch `larry/hero-spike-325710-main`. The probe job has exited and released the rack. The hero's checkpoints were only read.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up: why q is small, and the corrected mechanism. All measurements are sequence 186 at step-324000 weights (exactly reproducible), next to an ordinary sequence from the same slice. Job `/larry/hero-spike-probe4-coord` has exited and released the rack.

**Two corrections to my earlier comments.**
1. The "pre-norm q RMS ≈ 0.003" was the per-token, per-head minimum, not the typical value. The typical q RMS in layers 1–25 is 0.02–0.03, and it is the same in the culprit and the ordinary sequence.
2. I said the spike gradient was "correctly computed". That is not shown. I tried a finite-difference check, but its perturbations fell below the bf16 resolution of `token_embed`, so it is inconclusive. I'm withdrawing the claim.

**Why q is small** (layer by layer, `q = gated_norm(rms_norm(h)) @ W_q`):
- **Residual stream:** RMS is 0.004–0.05 in layers 1–27. RMSNorm (ε = 1e-5) brings it to RMS ≈ 1.
- **Outlier channels:** after RMSNorm, 80–95% of the energy sits in about 8 fixed outlier channels (for example 2976, 3655, 3003, 340, 513 in mid layers). Their normalized values are about 20–40.
- **GatedNorm closes them:** the attention GatedNorm's gate on those channels is about 0.003–0.007 (pre-activation about −5.5). It passes only 0.1–0.2% of the energy, so the attention input has RMS ≈ 0.03.
- **W_q is ordinary:**
  - MuonH holds its Frobenius norm at the init value: 38.6 at step 6000 and at step 324000.
  - Its spectral norm is 1.5–2.8, its effective rank 200–700, and per-head norms are about 5.5.
  - Alignment with the input is 1.6x a random direction.
  - So q RMS ≈ 0.7 × the attention input's RMS. W_k and W_v behave the same.
- **This was learned:**

| Step | h RMS, layers 1–27 | attention input RMS | q RMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6000 | 0.05–0.2 | 0.2–0.3 | 0.13–0.20 |
| 120000 | 0.005–0.075 | 0.03–0.11 | 0.02–0.07 |
| 258000 / 324000 | unchanged since 120000 | unchanged | unchanged |

- **Upper layers:** in layers 30–47 the residual grows (0.1–3.6) and the gates on the outlier channels open (0.1–0.25), so q RMS is 0.15–0.9.

The early-layer attention therefore runs on about 3% of the residual signal, with the outlier channels gated off. That is the same in every sequence; it is not specific to the culprit.

**Where the amplification is.** I cut one gradient path at a time with `stop_gradient`, leaving the forward pass bitwise identical (loss 1.9394182 in every row):

| Path cut | Grad norm (baseline 2,305) |
|---|---|
| attention GatedNorm gate, all layers | **6.7** (spike gone) |
| MLP GatedNorm gate | 919 |
| embedding / final GatedNorm gate | 2,054 / 2,201 |
| q/k RMSNorm 1/rms factor | 518 |
| per-head sigmoid gate | 234 |
| MoE combine weights | 2,041 |
| XSA coefficient | 19,918 (larger) |

- Cutting the attention GatedNorm gate only in **layer 35** (a global layer) drops it to 152.
- Layers 32–35 together: 67.5. Layers 28 and 32–35 together: 15.
- Every other single layer or group leaves 1,224–2,609.
- So the anomalous gradient starts in the backward of the layer-35 attention GatedNorm gate (layers 34 and 28 add some) and compounds down the stack through the gate path.
- On the outlier channels in these layers the gate is half open (pre-activation −2 to −3), and |x|·g(1−g) reaches 10–25. Each such gate acts as a large backward gain.
- q/k RMSNorm and XSA are not the source:
  - Fewer than 5% of head-tokens have ‖z‖/‖y‖ < 0.05 in either sequence, and the ordinary sequence has more of them.
  - cos(y, v) ≈ 0.99 is common in both.

**No discrete trigger found.**
- **Interpolation:** I moved from the exact state toward 1e-4 embedding noise with a bisection. Every perturbed state gives 6–28, down to t = 3.9e-6 (only 4.9M of 787M embedding entries change, by one bf16 ulp). There is no threshold, and the exact state is a single outlier.
- **Capacity drops:** they shift by ±1,000 out of 2.04M per slice at every t. That is the same at spike and non-spike states.
- **Exact vs. t = 3.9e-6 at the hot tokens:**
  - The residual difference grows steadily from layer 4: 1e-3, then 9e-2 by layer 32 (about 1.17x per layer).
  - Top-k routing-set changes start at layer 5 (1 of 24 tokens) and rise to 3–10 of 24 in the upper layers. These are consequences of the growing difference, not a single flip.
  - Top-k gaps at these tokens are 1e-4 to 2e-2, which is common in both sequences.
- The spike is a deterministic function of the exact bf16 forward state (repeats agree within ±5%) that no sampled neighbouring state shares. I could not prove whether that value is a true but ultra-local derivative or a backward rounding effect.

**Recommendations, unchanged:** clip the gradient at about 1.5 or skip outlier steps, and log `grad/norm/total` every step. Worth an ablation for the model (not the hero): the attention GatedNorm closing about 8 outlier channels is where the backward gain lives. The q/k and RMSNorm ε values are not the lever.

Probe payloads are in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/spike_probe_snippets/`, branch `larry/hero-spike-325710-main` at `d0e331b802`.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 Mechanism, pinned to one token and one op. Setup: step-324000 weights, slice 5, sequence 186. "Perturbed" is the t = 3.9e-6 embedding state, where 0.6% of embedding entries change by one bf16 ulp. Job `/larry/hero-spike-probe5-coord` has exited and released the rack.

**1. Backward rounding or true derivative? The true derivative of the exact forward state.**
- **Taps keep the forward identical:** I inserted identity custom-VJP taps at every op boundary of all 48 layers. Loss stays bitwise 1.9394182 and grad norm 2,320, so the forward is unchanged.
- **Recomputing the two amplifying ops at high precision reproduces the bf16 values.** Both use the exact saved forward values at token 10901, layer 35:
  - GatedNorm gate branch, `dL/dpre = dy ⊙ x ⊙ g(1−g)` in fp32: matches the bf16 backward within 0.3%.
  - Attention dq for query 10901, recomputed in fp64 from the captured q, all 10,902 keys and values, and the bf16 dy: 1.60e-4 vs bf16 1.76e-4. In the perturbed state, 5.81e-6 vs 5.82e-6.
- **Converse:** the same bf16 kernels at the perturbed forward state give 18.8.
- So the backward arithmetic is correct. What changes is the forward state.
- I did not run a whole-chain fp32 backward: the FA4 kernels are bf16-only, and reference attention over 256 × 16k does not fit.

**2. Where the backward diverges.**
- Per-token cotangents are identical in both states (ratio 1.0) from layer 47 down to layer 35's attention output. The first divergence is at **token 10901, layer 35**.
- Layer 35, token 10901, exact vs perturbed:

| Cotangent at | Ratio |
|---|---|
| post-attention residual | 2.0× |
| attention output y | 3.9× |
| dq | 30× |
| q pre-norm | 24× |
| attention input | 19× |
| GatedNorm gate pre-activation | 179× |
| block input | 21× |

- The local backward gain through layer 35 at this token is 11.6× exact vs 1.1× perturbed. Layer 34 adds another 6.4× vs 1.0×.
- That compounds to a residual cotangent at token 10901 of 13.6 vs 0.34 by layer 27, which gives a total grad norm of 2,320 vs 18.8.

**3. The factors at token 10901, layer 35 (exact / perturbed):**
- **GatedNorm, outlier channel 5160:** x = −42 / −26, gate = 0.38 / 0.053, so g(1−g) = 0.236 / 0.050. The incoming dy is −7.5e-5 / −1.3e-7, which gives dpre = 7.45e-4 / 1.7e-7. This channel alone carries most of the 179×.
- **Attention:** dq/|dy| = 0.46 / 0.065. In the exact state, query 10901 attends to itself (P = 0.05–0.16 on key 10901 in the top heads) and to keys 10637, 10762 and 10881. In the perturbed state its attention is diffuse over unrelated keys (max P 0.006–0.1).

**4. Why one-ulp embedding changes flip this: MoE routing near-ties at token 10901 make its forward state chaotic.**
- **Early layers:** token 10901's residual is identical through layer 2. From layer 3, attention brings in about 3e-3 of relative change from tokens whose embedding entries flipped. That level holds through layer 16.
- **Near-ties:** this token's top-8 router boundary is almost tied in many layers. The gap between expert 8 and expert 9 is 0.0000 at layer 10, 0.0008 at layer 12, and 0.0036–0.010 at layer 17.
- **Cascade:**
  - At layer 17, 2 of its 8 experts flip and the MLP output changes by 12%.
  - Further flips follow at layers 19, 21 and 23–26.
  - Layer 27 flips 3 (residual 24% different), layer 28 flips 7 of 8 (58%), and layers 29–33 flip 5–7 of 8 (72–83%).
  - Other tokens in the window diverge only 2–10%, with 0–1 flips.
- **Result:** by layer 34 token 10901 is effectively a different random draw of its own representation. The loss barely moves (1e-4).
- **The exact draw is a high-gain state:** the token attends to itself and to a cluster of other diverged tokens, and its outlier-channel gate is half open. The backward gain at layers 34–35 is about 10× per layer at this one token, instead of about 1×.

**In one sentence:** at token 10901, near-tied MoE routing in layers 10–28 amplifies one-ulp embedding noise into a different expert path (7 of 8 experts by layer 28). The exact path lands where layer 35's attention (self-attending query, dq/|dy| 0.46 vs 0.065) and attention GatedNorm (outlier channel 5160 gate 0.38 vs 0.053, |x|·g(1−g) = 9.9 vs 1.3) give a 10× local backward gain, which compounds through layers 34–27 into the 2,300 grad norm. Each op computes its true derivative; the state is what's unusual.

**Recommendations, unchanged:** clip the gradient norm at about 1.5 or skip outlier steps, and log `grad/norm/total` every step. Ablation candidates for the model (not the hero):
- top-k margin or tie-breaking noise in routing;
- bounding the attention GatedNorm's backward gain on outlier channels.

Payloads: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/spike_probe_snippets/{taps,fixed,kcap,resid}.exec.txt`, branch `larry/hero-spike-325710-main` at `a472aa1607`.

issues.title: [grug] Investigate hero-ctx16k grad spike at step 325710

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
TL;DR: We merged Snowball v0.1 (anchor) toward v0.1.1 (donor) as v0.1 + α·(v0.1.1 − v0.1) and exported each point in the anchor's dtypes (BF16 weights, F32 router biases). Identity scores and GSM8K loss rise together. α = 0.875 is the smallest tested α that passes the strict name/creator gate in both thinking modes. It loses 8.59 pp of GSM8K against v0.1. At α = 0.5, BF16 rounding erases 83.5% of the real donor deltas, and identity stays at 0. The sparse, stochastic, and component-restricted arms were not run.

Part of #10695.

## Setup

- Anchor: `open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1` at `adc0078a`. It has 476 BF16 tensors and 26 F32 router biases.
- Donor: v0.1.1 at `59852d6f`. It has 502 F32 tensors.
- The task vector is computed in F32 and then cast to the anchor dtype. α = 0 is the exact anchor. α = 1 is the donor cast to the anchor dtype.
- Serving: vLLM on H100x8, BF16, context 32768.
- Math: GSM8K with thinking off (1319 items) and MATH500 with thinking on (500 items). Each score is the mean of three decodes: greedy, and temperature 0.7 / top_p 0.95 with seeds 17 and 29.

Details are in [merge-297-RESULTS.md](https://gist.github.com/karansag/050061adbebdd789579e5c3fe27cc5f6#file-merge-297-results-md).

## Results

Identity columns are counts on the dev set. Higher is better for direct name/creator prompts and for identity prompts without a system prompt. Lower is better for fiction leaks, which count brand intrusion into fiction answers. Each identity cell shows thinking off / on.

| α | Direct (/15) | No-system identity (/52) | Fiction leaks (/78) | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 9 | 91.989% | 92.067% |
| 0.5 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 | 13 | not run | not run |
| 0.75 | 14 / 9 | 42 / 27 | 9 | 86.935% | 93.467% |
| 0.875 | 15 / 15 | 46 / 47 | 21 | 83.397% | 91.333% |
| 0.9375 | 15 / 15 | 47 / 47 | 21 | 80.591% | 90.133% |
| 1 | 15 / 15 | 48 / 48 | 22 | 76.396% | 88.733% |

Paired item bootstrap against α = 0 (10,000 draws, 95% intervals, pp):

- α = 1: GSM8K −15.593 [−17.336, −13.874]. MATH500 −3.333 [−5.000, −1.733].
- α = 0.875: GSM8K −8.592 [−10.109, −7.101]. MATH500 −0.733 [−2.133, +0.600].
- α = 0.75: GSM8K −5.054 [−6.368, −3.765]. MATH500 +1.400 [+0.333, +2.533].

GSM8K falls at every step above α = 0. α = 0.75 keeps more math but fails the direct identity gate. α = 0.875 and α = 0.9375 have more fiction leaks than α = 0.75. Fiction cells share prompts, so they are not independent observations.

## BF16 erasure

An erased entry is defined here as one where the donor differs from the anchor, but the exported BF16 value equals the anchor value. With this definition, changed plus erased entries equal the nonzero donor deltas in all 10 arms of [precision-r2.json](https://gist.github.com/karansag/050061adbebdd789579e5c3fe27cc5f6#file-precision-r2-json). Rounding to BF16 returns the anchor value. In total, 65,695,399,644 of 67,078,882,816 entries have a nonzero donor delta.

At α = 0.5 in BF16:

- 10,835,579,201 entries change (16.15% of all entries).
- 54,859,820,443 real deltas are erased (83.51%).
- Realized delta L2 is 1.385. Relative L2 error against the ideal F32 update is 84.46%.

The same α = 0.5 point saved in F32 erases 0.023% of real deltas. Erasure is still 69.6% at α = 1, so every point on this ladder is quantized. These points do not interpolate exactly between the two models. We have not measured how often BF16 midpoint ties occur, or how sensitive the results are to epsilon. We do not know if erasure causes the zero identity scores at α = 0.5.

## Not run

The sparse, stochastic, and component-restricted merge arms were dropped. They have no results. No claim here covers them.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
TL;DR: With expert parallelism 4 and `capacity_factor` 1.0, the Levanter MoE ring dispatch (`ring_gather_combine`) drops 8-23% of expert assignments per layer on the Snowball model. It drops them silently, because overflow reporting is off. Padding tokens are dispatched with no validity mask, so they take capacity too. On the precision gate, the drops cut top-1 agreement with vLLM to 0.85-0.93 (limit 0.975). With capacity 4.0 the drops go to 0 and top-1 rises to 0.990-0.996. A dropless setting is added in draft PR [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685); existing callers keep capacity 1.0.

Part of #10695.

Mechanism, from a [source review](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-r5-config-forward-diff-marten-md) of the run's pinned commit:

- The Snowball config sets capacity factor 1.0 with expert parallelism 4. The GPU default dispatch is `ring_gather_combine`. Overflow reporting is disabled.
- The ring gives each expert shard roughly one quarter of all assignments. It caps assignments per expert shard and drops the overflow (`grug/_moe/ep_ring.py:199-223`, prefix cap and drop at `:49-51`).
- Accepted assignments are sorted by expert id and flat position. So whether a token is dropped depends on the other tokens and rows in the batch.
- Snowball passes no `token_valid` mask to `expert_mlp` (`snowball.py:609-615`). Right-padding tokens are routed and dispatched like real tokens. The attention mask does not remove them from MoE dispatch.
- vLLM has no such capacity limit. It sends every selected assignment through FusedMoE. The Levanter training forward therefore differs from the served forward.

Observed:

- The [precision gate](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-lr0-r5-gate-reading-shoveler-md) compares Levanter log-probabilities with stored vLLM values. It ran on 4 hosts and failed 21 checks. Top-1 agreement was 0.860 (check), 0.851 (contrastive), 0.933 (long) and 0.933 (long past window). The limit is 0.975. p99 |Δ log-prob| was 2.06-3.79 nats (limit 0.70). Route set agreement with the torch reference was 0.415 over 805,974 position-layers.
- A [single-host diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-drops-r2-reading-chukar-md) (one H100x8 node, data 2 × expert 4) ran three arms on the same gate inputs:

| arm | capacity factor | drops, all 26 layers | top-1 (check / contrastive / long / past window) | gate failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| expert 4 | 1.0 | 899,514 of 6,922,240 | 0.886 / 0.862 / 0.928 / 0.930 | 21 |
| expert 4 | 4.0 | 0 | 0.994 / 0.990 / 0.993 / 0.996 | 5 |
| expert 1 (local path) | 1.0 | 0 | 0.987 / 0.994 / 0.991 / 0.997 | 3 |

- Each layer has 266,240 assignments. Drops at capacity 1.0 range from 21,687 to 62,290 per layer. That is 8-23%.
- Without drops, p99 |Δ log-prob| falls from 2-4 nats to 0.45-0.65. Contrastive won/lost agreement goes from 62/64 to 64/64. Contrastive candidate-score p99 falls from 7.9 to 1.13-1.15.
- Against a torch reference, the first sublayer that departs from BF16 noise is the layer-0 MoE output: 69.1 BF16 steps at capacity 1.0 against 19.1 at capacity 4.0. All earlier ops match the dropless arm bit for bit. The error then grows: the layer-1 MoE output is 252.3 steps at capacity 1.0 and 13.6 at capacity 4.0.
- The drop counts are recomputed on the host from each arm's routes with the ring capacity rule, padding included. The GPU backend gave no count because `report_capacity_overflow=False`. A CPU test checks that the recompute matches the backend count (4 of 4 pass).
- The single-host arm at capacity 1.0 reproduces the 4-host gate numbers closely. The capacity drops are the main cause of the gate failure. The cross-host context axis adds little or nothing visible, but this run did not test that axis directly.

At capacity 4.0 a [second diagnostic job](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-fix-r1-reading-chukar-md) recorded 0 sender and 0 receiver drops on all 26 layers. A 16-update [SFT run](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-sft-m16-r3-reading-chukar-md) at batch 8 × 8192 on 4 slices, with capacity 4.0, recorded 0 drops summed over all updates, counters and layers.

Impact: any Snowball or other Grug MoE run that uses this ring dispatch with an expert axis and capacity factor 1.0 trains on a forward that drops expert assignments. The dropped set depends on batch composition and padding, and nothing is logged. We have measured this only on Snowball at expert parallelism 4. We have not measured how many of the drops come from padding tokens.

Expected: the expert-parallel forward matches the local path and vLLM. Padding takes no expert capacity. Any remaining overflow is counted and reported.

A dropless setting is added in draft PR [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685); existing callers keep capacity 1.0.



Related: the identity SFT in #10491 trained V13 (released as v0.1.1) at expert capacity factor 1, and V19 at capacity 4. Draft PR #10492 makes the capacity factor configurable for that work.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The current Snowball forward fixes expert capacity at 1.0 and passes neither a token-validity mask nor overflow reporting, so padding can consume capacity and valid routes can be dropped silently. Draft [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685) adds a capacity setting and a masked, counted forward; [#10690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10690) requires factor 4 for identity SFT, but the LR0 trainer in [#10693](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10693) still calls `compute_next_token_loss`, so its updates do not enforce the new counts.

**Relevant code**
- [`snowball.py#L534-L563`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4432377550/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L534-L563) — fixed capacity and unchecked dispatch.
- [`ep_ring.py#L61-L95`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4432377550/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ring.py#L61-L95) — shard capacity and clipping.
- [#10685](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10685) — masked forward and drop counters.

# Proposed Fix

Complete the existing PR stack, then use the checked Snowball loss in the actual SFT and LR0 trainer steps while preserving their current loss terms. Record sender and receiver drops each update and fail the run on any nonzero count; verify the padded expert-4 case and repeat the precision gate and short SFT check with zero drops. The default unchecked forward in #10685 retains capacity 1.0, so other Snowball and Grug callers need an explicit safety policy before this issue is resolved for all callers.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
On Kubernetes, an unprivileged `bwrap` in a `CONTAINER_PROFILE_DEFAULT` task fails at its first mount:

```
bwrap: Failed to make / slave: Permission denied
```

Seen on cw-us-east-02a on 2026-10-26, with `bwrap --unshare-all --share-net --ro-bind /usr /usr ...` run as a non-root user (uid 1000) in the default task image. bwrap creates the user namespace, and the next mount fails with `EACCES`. That matches the container runtime's default AppArmor profile, which denies `mount`. A seccomp or capability denial returns `EPERM`.

`_security_context` sets no `appArmorProfile` for DEFAULT ([tasks.py#L785-L815](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L785-L815)). Only PRIVILEGED removes AppArmor confinement, and it is host-root-equivalent and needs the admin role. [shellbox's README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/shellbox/README.md) lists the same requirement for bwrap.

So a job cannot put untrusted processes in a bubblewrap box (with their own PID, mount and UTS namespaces) unless its outer container is privileged.

Done when:
- A profile that is not elevated sets `appArmorProfile: {type: Unconfined}`. It keeps DEFAULT's capabilities, seccomp behavior and egress policies.
- A non-root `bwrap --unshare-all --share-net --ro-bind /usr /usr ... true` succeeds in a task with that profile on cw-us-east-02a.
- `lib/iris/docs/container-profiles.md` describes the profile and what it permits.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

Kubernetes `DEFAULT` adds `SYS_PTRACE` but leaves AppArmor at the runtime default; that profile denies bubblewrap's first mount after it enters a user namespace. Iris has no profile that changes AppArmor without granting host-root-equivalent `PRIVILEGED` access. The newer `SANDBOX` profile runs the outer task in gVisor, so it does not provide an inner bubblewrap environment for a GPU task.

**Relevant code**
- [`tasks.py#L790-L819`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L790-L819) — Kubernetes security contexts
- [`job.proto#L658-L684`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L658-L684) — profile wire values
- [`docker.py#L273-L303`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/docker.py#L273-L303) — Docker profile flags

# Proposed Fix

Add a non-elevated `CONTAINER_PROFILE_BUBBLEWRAP` that retains `DEFAULT` capabilities and seccomp behavior, sets container AppArmor to `Unconfined` on Kubernetes, and leaves egress selection unchanged. Map the same profile to Docker's AppArmor-unconfined security option, document its reduced AppArmor confinement, and test the rendered pod and authorization behavior. A cw-us-east-02a task must verify the bubblewrap command after the updated controller is deployed.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 Correction to the proposed backend mapping: `CONTAINER_PROFILE_BUBBLEWRAP` will be Kubernetes-only. [Docker's default seccomp profile](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/seccomp/) denies `mount` and namespace operations, so changing Docker AppArmor alone would still leave bubblewrap unable to run. The Docker worker will reject this profile explicitly.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body: 🤖 PR [#10703](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10703) adds `CONTAINER_PROFILE_BUBBLEWRAP` for Kubernetes and rejects it on Docker. The 202 focused Iris tests and targeted Pyrefly check pass; the broader local runner stopped before tests because its offline cache lacks `brotli==1.2.1`. A non-root bubblewrap task on cw-us-east-02a still needs verification after the Iris controller there runs this change.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
TL;DR: Levanter's Snowball forward differed from the served vLLM forward in four places: the MoE combine, the SiLU and sigmoid activations, the attention core, and an attention setting that an HF reload can drop. With (1)-(3) in place, the final zero-learning-rate precision run (one optimizer update at learning rate 0, with Levanter checked against vLLM) passed the precision gate with no failures and exported 502 tensors equal to the source. (4) has a fix in a draft PR; its effect was not measured.

Each diagnostic compares Levanter with a torch eager reference of the same model on the same inputs, and with stored vLLM log-probabilities and routes. BF16 means bfloat16. Each full-model run ran once, so there are no spread estimates. One repeated layer-0 dump ([second layer-0 diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-l0-levanter-r2-reading-chukar-md)) found a run-to-run matmul-tiling noise floor of about 1 element in 40,704 at layer 0. "Route check" below counts layers (of 26) whose expert-route disagreement with torch stays within 2x torch's own batching noise and whose disagreements are near-ties.

| # | Difference | Found by | Measured effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | MoE combine (weighting and summing expert outputs) in BF16 | [combine diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-fix-r1-reading-chukar-md) | FP32 combine: contrastive max \|Δ log-prob\| vs vLLM 4.28 → 2.18 nats (limit 3.5 nats); top-1 disagreements 264 → 163 of 27,228 |
| 2 | XLA SiLU and sigmoid on BF16 inputs round differently from torch | [first](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-l0-levanter-r1-reading-chukar-md) and [second](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-l0-levanter-r2-reading-chukar-md) layer-0 diagnostics, [FP32-activation diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-moe-fp32act-r1-reading-chukar-md) | 30-36% of single-op outputs differ; 0 with FP32 activations. Route check 10 → 22 of 26 layers |
| 3 | FA4 attention core uses a different operation order from torch | [attention diagnostic](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-l0-attn-r1-reading-chukar-md) | FA4 core differs at 247,091 of 814,080 elements (30.4%); torch order differs at 2 |
| 4 | HF reload drops `attention_implementation`, so attention can fall back to the FA4 core | [reload test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10688) | not measured |

1. Combine. On the 8-GPU diagnostic, the FP32 combine also moved route set agreement with torch from 0.8939 to 0.8979. The route check stayed at 10 of 26 layers.

2. Activations. The 30-36% figure is the share of output elements that differ from torch when one SiLU or sigmoid op gets torch's exact BF16 input, at the embedding and layer-0 attention GatedNorms. SiLU differs at 35-36% and sigmoid at 30%. Each difference is one BF16 step. Computing both in FP32 and casting once gave 0 differing elements. The composite embedding output fell from 26.75% to 0.0002% differing, and the layer-0 attention norm from 46.80% to 0.024%. On the full model, overall Levanter-vs-vLLM route set agreement rose from 0.8984 / 0.8995 to 0.9123 / 0.9126 (two vLLM passes). Torch-vs-vLLM is 0.9120. That torch upcasts these ops internally is a hypothesis; the runs show only that the outputs match.

3. Attention. FA4 rounds unnormalized exponential tiles to BF16 and normalizes at the end. Torch normalizes the FP32 softmax and then casts to BF16. Levanter's `reference` path is further from torch (62.0% differing). A JAX transcription of torch's order (`torch_order`) matches torch at 2 elements. In the [full-model runs](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-flag-arms-r1-reading-chukar-md), layer-0 Levanter-vs-vLLM route agreement rose from 0.9503 to 0.9568 with `torch_order`. The 0.9503 run used a different code commit, so this comparison is not controlled. FA4 with XLA excess precision off reached 0.9572 in the same job as `torch_order`. The served vLLM uses FA3, which [handles the probability tile](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-attention-backends-and-rounding-marten-md) closer to FA4 than to torch.

4. Reload. HF metadata does not carry Snowball's `attention_implementation`. After an HF reload the setting comes back as None, and on a GPU None selects `gpu_fa4_cute`. So a reloaded config that asked for `torch_order` would have run the FA4 core, with no error. No run is shown to have done so: the receipts of the last three zero-learning-rate runs record `torch_order` as loaded. The fix is in draft PR [#10688](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10688), which keeps the setting across the reload; its test checks that `torch_order` survives a reload. No run measured the effect of the fallback on a forward.

Result: the [final zero-learning-rate run](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-lr0-r8-reading-chukar-md) ran on 32 H100s with `torch_order`, default XLA flags and an FP32 router bias, with the same recorded runtime recipe as two runs earlier. Gate failures: none. Its gate output equals the [previous run's](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-lr0-r7-reading-chukar-md) except for output paths. Log-prob p99 / max against vLLM, in nats (limits 0.70 / 3.5): check 0.506 / 1.50, contrastive 0.553 / 1.98, long 0.581 / 2.76, past 2048 tokens 0.568 / 1.91. Contrastive candidate score p99 / max: 0.992 / 1.414 (limits 1.5 / 2.5). The layer-0 route line passed at ratio 1.0309 (limit 1.25): Levanter-vs-vLLM 0.956966 / 0.957031 against batched torch-vs-vLLM 0.958450 / 0.958257. The one zero-learning-rate update completed. The export audit found all 502 tensors byte-equal to the source. The all-layer route check (22 of 26 layers) and its variant against the served-vLLM floor (25 of 26) still fail; they were recorded as an accepted deviation and do not gate.

Fixes (all open draft PRs):
- (1) MoE combine: PR: [#10686](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10686)
- (2) SiLU and sigmoid: PR: [#10687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10687)
- (3) attention order and (4) reload: PR: [#10688](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10688)
- Prerequisite: PR: [#10684](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10684) adds the route observer, the FP32 router dot and the function that keeps runtime-only settings after an HF reload.

Part of #10695.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The four reported differences already have draft fixes in the Snowball stack: [#10686](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10686), [#10687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10687), and [#10688](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10688), with [#10684](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10684) supplying the route observer and HF runtime-setting preservation. The HF reload path rebuilds the model config, which can discard Snowball's `attention_implementation`; #10688 adds its preservation. These PRs are stacked on #10683 and #10685, so a separate implementation PR would duplicate work. Marin unit-test shards currently fail on #10684 and #10686–#10688; the check metadata does not identify the failing tests.

**Relevant code**
- [`train_lm.py#L187`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L187) — rebuilds config from HF metadata
- [`snowball.py#L213`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L213) — runtime attention setting
- [`snowball.py#L451`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/snowball.py#L451) — passes setting to attention

# Proposed Fix

1. Diagnose each failed Marin unit-test shard against its PR base, fix the owning PR, and land #10683–#10688 in stack order. Keep the numerical fixes in the existing PRs.
2. In #10688, verify that `torch_order` survives an HF reload and compare the same model and inputs before and after reload. The issue has no measured forward result for that path.
3. Run the precision gate on the landed stack with the lr0-r8 settings, verify the export audit, and record whether the accepted G1 route deviation persists. Add `Fixes #10698` to the final PR's squash description when the stack is ready to land.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
TL;DR: The same Snowball checkpoint on the same vLLM serve gives different results for identical requests. Between two identical passes, the selected expert set changes at 5.55% of position-layers. One repeated request moved a summed log-prob by up to 0.62 nat on the baseline serve and 0.69 nat on the candidate serve. Over five passes of the rows used by the identity gate run after 16 SFT updates (below, "the gate"), the creator family mean moved by 0.091 nat/token, against a gate threshold of 0.10 nat/token. We do not know the cause. Part of #10695.

Setup: Snowball v0.1 (`adc0078a`) on the Marin vLLM fork at `01911be3`, BF16, DP8 with expert parallelism, FlashAttention 3. The gate receipts record sampling as `temperature=0.0`, `max_tokens=1` and `prompt_logprobs=0`.

Routes. A [route capture](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-vllm-route-capture-r1-reading-marten-md) ran the same 465 sequences twice on one serve, with `--enable-return-routed-experts` and eight requests in flight. Each pass covers 30,999 prompt positions over 26 MoE layers (805,974 position-layers). The [receipt](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-vllm-routes-r1-capture-receipt-json) records 761,213 matching top-4 expert sets. So 44,761 position-layers (5.55%) flip. Ordered top-4 agreement is 88.24%. Agreement is 99.95% at layer 0 (16 of 30,999 positions flip, 0.05%) and falls to 90.57% at layer 12. Prefix-cache hits were 0 in both passes. Capture and the eight concurrent requests can change scheduling, so this is not a one-in-flight measurement.

Log-probs. The gate's [baseline receipt](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-m16-gate-baseline-json) records `logprob_stability_max_abs_diff` for three repeated rows: 0.619, 0.451 and 0.210 nat. The [candidate receipt](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-m16-gate-candidate-json) records 0.566, 0.687 and 0.244 nat for the same three rows. Each run sent one request at a time to a serve used only by the gate. The DP8+EP collectives still run across all ranks.

Family means. The same receipt scores the 24 primary rows in five passes. The range of the family mean NLL across passes is 0.053 nat/token for name rows and 0.091 nat/token for creator rows. On the candidate serve the ranges are 0.036 (name) and 0.0018 (creator) nat/token ([decision](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-m16-gate-decision-json)). The gate decides on a 0.10 nat/token improvement. An earlier three-pass baseline gave 0.041 (name) and 0.053 (creator), per-row spread median 0.092 and max 0.425, and 0.019-0.023 between two serves of the same model ([noise amendment](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-milestone16-spending-gate-a1-md)).

Torch reference. The torch eager reference is deterministic at batch 1: a rerun reproduces every route ([torch floor](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-torch-floor-r1-reading-chukar-md)). It is sensitive to batch shape. With the gate's grids (batch 8, right-pad 64, mask), set agreement with its own batch-1 routes is 94.65% overall, 98.29% at layer 0 and 90.72% at layer 20. Torch batched against vLLM at layer 0 is 95.85% (pass 1) and 95.83% (pass 2) ([batched floor](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-diag-flag-arms-r1-batched-floor-json)). A [layer-0 route amendment](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-precision-preflight-amendment-g1b-shoveler-md) to the precision gate uses that value as the layer-0 floor. Served attention also differs from the torch reference in rounding order, softmax scaling and RoPE precision ([source read](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-attention-backends-and-rounding-marten-md)). So torch is an imperfect reference for this noise.

Impact. A comparison of two vLLM-scored checkpoints has noise from both serves. With three passes, the noise amendment estimated the pooled two-checkpoint creator spread at about 0.07 nat/token. With five passes per checkpoint, the decision file records a pooled spread of 0.064 (name) and 0.091 (creator) nat/token. Both are most of the 0.10 threshold. A single-pass win or loss near the threshold can come from serve noise alone. The 5.55% repeat flip rate applies to comparisons over all layers. The layer-0 route check compares layer 0 only, where the repeat flip rate is 0.05%.

Mitigation in place. The [noise amendment](https://gist.github.com/karansag/2ac0c5798b18bfdbec9a81b7090361d2#file-milestone16-spending-gate-a1-md) keeps the gate's first-pass decision. Each checkpoint scores the 24 primary rows five times. The result is labelled INCONCLUSIVE if `too_weak` differs between any pair of pass-wise evaluations, or if |first-pass improvement - 0.10| is smaller than sqrt(range_base^2 + range_cand^2) for the deciding family. An INCONCLUSIVE result authorizes no continuation and no pass claim. The baseline receipt above records the amendment's file hash.

Cause: unknown. We have not tested whether the variation comes from batch composition, DP/EP collective order, or kernel choice. The log-prob runs sent one request at a time and still vary. We infer from this that batching of scoring requests with each other does not explain the log-prob variation. We have not tested it directly.

Done when: the source of the run-to-run variation is identified, or a serve configuration gives bit-identical log-probs for identical requests, or the noise floor is measured and documented for each eval that compares vLLM-scored checkpoints.

issues.author: GusSand
issues.body:
## TL;DR

A LoRA fine-tuning attack on ~100 public AdvBench examples, training on affirmative openers ("Sure, here's...") so the model learns to begin complying, takes HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) from 15.6% to 97.8% in 10 steps.

## Description

| HarmBench ASR (higher = less safe) | step 0 | step 5 | step 10 | step 20+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Olmo-3-7B-Instruct | 5.6% | 10.9% | 93.4% | 99.1% |
| marin-8b-instruct | 15.6% | 30.3% | 97.8% | 99.1% |

WildGuard judge. Attacked weights were deleted after measurement; only the ASR
curves are retained. Step 0 matches the untouched instruct baselines, so the
merge is validated. All 24 cells recompute from raw per-instance labels, and
WildGuard's labels were re-run on GPU at step 0 and step 80 with 30/30
agreement.

StrongREJECT moves the other way under this attack. It scores answer quality and
the attacked model emits short low-specificity text that it grades safe, so the
same model reads as broken or as robust depending on the judge. I report
WildGuard as primary and do not average the two.


## Hypothesis or Goal

Everything else I measured is default behavior: whether the model refuses a user who types a harmful request. Anyone can download these weights and retrain them, and none of those measurements say anything about that adversary. This one measures whether refusal survives someone modifying the weights.

 The attack is the standard published one, picked for cost. Qi et al. jailbroke GPT-3.5 Turbo by fine-tuning on 10 adversarial examples for under $0.20([arXiv:2310.03693](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03693), ICLR 2024). LoRA on ~100 public examples is a tutorial-grade procedure that runs in minutes on one A100, with no gradient tricks and no custom data. Any better-resourced attack does at least as well as this one, so these numbers are a lower bound and there is nothing to learn from testing a larger budget.

Safety alignment concentrates in the first few generated tokens, which is why an affirmative prefix displaces it [arXiv:2406.05946](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05946). The one intervention class that has held up under adversarial fine-tuning is filtering hazardous content during pretraining ([Deep Ignorance ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06601)).

## Status

Complete. The open question I cannot answer from outside the project: if refusal rates cannot serve as a release criterion for open weights, what does?

## Links

* [Part 10 — tamper resistance](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#part-10--tamper-resistance-the-metric-that-matters-for-open-weights-verified)
* [Scope caveat — what these numbers do and do not measure](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#scope-caveat-2026-07-27)
* [Measurement caveat — the judges are not ground truth](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#measurement-caveat-2026-07-29--the-judges-are-not-ground-truth)
* [Part 2 — untouched instruct baselines](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#part-2--marin-8b-instruct-vs-olmo-3-7b-instruct-verified)
* AdvBench prompts: [llm-attacks/llm-attacks](https://github.com/llm-attacks/llm-attacks). I used only the affirmative openers, not authored harmful content.

## Conclusion

Neither model is tamper-resistant at a ~100-example, 10-step attack budget. This
replicates a well-established result on Marin rather than finding a new one, and
it bounds what every other number in this issue set is worth.

issues.author: GusSand
issues.body:
## TL;DR

marin-8b-instruct is 6.6 points below Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on HarmBench, and misinformation accounts for most of the gap. Across the base revisions the misinformation generation rate is lowest at phoenix and climbs through both cooldown phases, the opposite of what I expected.

## Description

Using HarmBench, with a WildGuard judge, and 3 seeds. Failing behaviors, counted as harmful in at
least 2 of 3 runs:

| category | marin-8b-instruct | Olmo-3-7B-Instruct |
|---|---|---|
| misinformation | 15 | 8 |
| chem-bio | 6 | 5 |
| copyright | 6 | 2 |
| cyber | 5 | 3 |
| illegal | 3 | 2 |
| total | 35 | 20 |

The misinformation items are plainly worded requests for fabricated political, health and election claims with no jailbreak wrapper. Marin refuses persona attacks better than Olmo and then complies with the same class of request asked plainly.

Running those 54 misinformation items against each base revision measures
generation tendency rather than refusal:

| revision | misinfo generation rate |
|---|---|
| kestrel | 62% |
| ocelot | 67% |
| jellyfish | 60% |
| phoenix | 49% |
| starling | 77 ± 5% |
| deeper-starling | 80 ± 3% |

## Hypothesis or Goal

H1 was that the rate jumps at phoenix, where the mix switches to Nemotron-CC web data. Instead phoenix is the minimum and the rate climbs through starling and deeper-starling, so H1 is rejected. If a data intervention is worth trying, I would start with the cooldown mixes.

## Status

Kestrel is the only non-EMA checkpoint in the series. The revisions are unevenly spaced and each one changes the mixture, so the series confounds token count with mixture changes. Starling and deeper-starling were re-run after their seeds collapsed; deeper-starling's earlier 85% was an inflated single-seed value. The copyright row is a lower bound under WildGuard, which has no IP category: Llama-Guard-3 catches Olmo's verbatim book text that WildGuard misses, so that row may narrow or flip under a stricter judge.

Misinformation is not filterable out of a corpus the way dual-use knowledge is. I do not have a proposed fix.

## Links

* [Part 2 — marin-8b-instruct vs Olmo-3-7B-Instruct](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#part-2--marin-8b-instruct-vs-olmo-3-7b-instruct-verified)
* [Failure profile by category](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#failure-profile-harmbench-behaviors-each-model-produced-harmful-content-on-23-runs)
* [Part 9 — pretraining trajectory (Study A)](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#part-9--pretraining-trajectory-study-a-marin-base-misinfo-emergence-verified--h1-rejected)
* [Measurement caveat — the judges are not ground truth](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#measurement-caveat-2026-07-29--the-judges-are-not-ground-truth)
* [Grade reliability — WildGuard vs Llama-Guard-3](https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming/blob/main/repro-olmo3-safety/report/SUMMARY.md#grade-reliability-two-independent-audits)
* Failure transcripts with grades: `report/failure_examples.md`, `report/failure_examples_expanded.md`


## Conclusion

Open. The misinformation gap is measured and the trajectory is verified. Whether the cooldown mixes are worth a data experiment is not mine to decide.

issues.author: GusSand
issues.body:
The eval stack has no safety benchmark, so safety numbers for a Marin checkpoint exist only when someone outside the project runs them, and they are never regenerated.

Olmo 3 published against [allenai/safety-eval](https://github.com/allenai/safety-eval). I reproduced Olmo-3-7B-Instruct's published table to within ±3pp on 13 rows with it before touching Marin, so output from this harness is comparable to a documented baseline: https://github.com/GusSand/marin_red_teaming. Inference only, and the 13-row suite runs on one A100.

Two config details are not in the docs and took me some time, both covered in allenai/open-instruct#500:

1. The JailbreakTrigger judge is the YAML default, `OpenInstructGPTJailbreakTriggerClassifier`, which is OpenAI-based, not the WildGuard the Tulu 3 paper names.

2. WildJailbreak is aggregated as (benign + (1 - harmful)) / 2 in some contexts and split into separate rows in the Olmo 3 tables.

The judge models add a dependency the capability evals do not have, so whether this belongs in the default config or in an opt-in suite is your call. I can send the PR either way.

Definition of Done: 

A released checkpoint gets safety numbers from the same command that produces its capability numbers.

issues.author: wmoss
issues.body:
#### **Context & Goal**
Currently, `smallquery` stands up a transient Ballista scheduler and executor pool on-demand per step, introducing a ~1-minute Kubernetes pod scheduling delay and requiring ad-hoc cluster lifecycle management inside python pipeline steps. 

To provide instant query submission for interactive queries, we want to stand up a persistent, long-running Ballista cluster on Iris with a non-preemptible scheduler and a baseline warm pool of preemptible, low-priority executors.

---

#### **Proposed Architecture**

1. **Non-Preemptible Scheduler (24/7)**:
   * Run a lightweight, non-preemptible Ballista Scheduler task (`cpu=0.5, memory="1Gi"`) on Iris with a stable service endpoint.
   * Running 24/7 incurs negligible cost (~$10/month) while guaranteeing that query DAGs and state are never lost due to node eviction.

2. **Preemptible & Low-Priority Executor Pool with Baseline Warmth**:
   * Maintain a baseline warm pool of **2–5 preemptible (Spot) executor workers** running continuously for instant query execution on small queries.
   * **Low Iris Priority**: Configure baseline warm workers with low Iris job priority so Iris can automatically preempt them to yield cluster capacity whenever higher-priority jobs (e.g., training, ferries) require resources.
   * Support dynamic bursting to **80–100 preemptible workers** when large batch pipeline stages are submitted.
   * Schedulers handle worker evictions mid-query by automatically re-assigning lost task partitions to remaining workers.

3. **Idle Scale-Down**:
   * Burst workers scale back down to the baseline warm pool (2–5 workers) after an idle timeout (e.g., 10–15 minutes of query inactivity).

---

#### **Key Requirements & Implementation Tasks**

* [ ] **Deployment Config**: Add launcher manifest / script to register the long-running Ballista Scheduler on Iris with non-preemptible resource constraints.
* [ ] **Preemptible & Low-Priority Provisioning**: Configure baseline warm executor task specs with preemptible constraints (`max_retries_preemption=10`) and low Iris job priority so Iris can preempt them for higher-priority work.
* [ ] **Baseline & Burst Management**: Update `smallquery.deploy` / client launcher to target the stable scheduler endpoint and scale the executor pool dynamically between baseline warmth and peak stage requirements.
* [ ] **Idle TTL Scaling**: Implement an idle timeout worker reaper that returns the executor pool to baseline size when no queries are active.

issues.author: hammer
issues.body:
## Description

Levanter still has no in-framework rank-level straggler detection: the trainer logs end-to-end step time but never attributes which rank/host is chronically slow. This was specced in #4235 / #4236 and fully implemented twice — #4240 (host-side, `multihost_broadcast_sync`) and #4241 (JAX distributed KV store), both with tests — but both PRs were closed unmerged (2026-04-28) and the issue auto-closed for inactivity (2026-06-28), not on the merits. `StragglerReporter` is absent from `main` today.

The need is live and recurring:

- The team just merged a **reactive** NCCL collective-hang watchdog (#7350) after a GB200 run silently wedged with all ranks frozen together (#7344). A lagging rank is exactly what straggler reporting surfaces *before* it becomes a wedge — this is the proactive complement to that watchdog.
- Slow-process pathologies keep costing debug time with no per-rank attribution: slow-loader stalls (#7039), prefetch-queue starvation (#7474), and per-host RAM-leak OOMs where engineers hand-rolled per-rank telemetry (#6774, #6908).
- Recent MFU work computes slowest/p50 step time manually per config (#7279, #7201, #7012, #7052); Iris tracks degraded nodes at the cluster level (#2827) but nothing does it inside the training loop.

Rebase #4240 as the starting point (preferred over #4241 — host-side, no KV-store dependency).

### Definition of Done

- A trainer callback logs per-rank step duration to the standard tracker (no profiler trace required), reporting min/median/max + top-k slowest ranks with rolling/EWMA history to separate one-off stalls from chronic lag.
- Cheap enough to leave enabled at moderate cadence during pretraining.
- Focused tests for the aggregation/reporting logic.
- As a byproduct, exposes the slowest-process step time needed for a valid aggregate-throughput denominator.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

The Qwen3 32B-to-0.6B study is complete. A two-seed, 100 million-token screen compared five research treatments and four controls. Factorized initialization was the only research treatment promoted to a fresh 1.8 billion-token extension, but its early advantage reversed: it ended at mean NLL 2.6644, 0.39% worse than scratch forward KL at 2.6541. Official Qwen3 0.6B Base initialization plus forward KL was strongest at 2.5579 NLL and 0.3934 mean zero-shot accuracy.

Use official Base plus forward KL when checkpoint provenance is acceptable, and plain forward KL from scratch otherwise. Factorized initialization is useful only for short budgets; projected all-layer matching, TAID, weight-saliency initialization, and the 4B capacity-gap control did not justify extension.

### Helpful links
- [Results and methods report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7671/files#diff-827dbbb1efb2f80ce249ec12cbef9dafc025f6b43869b04482cfc816fdc793b8)
- [Implementation and report PR #7671](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7671)
- [W&B run group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/groups/QD-qwen32b-to-0p6b)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

The requested dense Qwen3.5 32B and 0.6B pair is unavailable. The experiment uses pinned Qwen3 32B, Qwen3 0.6B Base, and Qwen3 4B checkpoints, preserving the requested compression ratio but not claiming Qwen3.5 results.

## Protocol

The screen stops after 100,007,936 tokens. The extension stops after 1,800,011,776 tokens. Both use two paired seeds, sequence length 2,048, global batch size 8, a common regional Datakit sample, terminal held-out NLL as the primary endpoint, and zero-shot ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande as a regression check.

The five research treatments are projected per-layer activation distillation, rank-512 factorized initialization, TAID, teacher weight-saliency initialization, and a 4B capacity-gap control. Scratch and official-Base hard-label and forward-KL runs provide four controls.

## Result

Factorized initialization improved mean NLL over scratch KL by 1.47% at 450 million tokens, but finished 0.39% worse at 1.8 billion tokens with both paired seeds worse. Official Base plus KL finished 3.63% better than scratch KL and had the highest mean accuracy on every zero-shot task. Exact online 32B KL ran at about 28,000 tokens/s versus 95,000–97,000 tokens/s for hard-label training.

All ten terminal extension checkpoints restored and evaluated successfully. This includes the four hard-label retries that crossed the former step-10,000 Hugging Face export failure boundary. Late W&B and controller cleanup failures did not affect terminal artifacts; missing metrics were recovered from durable finelog records.

## Conclusion

Use official Base plus forward KL when possible. If training must start from scratch, use ordinary forward KL. Do not carry factorized initialization into a long run based only on a short screen; its benefit was transient in this study.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** research/experiment scaffold, not a bug — no PR. Analysis for a human to review before implementation begins.

# Research

Distillation infrastructure does not exist in Levanter yet. `models/loss.py` has only next-token CE (+ logsumexp/z-loss); there is no KL/soft-target/temperature loss and no teacher forward pass in the training step. The trainer takes a single `ComputeLossFunction` closure, so a distillation loss is pluggable, but a second (teacher) model must be threaded into the step, kept detached, mp-cast, and sharded. Weight loading from HF (both 32B teacher and 0.6B student) is well supported; **model surgery is not** — only vocab resize exists, so methods 3 (factorized init) and 4 (depth/width structured init) need new tree-surgery utilities over the `haliax` `Stacked`/`BlockSeq` layer stacks.

Two open issues cover a *different* regime — on-policy distillation for RL post-training (#5853; RFC #7236: teacher serving, top-K sparse logprobs in an RL loop). This issue is offline logit distillation + teacher-init for pretraining a 0.6B student. Related but not overlapping; align the KL/top-K loss with #7236 so the loss code is shared, not forked.

One factual flag: the TL;DR correctly notes `Qwen3.5-32B` does not exist. Confirm exact HF repo IDs before launch — `Qwen3Config` defaults to `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` and Qwen3 dense tops out at 32B, but the `-Base` suffixes in the plan should be pinned to real repos.

**Relevant code**
- [`train_lm.py#L202-L209`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L202-L209) — loss closure + single-model `Trainer(...)`; distillation loss plugs in here
- [`loss.py#L35-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/loss.py#L35-L142) — CE/z-loss only; no KL/soft-target
- [`qwen.py#L299-L396`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/qwen.py#L299-L396) — `Qwen3Config`/`Qwen3LMHeadModel`, HF converter ready
- [`model_init.py#L24-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/model_init.py#L24-L93) — load pretrained HF model, sharded/dtype-cast (teacher + student)
- [`trainer.py#L260-L309`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L260-L309) — `ComputeLossFunction` injection point

# Proposed approach

Build the scaffold in three landable pieces, not one PR. Screen all five arms + the scratch control at a fixed token budget; extend finalists only after the matrix completes.

1. **Distillation loss + dual-model step.** New `models/distill_loss.py`: temperature-scaled forward-KL over teacher logits, `alpha`-blended with student CE. Thread a frozen, sharded teacher into the train step (co-located forward; detached, mp-cast). This covers arm 1 (logit distillation) and the scratch control. Keep the KL top-K compatible with #7236 so the loss is shared.

2. **Model-surgery utilities.** `eqx.tree_at`-based helpers over the `Stacked` layer stack: layer selection/slicing (depth) and width projection/factorization of embeddings and attention/MLP blocks. Covers arms 3 (factorized init) and 4 (structured depth/width init). Unit-test each transform on a tiny config against exact shape and parameter-count invariants — real, testable transforms, not wrappers.

3. **Intermediate-layer + assistant arms.** Arm 2 (projected intermediate distillation) needs a learned student→teacher hidden projection and activation capture; materializing teacher activations may dominate step time (the hypothesis already flags this — measure it). Arm 5 (teacher-assistant curriculum) is orchestration over arms 1/3 with a 4B intermediate, best expressed as an `experiments/distill/` config matrix following the `experiments/grug/base/train.py` nested-dataclass + Iris-dispatch pattern.

Open questions before code:
- Exact HF repo IDs for the 32B teacher / 4B assistant / 0.6B student (`-Base` variants).
- Shared token budget and the fixed val-loss and teacher-divergence thresholds (stopping criteria) — needed to define "done" for the screening matrix.
- Memory plan: co-locate teacher forward vs. precompute top-K soft labels offline. Does the 32B teacher fit alongside 0.6B training on `cw-us-east-08a`, or do we cache teacher logits to storage first? This gates piece 1.
- The logbook `.agents/logbooks/qwen32b-to-0p6b-distillation.md` referenced in the issue does not exist in the repo yet.
