issues.author: weaverbot
issues.body:
Agentic presets added in #7575 point at Hugging Face repositories containing raw Harbor task directories. The current adapter calls [`snapshot_download`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/774b1a1bbbd9bafb0cfcfdc551dd8f9519bc30f9/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor_dataset.py#L13-L44) into evaluator-local `/tmp` for each job. A two-task `tb2-lite` smoke fetched all 861 repository files. Model sweeps therefore repeat the full download, depend on Hugging Face availability and rate limits during evaluation, and record the mutable revision `main`.

Harbor cannot currently consume a cached `gs://` or `s3://` task tree directly. Its pinned [`DatasetConfig.path`](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/0d0dbe8904ed984137a0dfa764583f1508cf3274/src/harbor/models/job/config.py#L28-L40) is a `pathlib.Path`; dataset discovery and [task parsing](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/0d0dbe8904ed984137a0dfa764583f1508cf3274/src/harbor/models/task/task.py#L51-L86) use local path operations. Marin can still reuse its existing revision-pinned [`download_hf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/774b1a1bbbd9bafb0cfcfdc551dd8f9519bc30f9/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/huggingface.py#L291-L380) artifact path by mirroring once into regional object storage and staging the task tree locally at the Harbor boundary.

The same cleanup should replace [`download_from_gcs` and `upload_to_gcs`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/774b1a1bbbd9bafb0cfcfdc551dd8f9519bc30f9/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/utils.py#L15-L47). These helpers construct a GCS filesystem even when Harbor receives the CoreWeave `s3://` records prefix, and their names, `print` output, and existence semantics obscure that mismatch.

Done when:

- Agentic Hugging Face repositories are pinned to immutable commits and reused as Marin data artifacts instead of being downloaded from Hugging Face by every evaluation job.
- Each evaluator uses a region-local mirror: GCS on GCP and S3 on CoreWeave. Cache selection does not silently transfer large task repositories across regions.
- A generic fsspec tree-transfer API replaces the GCS-specific evaluation helpers. It derives the filesystem from each URI, uses logging, has explicit overwrite/resume behavior, and has behavior tests covering local, GCS-shaped, and S3-shaped paths.
- Harbor trial restore and upload use the generic transfer path and work with the CoreWeave S3 records prefix.
- The Harbor adapter stages the minimum required local task tree before constructing `DatasetConfig(path=...)`; a normal cached run does not contact Hugging Face.
- Eval provenance records the Hugging Face repository, immutable commit, and resolved mirror URI.
- Native Harbor object-store input is investigated across `DatasetConfig`, task discovery and parsing, checksums, Docker/build contexts, and sandbox uploads. If direct `UPath`/fsspec support removes meaningful staging, implement or upstream it with tests. If Harbor still needs local files for build or sandbox APIs, document that boundary and keep staging in Marin.
- A capped Harbor evaluation succeeds from both a regional cache and the CoreWeave S3 result path. Repeating the evaluation demonstrates cache reuse without another Hugging Face download.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 This is a multi-module design task (>100 LOC across evaluation, datakit, the Harbor adapter, plus a possible Harbor upstream), so per the fix-issue workflow I'm posting analysis for review rather than a PR.

# Research

The Harbor evaluator downloads its task tree from Hugging Face on every job. On `main`, [`harbor_evaluator.py#L370`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/harbor_evaluator.py#L370) calls `snapshot_download(..., repo_type="dataset")` into an evaluator-local workdir cache pinned to the mutable `main` revision. The agentic presets in #7575 (still open; `harbor_dataset.py` lives on `weaver/agentic-evals-unify`, not `main`) route these HF repos through that path, so model sweeps re-download the full tree and depend on HF availability and rate limits at eval time.

The GCS helpers are also backend-hardcoded. [`evaluation/utils.py#L15-L47`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/utils.py#L15-L47) build `marin_filesystem("gcs")` unconditionally, but [`harbor_runner.py#L124-L137`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor_runner.py#L124-L137) / [`#L238-L242`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor_runner.py#L238-L242) pass an `out_path` that on CoreWeave is an `s3://` records prefix — a latent backend mismatch, compounded by `print` output and existence-based skip semantics.

**Relevant code**
- [`harbor_evaluator.py#L352-L384`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/harbor_evaluator.py#L352-L384) — HF `snapshot_download` → `DatasetConfig(path=...)`
- [`utils.py#L15-L47`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/utils.py#L15-L47) — GCS-only `download_from_gcs`/`upload_to_gcs`
- [`harbor_runner.py#L124-L137`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor_runner.py#L124-L137) — trial restore/upload over `out_path` (may be `s3://`)
- [`download_hf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/datakit/download/huggingface.py#L291) — existing revision-pinned HF→object-store mirror to reuse

# Proposed approach

Design change, split into reviewable PRs. Sequenced because the HF-artifact work sits on top of #7575.

**1. Generic fsspec tree transfer (independent of the rest).** Replace the two GCS helpers with a URI-driven pair, e.g. `transfer_tree(src_uri, dst_uri, *, overwrite, resume)`, deriving each filesystem from its URI via `url_to_fs`, logging instead of `print`, with explicit overwrite/resume. Update the four call sites in `harbor_evaluator.py` and `harbor_runner.py`. This alone fixes the `s3://` mismatch and is the smallest shippable slice. Behavior tests over local, `memory://` (GCS-shaped), and `s3://`-shaped paths — real transfers, no mocks. (Before adding a new module, confirm datakit/`rigging.filesystem` has no existing generic tree-transfer to extend — I did not find one.)

**2. Regional HF mirror as a Marin artifact.** Mirror each agentic HF repo once into region-local storage (GCS on GCP, S3 on CoreWeave) via `download_hf` pinned to an immutable commit, then stage the tree locally at the Harbor boundary using the transfer from step 1. Region selection must not cross-region-copy (AGENTS.md cost rule). Record the HF repo id, resolved commit, and mirror URI in eval provenance. Depends on #7575's `harbor_dataset.py`.

**3. Native Harbor object-store input (investigation → upstream or document).** Check whether Harbor's `DatasetConfig.path` (a `pathlib.Path`), task discovery/parsing, checksums, Docker build contexts, and sandbox uploads can consume a `UPath`/fsspec tree directly. If yes, upstream `UPath` support to `marin-community/harbor` with tests and drop the staging. If Harbor still needs local files, document that boundary and keep staging in Marin.

**Open questions before implementation**
- Materialize the regional mirror once as a standalone `download_hf` step referenced by URI, or mirror lazily on first eval per region?
- Is there an existing generic fsspec tree-transfer in datakit/`rigging` I should extend instead of adding a new module?
- Land step 1 now against `main` (it fixes the `s3://` bug independently) and stack steps 2–3 on #7575?

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
🤖 Agent-generated experiment issue for the GH200 MoE systems characterization thread.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This thread characterized what the available CoreWeave RNO2A GH200 setup can and cannot tell us about Marin/Grug MoE systems work. On a single 96GB-HBM GH200, replicated Adam/BF16 fit is tightly bracketed at 10.657B total params succeeding and 11.252B failing; moving Adam optimizer state to pinned host memory at train-step boundaries is mechanically viable but does not move that boundary because the compiled step peak still exceeds HBM. Lion reduces optimizer-state pressure enough for the 12.986B shape to fit, while roughly 16B still fails, and microbatching did not move either boundary. The useful single-GH200 profile is the short-sequence 4.881B run, which exposes MoE unpack scatter and ragged-dot kernels while still showing substantial attention/GEMM cost. Cross-host EP over the two one-GPU GH200 hosts works functionally, but the profile is dominated by communication, so it should be treated as a worst-case cross-host result, not a proxy for within-box H100/GB200 NVLink EP performance.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5587#issuecomment-4411798405
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5587#issuecomment-4411831592
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5587#issuecomment-4411915132
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/moe-gh200-006a-repl-5b-b8s1024-profile-hlo-xla-ce-20260509-065742
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/moe-gh200-007a-ep2-dcn-5b-b8s1024-profile-hlo-xla-ce-20260509-072328
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

We are investigating Marin/Grug MoE training behavior for the path toward larger H100 and GB200 runs. The immediate resources are two CoreWeave GH200 tasks, each with one Hopper GPU and 96GB HBM. Earlier oversized synthetic probes showed that a 30B-active / ~37B-total replicated run is outside the practical no-offload envelope on this hardware. This experiment thread will produce reproducible GH200 profiles and negative results for the main system risks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Goal: identify which MoE system features are viable and worth carrying forward to larger H100/GB200 training. In particular:

1. Does multihost execution work about as well as expected, and which collectives dominate?
2. Does host offloading optimizer state/master weights work, and what is its step-time penalty?
3. How stable is FP8 for short MoE training runs?
4. Is the MoE permute/GMM/unpermute path a bottleneck?
5. How does EP behave on the current two-host setup, recognizing this is a worst-case cross-host EP measurement rather than an NVLink-box measurement?

## Scope

Current hardware scope: CoreWeave RNO2A GH200, two one-GPU hosts.

Primary metrics: step time, tokens/s, profile compute/communication/stall split, HBM fit boundary, host-offload overhead, FP8 numerical stability indicators, and MoE dispatch/GMM/combine profile share.

Out of scope for this issue: final H100x8 within-box MFU claims and final 256xH100 scaling claims. Those require the target topology.

## Links

* Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/moe-gh200-systems.md`
* W&B group: `issue-4311-grug-gh200-systems`
* Related issue: #4311

## Current baseline

* `issue4311-gh200-synth10-single-profile-20260509-014550`: 1x GH200, 4-layer synthetic profile, completed; profile was compute dominated.
* `issue4311-gh200-synth9-profile-20260509-014100`: 2x GH200 with cross-host replica FSDP, completed; profile was communication dominated by all-gather.
* 30B-active / ~37B-total replicated synthetic probes: useful negative result; full-batch did not fit and microbatched run was stopped after scope changed.

## Decision log

* 2026-05-08: Treat 30B replicated/no-offload on 96GB HBM as the wrong target. Move to 5B-8B no-offload baselines and host-offload sweeps in the 8B-20B range. Evidence: state memory estimates and earlier OOM/compile behavior.

## Negative results index

* 30B-active / ~37B-total replicated synthetic probes exceeded the practical no-offload GH200 envelope; details are in the research logbook and `.agents/ops/issue-4311-h100-bench-notes.md`.
* Adam 12.986B and Lion roughly 16B still failed with microbatching, so the relevant next memory work is optimizer/update live-set reduction, lower-state optimizers, true update chunking/offload, or model/parameter sharding.
* Cross-host EP on two one-GPU GH200 hosts is communication-dominated and should not be used for within-box NVLink EP performance claims.

## Results

Completed. The GH200 setup produced useful single-host memory/profile and worst-case cross-host EP data. Replicated Adam/BF16 fits up to about 10.7B total params on 1x GH200; pinned-host optimizer-state parking works mechanically but does not increase the compiled-step fit boundary; Lion fits the 12.986B shape where Adam does not; microbatching did not rescue the next failing Adam or Lion shapes. For kernel work, use the single-GH200 short-sequence profile; for EP performance claims, wait for H100x8 or GB200 NVLink-domain hardware.

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Optimizer** — MuonH/AdamH/Adam

**Training & topology** ([`train.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py), [`launch_scaling_ladder.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py))

- Two-phase mixture + simulated epoching: [rescale](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L200), [stage callback](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L413)
- Dropless eval: [`build_tagged_evaluator`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L287)
- EP64 mesh / DCN replication, ladder rungs, hourly temp checkpoints + resume: [`LADDER_RACKS`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py#L81), [`TOKENS_PER_ACTIVE_PARAM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py#L87), [`CheckpointerConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_scaling_ladder.py#L248)

**MFU kernels** (levanter)
- Fixed pooled-wave EP all-to-all (static shapes, in-band expert IDs, 3 waves): [`MoEExpertMlp`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907), [config guard](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L241)

- Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward, streamed vocab blocks): [`fused_cross_entropy_loss`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss)
- Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas): [`short_conv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/short_conv)
- Muon symmetric-GEMM Newton–Schulz (QuACK SM100, `use_syrk`): [`_newtonschulz_batched_syrk`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L182) → [`quack_symmetric_gemm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/quack_symmetric_cute.py)
- Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack, no matrix-dim gather): [3D padded stack](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L298), [4D expert-stack distribution](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L211), [intra-rack axis selection](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/grugmuon_hero.py#L32)

## 7. Outputs (pending — run in progress)
- **Checkpoints**: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/<run>/…/checkpoints` (permanent every 6000 steps for the hero; output-only).
- **W&B**: pending.
- **Final evals** (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`, `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb`, `eval/uncheatable_eval/macro_loss`): pending.
- **Throughput** (mean over last 100 steps): pending. Reference from the d2048 rung: compute-step ~24M tok/s (MFU p50 ~13.6%), sustained ~17M tok/s (the gap is bursty cross-rack all-reduce over DCN, not evals/logging).

comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

The earlier fixed-evaluation `a1` runs omitted each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. They are superseded by the corrected `a2` runs above. The separate evaluation-path problem is tracked in [#9352](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9352).

The isolated timing covers only the saved-input router dot and gradient. It is not a whole-step measurement.

**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

issues.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens

issues.author: ClassicLarry
issues.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids
B × 4096, packed documents"] --> emb["token embedding
16384 × 512"] emb --> en["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] en --> S0(["source 0
embedding"]) S0 --> L0 subgraph STACK["6 layers: local KDA ×4, global MLA ×2 (every 4th + last)"] direction TB L0["layer 0 · KDA + MoE"] --> L1["layer 1 · KDA + MoE"] --> L2["layer 2 · KDA + MoE"] L2 --> L3["layer 3 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] --> L4["layer 4 · KDA + MoE"] --> L5["layer 5 · MLA + Inkling + MoE"] end L0 -. "block sum b0" .-> H L1 -. "b1" .-> H L2 -. "b2" .-> H L3 -. "b3" .-> H L4 -. "b4" .-> H S0 -.-> H H[("AttnRes history, read by every gate
[embedding, b0 … b(i−1)]
+ running partial")] L5 --> FG["final AttnRes gate
softmax over embedding, b0…b4, partial"] FG --> fn["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] fn --> head["lm_head (untied) 512 × 16384
fused CE, vocab tile 8192, z-loss 1e-4"] head --> loss(["next-token loss"]) ``` **2. One layer.** The two sublayers each have an AttnRes gate. The MoE gate also sees the attention output written just before it, as the running partial. ```mermaid flowchart TB Hin[("history
embedding + b0…b(i−1)")] --> GA subgraph GATE["AttnRes gate (one per sublayer, 13 at d512)"] direction TB GA["logit_n = q · rms_norm(source_n)
q ∈ ℝ⁵¹², zero-init (uniform mix)
frozen key norm"] --> SM["softmax over sources
weighted sum of raw sources"] end SM --> A1["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] --> MIX{{"mixer
KDA (local) or MLA + Inkling (global)"}} MIX --> SCA["ShortConv (MLA layers only)"] --> PA(["partial = attn out"]) PA --> GM["AttnRes gate
history + partial"] Hin --> GM GM --> M1["RMSNorm → GatedNorm"] --> MOE{{"LatentMoE + 2 shared experts"}} MOE --> SCM["ShortConv"] --> PB(["block b_i = attn out + MoE out"]) PB --> Hout[("appended to history")] ``` **3a. Kimi Delta Attention, the local mixer (layers 0, 1, 2, 4 at d512; D = 512, 4 heads × 128).** ```mermaid flowchart TB kx["x"] --> kq["q = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_q))"] & kk["k = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_k))"] & kv["v = SiLU(ShortConv(x W_v))"] kx --> kg["decay g = −5 · σ(exp(A_log) · (x W_a↓ W_a↑ + dt_bias))
rank-128 gate, per channel; A_log per head"] kx --> kb["write strength β = σ(x W_β), per head"] kq & kk --> kn["L2-norm q, k; q × 1/√128"] kn & kv & kg & kb --> rec["delta rule, chunked Pallas kernels (chunk 16)
S_t = (I − β k kᵀ) Diag(e^g) S_{t−1} + β k vᵀ
o_t = S_tᵀ q_t · state resets at document starts"] rec --> kon["per-head RMSNorm (shared 128-wide scale)"] --> kog["× σ(x W_g), per channel"] --> ko["W_o → sublayer out
no RoPE, no window, no output ShortConv"] ``` **3b. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. comments.body:
Some ideas to get started. Treat this as a general pool of ideas, that indicates the spirit of what can be tried.
1. https://blog.tilderesearch.com/blog/online-kl-shampoo. Consider interactions with hyperball and selectively replace matrices.
2. Add a second embedding table with its own random init. Attn residuals queries both embedding tables, treating them as unique inputs.
3. Lets add value embeddings. That is, a second embedding table that gets added to V on the MLA layers. So take KV latent-> project to num_heads of size 128. Then do values = lambda1*values + lambda2*value_embeds[layer_i]. lambda 1 init to 1, lambda2 init to 0. value_embeds has [vocab_size, num_heads*head_dim, num_mla_layers] dimension. Can also try gated value embeds, where instead of lambda2, its conditional on residual stream via sigmoid(linear(x)).
4. Add learnable scalars to each submodule output, that feeds into attention residuals. May be worth tracking and plotting these in wandb, to see if indicates any architecture changes will help.
5. Try different variations of linear attention to replace KDA.
6. It has been shown in many places that the final couple layers of attention dont prefer to attend to outputs from the final MLPs. See if there is any change to attention residuals to help make this more natural.
7. Adding an lm_head auxillary loss to the output of layer 1 for the first X (say 500) steps can help give the routed experts a cleaner role early. Unclear how this interacts with attention residuals.
8. Hash routing on first layer.
9. Instead of Adam/AdamH on embed and lm_head, look into other optimizers here that have shown promise in literature.
10. Do any weights benefit from extremely different beta1/beta2/momentum terms, or swapping their optimizer group.
11. Update the router behavior (sigmoid vs softmax), normalizing over picked experts vs not, sampling over experts instead of top k).
12. Null routing (enable tokens to select null experts which skips their computation, dynamic compute per token).
13. Multi-token-prediction.
14. Sparse attention.

If users give comments with singular specific ideas, give it priority over this laundry list.

🤖 **Batch 1: cheap architecture adds from the idea list, an LR check, and a noise and profile baseline** (d512, 2475 steps) — **done**

**Goal.** Test the lowest-cost ideas from @ClassicLarry's list: `#2` (second embedding table), `#3` (value embeddings, both forms), and `#4` (learnable sublayer output scalars, logged to W&B). Also check whether the `MoeHeuristic` LR, which was fit on the old baseline architecture, is still right for KMA (×1.5 and ×0.67 on both LRs). Add a seed-1 baseline to calibrate noise, and a 60-step profile to find speed levers. Speed counts as a win under the fixed-time objective.

**Assumption (I'll correct it next batch if it's wrong).** None of these changes adds meaningful compute, so all runs use the baseline's 2475 steps instead of a separate probe. After each run I check its steady-state ex/s. If it is more than about 1% below 660, I rerun at `round(480 × ex/s / 128)` steps. Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch01`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/eb26f3cbc9) @ `eb26f3cbc9`: every change is gated by a `--model-set` / `--opt-set` flag and defaults to off.

**Implementation details**
- **ve:** each MLA layer gets a [16384 × N·128] table, and `v = λ1·v + λ2·VE[token]` (λ1 = 1, λ2 = 0 at init). The tables, λ and the gate go to Adam at the Adam LR, like `token_embed`.
- **veg:** `v = λ1·v + sigmoid(x·W)·VE[token]`, with one gate per head. `W` is zero-initialized, so the gate starts at 0.5.
- **osc:** a scalar initialized to 1 on each attention and MoE sublayer output before it enters the AttnRes history (Adam). Logged as `train/attn_res/scale_{attn,mlp}_L*`.
- **emb2:** a second randomly initialized table → learnable RMSNorm, prepended as an extra AttnRes block that every gate can read.

| baseline profile, 60 steps, no eval | [`eb26f3cbc9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/eb26f3cbc9) | [lc1-b01-prof](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b01-prof) | 60 | 686 | — | — | — |

**Takeaway.**
- **Noise is the story.** The identical-code seed-1 baseline landed at 3.1195, 0.0056 below seed 0. Against the two-seed baseline mean of 3.1223, none of the architecture changes clears noise: emb2 −0.005, veg −0.004, osc −0.002, ve −0.002. ve, veg and emb2 also ran 7–13% slower, so at a fair 8-minute step count they would lose part of that.
- **The LR heuristic holds for KMA.** Both ×1.5 and ×0.67 are clearly worse.
- **The learned scalars in osc point at the MoE output.** Its final values: MoE outputs grow to 1.2 / 1.4 / 1.5 / 2.1 / 1.7 / 1.9× by layer, the early KDA outputs shrink to 0.48×, and the MLA outputs stay near 1.0. The routed-expert output magnitude is capped by MuonH's sphere and the 2.5 combine renorm, and it wants to grow.
- **Profile (8×H100, d512, ~187 ms/step).** Compute is ~155 ms: elementwise fusions ~61, GEMMs ~43, sort/scatter/gather ~23, KDA ~14, FA4 ~7. Exposed EP all-to-all is ~18 ms, and the host gap between steps is ~6 ms.
  - **One kernel is a bug:** the token-embedding gradient takes **~11 ms/step**. Under the bf16 compute policy, the gather's transpose scatter-adds every token's cotangent directly into a **bf16** table. That means contended bf16 atomics, with frequent tokens' gradients rounded at every add. A single-GPU microbenchmark puts the fp32 scatter at 0.2 ms. The same scatter is why ve, veg and emb2 were slow: each extra table adds one.

**Next (batch 2).**
- Fix the embedding backward with an fp32 scatter-add plus a psum: [`ladderclimb_v1_batch02` @ `269387e86b`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/269387e86b). It is a pure speed and precision change, so it is a baseline candidate in its own right.
- Probe throughput with the fix, then rerun ve, veg and emb2 on it at fair step counts, with replicate seeds.
- Test MoE output-magnitude variants: combine renorm sum 2.5 → 4, sigmoid without renorm, softmax combine, and K3's normalized LatentMoE.
- In response to the literature-scan comment: a background scan turned up these candidates for later batches: K3 normalized LatentMoE, per-head Muon, NorMuon-style row normalization, Engram n-gram memory, null experts, and FP8 lm_head.
**Next batch (tentative):** act on the profile. Validate any win above 0.005 at d768. Try combinations of the winners, MTP, and router variants (`#11`).

**Goal.**
1. Make the **fp32 embedding backward** the new baseline candidate. The embedding gather's backward now scatter-adds in fp32 inside each shard and then psums, instead of scatter-adding bf16 cotangents into a bf16 table. On an 80-step probe that is **+9.9% ex/s** (754 vs 686), and it also makes the embedding gradient more precise. Replicated over 2 seeds, because noise is about 0.005.
2. Rerun **ve, veg and emb2** on the fix, where their extra tables are nearly free (probes: 750 / 744 / 735 ex/s).
3. Follow the batch-1 osc signal that the **MoE output wants to be larger**: combine renorm sum 4.0 instead of 2.5; sigmoid without renorm (`2.5·σ/(K/2)`, so the per-token total can vary); softmax combine (idea `#11`); and Kimi K3's normalized LatentMoE (a learnable RMSNorm before `W_latent_up`, from the literature scan @ClassicLarry asked for). osc is rerun on the new base.

**d768 validation (gate 1):** the d768 baseline (`fasttrack-moe-kma-d768`) ran 6929 steps at 288.9 ex/s, about 48 minutes of train-step time. An 80-step probe of the fix sets its steps at `6929 × probe ÷ 288.9`, and the full run follows.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 5: @ClassicLarry's three requests: z-loss weight, projection biases, and freezing QB at 50%** (d512, 2817 steps; reference = batch-3 base mean **3.0990**)

**Addresses** the comment asking to vary the logit z-loss, add biases to some weight matrices, and freeze QB updates halfway through training. All runs build on the fp32-embedding base, branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch05`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02).
- **z-loss:** the current weight is 1e-4 (`--z-loss-weight`). One run turns it off, one raises it 10×.
- **Biases:** zero-initialized and trained with Adam, at three sites:
  - Qwen-style q/k/v: KDA q/k/v before their ShortConvs, and MLA q plus the KV latent before its RMSNorm.
  - The attention sublayer output.
  - The MoE sublayer output.

  If the combined run moves, I'll split the sites next batch.
- **QB freeze:** from step 1408 on, the router bias keeps its last quantile-balanced value (`qb_freeze_step`). Routing can then drift, and load balance is no longer enforced.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| z-loss weight 1e-3 | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-z1e3](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-z1e3) | 2817 | 749 | 3.4029 | 3.1046 | +0.0056 |
| biases: q/k/v + attention out + MoE out | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-bias](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-bias) | 2817 | 742 (−1%) | 3.3913 | 3.0993 | +0.0003 |
| freeze QB router biases at step 1408 (50%) | [`ea0592bd02`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ea0592bd02) | [lc1-b05-qbfrz](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-qbfrz) | 2817 | 751 | 3.3924 | 3.1059 | +0.0069 |
| **AttnRes logit bias** per (gate, source), zero-init, Adam at 0.1× (human, 2nd comment) | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arb](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arb) | 2817 | 751 | 3.3954 | 3.1001 | +0.0011 |
| AttnRes logit bias + AttnRes z-loss 1e-3 | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arbz3](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arbz3) | 2817 | 748 | 3.3996 | 3.1045 | +0.0055 |
| AttnRes logit bias + AttnRes z-loss 1e-1 | [`f1734ddcdf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/f1734ddcdf) | [lc1-b05-arbz1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b05-arbz1) | 2817 | 746 | 3.4570 | 3.1475 | +0.0485 |

**AttnRes logit bias and z-loss** (added for the follow-up comment). Each of the 13 gates gets a zero-init bias per source it reads: one per completed block, plus one for the running partial. It is added to the logit before the softmax and trained with Adam at 0.1× the Adam LR, the same as the queries. The z-loss is the mean over tokens of logsumexp(gate logits)², averaged over gates, and added to the loss. Every run now logs the pseudo-query norms: `train/attn_res/query_norm_{mean,max,gNN}` plus the unweighted `train/attn_res/z`. One caveat: a z-loss can be satisfied by shifting a gate's biases down together, which leaves the mix unchanged. I'll compare the q norms across the three runs.

**Correction:** the AttnRes z-loss runs' eval losses also included the z-loss term (the same bug, found in batch 18). That inflated them by weight × z: about +0.0012 for 1e-3 and +0.001 for 1e-1. Their deltas are about +0.004 and +0.047 instead of +0.0055 and +0.0485, so both are still worse.

**Takeaway (all done).**
- **AttnRes logit bias is neutral (+0.0011).**
- **The AttnRes z-loss hurts:** +0.0055 at 1e-3 and +0.049 at 1e-1.
- **It raises the pseudo-query norms rather than lowering them.** Final values:

  | run | AttnRes z (unweighted) | query norm mean | query norm max |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | bias only | 6.31 | 0.227 | 0.377 |
  | bias + z 1e-3 | 1.23 | 0.286 | 0.583 |
  | bias + z 1e-1 | 0.01 | 0.332 | 0.565 |

  The z-loss is minimized by pushing every logit down. With keys that are RMS-normalized but not mean-centred, the query does this by growing along the direction opposite the common component of the sources, instead of shifting all biases together. That distorts the mix.
- The other results from this batch:
  - Freezing QB at 50%: +0.007.
  - lm_head z-loss 1e-3: +0.006.
  - lm_head z-loss 0: −0.002.
  - Projection biases: neutral.

comments.body: Try a simple version of looped models (w/ and wo/ growing, a la https://github.com/qlabs-eng/slowrun/pull/92 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) with untying and see if that improves performance. Make sure to include the input injection as well!

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 9: looped models (@neel04's request): tied looping, with and without growth, with input injection** (d512, paired seed 0 vs qk_mult-2.5 base **3.0858**)

**Addresses** @neel04's comment. It follows [slowrun#92](https://github.com/qlabs-eng/slowrun/pull/92) (1× for 70% of training, then 2×) and [arXiv 2609.19107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) (boundary operator `Norm(h) + α·e`, growth partway through training, backprop through all passes, and FLOPs of every pass counted). Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch09`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0).

**How it maps onto KMA** (`loop_passes`, `loop_grow_step`):
- **The looped core is the whole 6-layer stack**, weights tied. Each pass extends the Block AttnRes history. Pass 2's gates read the embedding, every pass-1 block, and the pass-2 blocks so far. Pass 2 has its own zero-initialized AttnRes pseudo-queries, so its gates start as uniform averages over that longer history.
- **Input injection.** At the start of each extra pass, the running partial is initialized to `α·e`, where e is the normalized embedding source and α is learned (init 1, Adam), and the pass's layers write onto it. The AttnRes gates already see e as source 0. This is the explicit re-injection from both references. The AttnRes softmax already normalizes what each sublayer reads, which plays the part of `Norm(h)`.
- **Growth** uses a step-gated `lax.cond`. Before the growth step only pass 1 executes, at full base speed. After it both passes run, with gradients through both. The router biases are shared per physical layer; their QB statistics are averaged over the passes.
- **Fixed-time steps.** Two passes run at 0.506× the base throughput (80-step probe: 381.8 vs 754.1 ex/s), so every run is given 8 minutes of train-step time:
  - loop2 throughout: 1426 steps.
  - Grow at 70%: N solves `0.7N/751 + 0.3N/380 = 480/128`, so N = 2179 and growth is at step 1525.
  - Grow at 50%: N = 1892, growth at step 946.
- **Not in this batch: untied growth**, where the core is copied at the growth step and the copies train separately. It changes the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run, so it needs trainer work. It's next if tied growth looks promising.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| loop ×2 throughout (tied, injection) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-loop2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-loop2) | 1426 | 381 | 3.5052 | 3.1766 | **+0.0908** |
| grow 1→2 passes at 70% of steps (step 1525) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-grow70](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow70) | 2179 | | | OOM: 79.8 GiB (lax.cond kept both branches' buffers); fixed, rerun below | |
| grow 1→2 passes at 50% (step 946) | [`c2803601b0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0) | [lc1-b09-grow50](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow50) | 1892 | | | OOM: 79.8 GiB (lax.cond kept both branches' buffers); fixed, rerun below | |
| grow 1→2 at 70% (step 1525), static per-phase programs | [`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9) | [lc1-b09-grow70b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow70b) | 2179 | 747 → 380 | 3.5435* | 3.1065 | +0.0207 |
| grow 1→2 at 50% (step 946), static per-phase programs | [`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9) | [lc1-b09-grow50b](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b09-grow50b) | 1892 | 747 → 380 | 3.5647* | 3.1195 | +0.0337 |

The mid-run eval always runs every pass, so for the growth runs the mid loss evaluates a model that has not trained its second pass yet. Only the final loss is comparable.

**Takeaway.**
- **Looping loses at d512 fixed time**, in every variant:

  | variant | Δ |
  |---|---|
  | 2× throughout | +0.091 |
  | grow 1→2 at 50% | +0.034 |
  | grow 1→2 at 70% | +0.021 |

  The less time spent in the 2× slower phase, the smaller the loss. The measured phase throughputs, 747 then 380 ex/s, match the budget, so all three got 8 minutes. \* marks mid losses from evals that ran both passes before the second pass had trained.
- **Why it loses.** The paper's gains are compute multipliers at ≥1e20 FLOPs with 7–8 tokens per parameter for its growth variants. Here the whole run is about 1e17 FLOPs and data-limited: in 8 minutes the model sees only about 1.1B tokens. An extra pass costs tokens, which are the scarce resource at this rung. Untied growth has the same FLOP cost after growth, so I'm not building it for d512. It is a better fit for a hero-scale study.

**Earlier notes.**
- **Fixed 2× looping throughout is much worse at fixed time: +0.091.** It gets only 1426 steps. At d512, one pass of the 6-layer stack is not the bottleneck; tokens seen are.
- **The growth runs first OOMed.** The step-gated `lax.cond` allocated 79.8 GiB, because XLA holds buffers for both branches. I replaced it with two statically compiled train steps, a one-pass program before the growth step and a two-pass one after, chosen per step in Python ([`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9)). Its CPU check matches the plain model exactly.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 10: slimming ablations (@ClassicLarry's request)** (d512, 2817 steps, paired seed 0 vs the qk_mult-2.5 base **3.0858**)

**Addresses** the comment asking to drop the GatedNorm on the embedding, drop the GatedNorm on the lm_head input, and make the KDA output gate per head instead of per channel. Each runs independently on top of qk_mult 2.5. All three remove compute, so running them at the base's 2817 steps slightly under-credits them, which is the conservative direction.
- `embed_gated_norm=false`: embedding → RMSNorm only.
- `final_gated_norm=false`: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → lm_head.
- `kda_gate_per_head=true`: `W_g` becomes [D, N] instead of [D, N·128], and `σ(x W_g)` is broadcast over each head's 128 channels. It stays on MuonH, like `W_β`.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no GatedNorm on the embedding | [`afa837be5f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/afa837be5f) | [lc1-b10-noembgn](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b10-noembgn) | 2817 | 748 | 3.3773 | 3.0863 | +0.0005 |
| no GatedNorm before the lm_head | [`afa837be5f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/afa837be5f) | [lc1-b10-nofingn](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b10-nofingn) | 2817 | 749 | 3.3822 | 3.0864 | +0.0006 |
| KDA output gate per head (not per channel) | [`afa837be5f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/afa837be5f) | [lc1-b10-kdagh](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b10-kdagh) | 2817 | 705 (−6%, see below) | 3.3877 | 3.0912 | **+0.0054** |
| both GatedNorms removed (embedding + lm_head input) | [`0d023baad9`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0d023baad9) | [lc1-b10-nogn2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b10-nogn2) | 2817 | 752 | 3.3803 | **3.0821** | **−0.0037** |

**Takeaway.**
- **Both GatedNorm removals are neutral** (+0.0005 embedding, +0.0006 lm_head input), so they are free simplifications. **Removing both gives 3.0821 (−0.0037)**, so they stack. The model is simpler and, if anything, better. The batch-12 bundle drops both.
- **The per-head KDA output gate is worse: +0.0054 at the same 2817 steps.** The per-channel gate carries information. It also ran 6% slower, because my `jnp.repeat` broadcast of the gate didn't fuse; a reshape to `[B, S, N, 128]` would avoid that. The step count was the same as the base, so the loss comparison is fair either way. Not pursuing it.
