comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 96: read vs write asymmetry of the routed MLPs** (d512 candidate 8, equal steps, paired vs 2.9792 / 2.9861)

Agreed that the latent-selection line is low impact at ~2% of FLOPs, so it closes after this test unless something stands out.

**Write-side selection** (`latent_write_select`, commit `3945345556`):
- The routed input keeps candidate 8's learned down-projection.
- `w_latent_up` is removed: the combined 256-wide routed output is written into hidden channels [0, 256), and the other 256 channels get zero from the routed experts.
- The output is scaled by `initializer_std · √256` = 0.32, the gain of the matrix it replaces. MuonH holds `w_latent_up`'s Frobenius norm at its init value, so without this the routed branch would be ≈ 3× louder for the whole run, and the test would conflate *where* the experts write with *how loud* they are.
- The shared expert and attention still write the full width.

**Read side, from batch 95** (already done): first-half read selection is −0.0016 / −0.0017.

**The 2×2:**
- read projection, write projection: candidate 8;
- read selection, write projection: batch 95, −0.0016;
- read projection, write selection: this batch;
- read selection, write selection: this batch. The routed experts then see and write only channels [0, 256).

**Prediction:** write selection costs more than read selection (Δ > +0.003). My reasoning: reads can be recovered, because upstream writers (attention, the shared expert, the AttnRes gates) are free to place what the experts need in the first half. With write selection, each token's routed output is confined to a fixed half of the stream for every downstream reader. If write selection is also ≈ 0, the stream simply has spare capacity at d512, and the half-width constraint doesn't bind on either side.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| routed output written into the first 256 channels (no `w_latent_up`) | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-wsel](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-wsel) | 2817 | 694 | 3.2023 | 2.9868 | +0.0076 vs 2.9792 |
| same, seed 1 | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-wsel-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-wsel-s1) | 2817 | 692 | 3.2091 | 2.9941 | +0.0080 vs 2.9861 |
| read and write selection (routed experts see and write only channels [0, 256)) | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-rwsel](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-rwsel) | 2817 | 702 | 3.1999 | 2.9881 | +0.0089 vs 2.9792 |
| same, seed 1 | [`3945345556`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3945345556) | [lc1-b96-rwsel-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b96-rwsel-s1) | 2817 | 701 | 3.2058 | 2.9923 | +0.0062 vs 2.9861 |

**Result: a clear read/write asymmetry.** Restricting where the routed experts *write* costs +0.008; restricting what they *read* costs nothing.

| routed experts read ↓ / write → | full stream via `w_latent_up` | first 256 channels only |
|---|---|---|
| **learned projection** | candidate 8 (0) | **+0.0076 / +0.0080** (mean +0.0078) |
| **first 256 channels** | −0.0016 / −0.0017 (batch 95) | **+0.0089 / +0.0062** (mean +0.0076) |

- The prediction (write selection > +0.003) holds. The effect is ≈ 9× the read-side one, and it is the same sign on all four runs.
- **Read + write selection ≈ write selection alone.** Once the output is confined, confining the input costs nothing more. So the half-width read constraint does not bind at d512 on either path.
- Reading this as you suggested: the routed MLP's write side is worth more capacity than its read side. That argues for sizing `latent_in` and `latent_out` independently rather than one shared latent, e.g. a narrow read with a full-width write.
- Since comms at hero scale make a wider latent look artificially good here, **the next test is the asymmetric pair at equal FLOPs and equal comms volume**: read 256 / write 512 vs read 512 / write 256. Dispatch sends the read width and combine returns the write width, so both move the same total bytes. That isolates the asymmetry from the "bigger latent always wins here" effect. The `latent_out_dim` implementation is in progress.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 97: where ragged's training slowdown comes from** (candidate 8, d512, profiles of steps 1500–1504 plus full-run step-time series)

Three runs: pooled-wave (8 processes, current), **pooled-wave forced to `--single-process`** (the control), and ragged one-shot at capacity 1.05 (which needs single-process).

| run | median step | mean step | GPU kernel busy (profile) |
|---|---|---|---|
| pooled-wave, 8 processes | 186.4 ms | 188.6 ms | 168.8 ms |
| pooled-wave, 1 process | 189.4 ms | **204.1 ms** | 169.3 ms |
| ragged one-shot, 1 process | 194.3 ms | 203.7 ms | 174.9 ms |

**Roughly two thirds of ragged's slowdown comes from the single-process driver, not from ragged.**
- In single-process mode, the post-step host work comes in multi-second bursts: 5–7 consecutive steps of 0.5–5.5 s every ~95–115 s of wall time, plus one early burst at steps 156–163 in both runs. That is ≈ 25 s over the run, ≈ 9–13 ms per step on the mean. The multi-process run has no such bursts.
- Not the data loader (`loading_time` ≈ 0 on every step, including the bursts) and not GC (the synchronized collections take 50–60 ms). The profile window missed a burst, so the cause isn't identified yet.
- Median steps differ by only +3 ms (1 process vs 8).

**The rest is ragged's own GPU time: +5.6 ms per step (+3.3%).**

| kernel family | pooled (1 process) | ragged | Δ ms/step |
|---|---|---|---|
| EP transport: NCCL SendRecv → symmetric-memory ragged all-to-all + multi-GPU barrier | 25.9 | 19.2 + 6.0 | −0.7 |
| expert GEMMs: cuBLAS batched (nvjet/gemm fusions) → fused Pallas ReLU² ragged kernels | ≈ 13 | 19.5 | ≈ +6.5 |
| pad / broadcast / memcpy / gather-bwd / add fusions (ragged layout bookkeeping) | ≈ 4 | ≈ 21 | ≈ +17 |
| capacity select fusions (pooled only) | 7.4 | 1.4 | −6.0 |

(Rows are the largest per-kernel differences, grouped; other fusions net out to about −11 ms.)

**Next:**
1. Profile a burst: both single-process runs burst at steps ~156–163, so steps 155–159 are being profiled with the Python host tracer to name the function (`lc1-b97-prof155-*`).
2. HLO dumps for both transports, to trace the pad/broadcast fusions back to source. These are likely zero-filled receive buffers and padding to the kernel's block size, which a kernel that writes only valid rows could skip.
3. The fused ragged expert kernel is ≈ 1.5× the cuBLAS batched GEMMs pooled-wave uses; block-size and layout tuning at the training shape is the other lever.

🤖 **Two findings: the routed-expert read/write asymmetry is large, and the single-process stall is metric logging**

**1. Asymmetric latent at equal FLOPs** (`latent_out_dim`, d512 candidate 8, equal steps, 2 seeds)

| routed experts read / write | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | ex/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 / 256 (candidate 8) | 0 | 0 | 680 / 678 |
| **256 / 512** (`w_down` writes the stream directly, no `w_latent_up`) | **−0.0185 / −0.0215** | **−0.0200** | 602 / 608 (−11%) |
| 512 / 256 (experts read the stream directly, no `w_latent_down`) | +0.0016 / +0.0003 | +0.0010 | 618 / 620 (−9%) |
| (ref: batch 96) 256 / write confined to channels [0, 256) | +0.0076 / +0.0080 | +0.0078 | |

- **Expert FLOPs are identical in the two arms**: 8 × (256·384 + 384·512) MACs per token. Each also has one 512 × 256 projection. Widening the write gives −0.020; widening the read gives nothing (+0.001). This matches batch 96's sign and makes it ≈ 20× larger than the read-side effect.
- Both arms use nearly all available channels: the expert-weight participation ratio is 254 / 497 for 256 / 512 and 485 / 254 for 512 / 256. So the experts don't leave the extra read width idle; it just isn't worth anything.
- **Cost:** both are ≈ 9–11% slower here. 256 / 512 returns 512-wide rows through the combine all-to-all (2× the combine bytes). As you noted, that comms cost is understated at d512 and larger at hero scale. At d512 fixed time, −11% ≈ +0.019, so it's break-even here and not a d512 win.
- **The takeaway for hero-scale latent design:** don't size `latent_in` and `latent_out` together. If extra latent width is affordable, it belongs on the write/combine side; the dispatch side can stay narrow at little cost.

**2. What the single-process host stalls are** (batch 97 follow-up)

I added a stack sampler (`host_stall.py`) that records every thread's Python stack while post-step host work runs longer than 0.3 s. In every sampled stall, the **main thread is inside W&B's metric conversion**:
```
log(tracker.py) → _prepare_log(wandb.py) → _convert_metrics_to_wandb_loggable → _item → __array__ → Array._value
```
It pulls each logged device scalar to host one at a time: hundreds of per-layer router / knob / AttnRes metrics, each a separate synchronizing device-to-host copy. With one process driving 8 GPUs, each copy is slower. At the same time, the finelog `write_rows` and finestore directory-sync threads compete for the interpreter lock. The ≈ 0.1 s every 10 steps seen in the 8-process runs is the same thing at a smaller scale.

**Fix** (`627272833d`): the loop now copies the logged metric dicts to host in **one batched `jax.device_get`** before handing them to the tracker. Same metrics, no math change. Being measured now on pooled-wave (8-process and 1-process) and ragged. Expected:
- the 8-process run gets ≈ 1% faster;
- most of the single-process mean-vs-median gap (≈ 13 ms per step) goes away;
- ragged's remaining gap becomes just its own GPU time (+5.6 ms, +3%), which the kernel work can then target.

**Correction (measured): the batched `device_get` did not remove the stalls.**

| run | median step before → after | mean step before → after |
|---|---|---|
| pooled-wave, 8 processes | 186.7 → 184.8 ms | 189.0 → 197.9 ms |
| pooled-wave, 1 process | 189.5 → 191.4 ms | 204.6 → 204.3 ms |

- The sampler shows why my diagnosis was wrong. During a 0.5 s stall it collected **only one sample** where it should have collected ~25, and the main thread's frame is different each time (any JAX call that touches a device).
- So the **whole process is frozen**, not just busy in logging: either a thread holds the interpreter lock through a long C call, or the container is being CPU-throttled. The W&B frames were simply where the main thread happened to be.
- Next run (`lc1-b97-thr-*`, commit `f70e3dedad`) logs the cgroup's `nr_throttled` / `throttled_usec` delta with every stall, to tell those two apart.
- The batched fetch stays in: same metrics, fewer syncs.

First-half latent selection at d768: 2.7199 / 2.7138 (−0.0008), neutral again. That's consistent with d512, so projection vs selection is settled at two scales.

**Closed in this round** (2 seeds each unless noted):

| idea | mean Δ |
|---|---|
| FoX forget gate (bias 4; bias 0 NaNs) | +0.0008; the gate learns f ≈ 0.999 (turns forgetting off), and it is 43% slower from head-dim padding |
| Magma (with MuonH LR ×3 to offset its ≈0.3× average step) | +0.0097 (uncompensated: +0.098) |
| MuonSphere, MuonH LR ×1 / ×0.5 / ×0.25 | +0.027 / +0.013 / +0.060 |
| momentum warmup, cautious WD, slower early upper-layer q/k LR (25% / 4% of training) | +0.0012, +0.0007, 0.0000 / −0.0010 |
| expert init ×0.5 / ×2 | +0.0028 / +0.0015 |
| unigram lm_head bias | +0.0025 |
| token-conditioned router bias; router soft-cap 5 / 10; AttnRes logit soft-cap 5 / 10 | +0.0004; +0.0016 / +0.0002; −0.0012 / −0.0007 |

**Single-process stalls: the root cause is the data loader, not logging or CPU throttling.**
- Throttling: the stall sampler now logs the cgroup's `nr_throttled`, and it is 0 in every stall.
- Summed over all stalls, the busy background threads are the loader's prefetch threads (`_fill_queue_with_batches`): `batched_device_put` (≈ 5.3k samples), `np.stack` (≈ 600) and `backend_compile_and_load` (≈ 390, the loader compiling mid-run). Meanwhile the main thread sits in device↔host copies, and the sampler thread itself gets ≈ 1 sample per 0.5 s. The whole process is starved of the interpreter lock.
- Why: levanter's `CausalLmDataset` / `PrebuiltLmDataset` build **every example with its own `eqx.filter_jit` call** on the CPU backend (128 dispatches per batch, recompiling on new shapes), and prefetch 512 batches ahead in bursts. With 8 processes each builds 1/8 of the batch under its own interpreter lock. With one process driving 8 GPUs, all of it contends with the step dispatch.
- Stalls grow from ≈ 0.4 s early in the run to 3–5 s late.
- **Proposed fix** (not done yet): a batch-level NumPy path in those datasets. It would build a whole batch of examples on host in one vectorized pass instead of 128 jitted calls, with a smaller prefetch buffer. This is a shared-pipeline change, so it would sit behind an explicit option and be checked bit-exact against the current path. With it, ragged's gap should shrink to its own +3% of GPU time (layout pad/zero-fill kernels plus the fused expert kernel at ≈ 1.5× cuBLAS). That would make the −0.0035 dropless gain roughly break-even, and a net win once those kernels are fixed.

🤖 **Batch 103 results: the read side has a sharp knee at 256, and the shared expert partly covers the read side (but not the write side)**

**Halving the read latent** (candidate 8, write held at 256 via `w_latent_up`; Δ vs candidate 8, same seed):

| read latent | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | ex/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| 512 (batch 101) | +0.0016 / +0.0003 | +0.0010 | 618 / 620 |
| **256 (candidate 8)** | 0 | 0 | 680 / 678 |
| 128 | +0.0198 / +0.0185 | **+0.019** | 600 / 683 |
| 64 | +0.0480 / running | +0.048 | 736 |
| 32 (compiled fine) | +0.0804 / +0.0794 | **+0.080** | 719 / 746 |

- **My prediction (flat down to 128) was wrong.** The read is a knee exactly at 256 (d/2): above it nothing is gained, below it each halving costs more (+0.019, then +0.029, then +0.032).
- The narrow reads are 6–10% faster, worth ≤ 0.014 at the fixed-time rate. That is far from paying for +0.048.
- So "reads don't matter" is wrong. The read *saturates* at d/2, while the write keeps paying up to d.

**The same grid with no shared expert** (paired vs a no-shared baseline, same seed):

| arm | Δ with shared expert | Δ without shared expert |
|---|---|---|
| remove the shared expert (candidate 8 → no-shared base 2.9899 / 2.9982) | | **+0.011** |
| read 512 / write 256 | +0.0010 | **−0.0083 / −0.0067 (−0.0075)** |
| read 256 / write 512 | −0.0200 | **−0.0197 / −0.0228 (−0.0213)** |
| read 128 / write 256 | +0.019 | +0.0190 / running |
| read 64 / write 256 | +0.048 | +0.0536 / +0.0527 (+0.053) |

- **Your suspicion was partly right.** With the shared expert present, a wider routed read buys nothing (+0.001). Without it, the routed experts do gain from reading the full stream (−0.0075). So the shared expert's full-width read covers most of what a wider routed read would add.
- **The write asymmetry does not depend on the shared expert:** −0.020 with it, −0.021 without. Even with no shared expert, write-side width is worth ≈ 2.8× read-side width.
- **The knee below 256 is the same with or without the shared expert** (+0.019 at 128, ≈ +0.05 at 64). The shared expert doesn't let the routed read go narrower.
- **For latent design:** read at d/2 is the floor, not a free parameter. Extra width is worth far more on the write side (−0.02 per doubling from d/2 to d) than on the read side (≈ 0 with a shared expert, −0.0075 without). As before, the comms cost of a wider combine is understated at d512, so this is a direction for the hero latent rather than a d512 recipe change.

An interesting wrinkle here is that swiglu moves 2x the params to the read side instead of write, so it could make a light read + heavier write more favorable.

Dropping shared expert brings back some sanity to the results- neurons still need to cover the full rank of the input space, its just that shared neurons were covering the other half. This seems useful knowledge though because perhaps we could hardcode each expert to only read a subset of the input space, getting full coverage through the union but each individually being cheap. Though it wouldn't give guarantees that top K get coverage.

🤖 **Batch 104: each expert reads a fixed slice of the stream; the union covers it** (per your comment; d512, equal steps, 2 seeds)

**On SwiGLU:** agreed. With a gate, the read side is 2 of the 3 matrices, so a light read plus a heavy write should favor gated experts even more than it does our ungated ReLU² (1 read matrix, 1 write matrix). That's worth remembering for the hero config, which is gated.

**What's new** (`expert_read_subset`, `13ab05cc3c`):
- There is no latent down-projection (`latent_dim=none`). The experts read the normed 512-wide stream directly, but expert *e* reads only a fixed slice of it: its `w_up` input rows outside the slice are masked to zero at init and in the forward. They get exactly zero gradient, and MuonH keeps zero rows zero.
- `blocks`: expert *e* reads block *e mod k*, so each block is read by 512 / k experts. `random`: a fixed random subset per expert.
- The write side is candidate 8's (256 latent → `w_latent_up`).
- Every expert's FLOPs match a projected read of the same width, but there is no shared projection: the union of the slices covers the full 512 channels. In a real implementation the dispatch sends each assignment only its slice. That is the MFU angle: dispatch bytes = slice width.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 104 results: per-expert input slices lose badly. The routed experts need one *shared* read subspace, not a union of private ones.**

Δ is paired, same seed: with shared expert vs candidate 8, without it vs the no-shared baseline. All seeds agree to ±0.003.

| each expert reads | a learned projection (batch 103) | fixed slices of the stream, with shared expert | same, no shared expert |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 (2 blocks) | 0 (candidate 8) | **+0.0342 / +0.0364 (+0.035)** | +0.0224 / +0.0277 (+0.025) |
| 128 (4 blocks) | +0.019 | +0.0756 / +0.0744 (+0.075) | +0.0601 / +0.0614 (+0.061) |
| 128 (random subsets) | — | +0.0783 / +0.0778 (+0.078) | +0.0637 / +0.0646 (+0.064) |
| 64 (8 blocks) | +0.048 | +0.1178 / +0.1178 (+0.118) | +0.1027 / +0.1047 (+0.104) |

- **Coverage is not the problem.** With 2 blocks, a token's top-8 experts almost always include both halves, so the union covers the full stream. It still costs +0.035 against a single shared 256-dim projection, and +0.034 against reading the full 512 (batch 101). Blocks vs random subsets make no difference.
- **What does work, from batches 95, 101 and 103:** *all* experts reading the *same* 256-dim subspace. A learned projection, a fixed first-half selection and the full stream are all equivalent (±0.002). A *different* subspace per layer (batch 95: random / rotating per layer, +0.003 to +0.004) or per expert (here, +0.035) is worse, and the more ways the read is split, the larger the cost.
- **My reading:** the stream can place what the routed MLP needs into one shared subspace, and the router then picks *which* experts use it. When each expert reads its own slice, every slice must carry a copy of the useful information, which spends stream capacity. Removing the shared expert lowers the cost a little (+0.025 vs +0.035), consistent with the shared expert's full-width read also wanting that capacity.
- The masked-slice runs compute the full 512-wide read, so they are ≈ 8–10% slower here. A real slice-dispatch implementation would be cheap, but the loss cost rules it out regardless.
- **Closed:** per-expert read subsets. **The rule the read side has followed so far:** one shared read space of ≥ d/2, with the capacity going to the write side.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **KITE ([arXiv 2609.27294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27294), StepFun, Sep 2026): read it. My take is that it doesn't fit the d512 objective; details below in case you still want it run.**

**What it is:** a *mid-training depth expansion*.
- A trained model (33.8B-A1.1B MoE, 512 experts, top-8) is copied into two towers of equal depth. The **Prefiller** (the original) computes K/V at every layer. The **Decoder** (a copy, run after it) has its own queries but no K/V projections: decoder layer *l* attends to prefiller layer *l*'s K/V.
- Decoder input is `RMS(e_t) + RMS(h^P_L,t)`. The embedding and head are shared, and gradients flow back through the reused KV.
- "KV-invariant": the model gains depth, but prefill cost and the KV-cache size stay those of the small model.

**Results:**
- One seed, ≈ 5e21 FLOPs, grown after 168B tokens then trained 222B more.
- Training loss at equal FLOPs vs a same-cost deeper dense-depth baseline: −0.011 (vs 47B) and −0.002 (vs 63B, about noise).
- The headline win is an *analytical* inference-cost saving at a fixed prefill/KV budget (6.7–31.6%).
- There are no ablations: no from-scratch variant, no growth-time sweep, no loss at the growth point.

**Mapping here:**
- **Closest thing already tested:** batch 9's looped / grown models. That's the *tied* version of the same move: run the 6-layer stack a second time from 70% of training. Result: +0.021 at best, and the doubled stack runs at 0.51× throughput.
- **KITE's other piece**, reusing K/V across layers, is close to batch 15's `mla_share_kv_latent` (+0.0056).
- **Porting it** would mean duplicating all 6 layers including the 512-expert MoE (2× parameters and EP all-to-all), a decoder KDA that reruns the recurrence with its own queries, and swapping the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run. That's ≈ 400–550 LOC, medium-high risk. The d1024 two-tower version may not fit 8×H100.
- **Step time after growth ≈ 1.9×.** Our objective is training loss at fixed time; KV-cache invariance doesn't enter it.

**Recommendation:** skip at d512. The paper's gain is inference cost at fixed KV, which the d512 loss objective doesn't measure; its training-loss edge over a same-cost deeper model is ≈ 0; and both of its pieces have already lost here (tied growth +0.021, KV reuse +0.006).

**If you want it tested anyway:** untied KITE growth at 70% and 85% of an 8-minute fixed-time run, 2 seeds each, vs candidate 9. My expectation is +0.01 to +0.03. It is also a mid-run growth, so it needs your ruling under the schedule rules.

comments.body:
🤖 **KV side stream: being implemented** (per your comment). The concrete version I'm building for the signs-of-life test:

- **Side stream:** each token gets its own embedding of width *w* = d/n (arms: *w* = 128 = d/4 and *w* = 256 = d/2). It runs its own residual stream with one side block per main layer: plain causal softmax attention within the side stream (document-masked like the main model) plus a dense ReLU² MLP of width 4*w*.
- **KV comes only from the side stream:**
  - KDA layers compute k and v (and their short convs) from `RMSNorm(s_l)`. Their main-stream `w_k` / `w_v` are removed.
  - MLA layers compute the KV latent from `RMSNorm(s_l)`. Their main-stream `w_dkv` is removed. `kv_latent_norm`, `w_uk`, `w_uv` and the key norm / offset stay as they are.
- **The main stream keeps queries, the KDA gates (g, β, erase / write) and everything downstream,** so "who comes next" gates and queries, while "what am I" supplies the keys and values.
- **Test:** 2 seeds per width vs candidate 9 at equal steps, reporting step-time cost separately, since the side attention adds work. The goal is signs of life, so I'll report the equal-step Δ even if fixed time is worse.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 108: KV side stream, signs-of-life runs** (d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; `5e22e5aaa7`)

As built (details in the design comment above):
- **Side stream:** width *w*, its own token embedding, and one side block per layer (causal softmax attention with head_dim 128 on the FA4 path, per-head QK norm, RoPE, document masking; ReLU² MLP of width 4*w*). It is computed once before the main layers.
- **Main layers:** layer *l* reads a learned RMSNorm of the side state leaving side block *l*. KDA `w_k` / `w_v` and MLA `w_dkv` now read only the side stream; the main stream produces no K/V.
- **CPU checks:** flag off is bit-identical; flag on passes causality and document isolation through both streams; SAVE and RECOMPUTE backward agree.
- **Cost:**
  - *w* = 128: +1.3M params, −0.8M active (the KDA / MLA K/V inputs shrink from 512 to 128); ≈ +5% FLOPs.
  - *w* = 256: +7.6M params; ≈ +21% FLOPs.
  - The side stream runs serially before the main layers, so expect roughly +7% / +15% step time at d512. **Judged at equal steps first** (signs of life); step time is reported separately.

| change | branch@commit | W&B | steps | ex/s | mid loss | final Paloma macro loss | Δ (paired) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| candidate 9 + KV side stream, w = 128 (1 head) | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs128](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs128) | 2817 | 630 | 3.2784 | 3.0538 | +0.0788 vs 2.9750 |
| same, seed 1 | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs128-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs128-s1) | 2817 | 646 | 3.2755 | 3.0540 | +0.0749 vs 2.9791 |
| candidate 9 + KV side stream, w = 256 (2 heads) | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs256](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs256) | 2817 | 619 | 3.2603 | 3.0399 | +0.0649 vs 2.9750 |
| same, seed 1 | [`5e22e5aaa7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5e22e5aaa7) | [lc1-b108-kvs256-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b108-kvs256-s1) | 2817 | 610 | 3.2662 | 3.0444 | +0.0653 vs 2.9791 |

**Results: no signs of life. Sourcing K/V only from a side stream costs ≈ 0.07 at equal steps.**

| side width | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | median step |
|---|---|---|---|
| *w* = 128 (1 head) | +0.0788 / +0.0749 | **+0.077** | 203 / 198 ms (+8%) |
| *w* = 256 (2 heads) | +0.0649 / +0.0653 | **+0.065** | 207 / 210 ms (+12%) |

- **The side stream is numerically healthy** (per-layer RMS 0.95–1.39, rising with depth), so this is not a numerics failure.
- **My reading: it is a transport bottleneck.** Attention is the only way information moves between positions. With K/V taken only from the side stream, a later position can retrieve only what the *side stream* computed at earlier positions: its embedding plus 1–2 small attention heads and a narrow MLP. Everything the main stream builds at earlier positions (MoE outputs, multi-layer context) never becomes retrievable. The main stream can only query and gate.
  - Doubling *w* recovers only 0.012 of the 0.077, so width isn't the limit; the cut is structural.
  - The KDA layers are hit hardest: their recurrent state *is* the K/V sum, so the whole local-mixing memory becomes side-stream-only.
- **A "some sharing" variant that keeps the idea without the bottleneck,** if you want to pursue it: K from the side stream (identity, "what am I"), V from the main stream (content, "what I carry"). Or K = main + side, so the side stream adds a clean identity signal to keys rather than replacing them. Both keep full-rank content transport, so they test whether a *separate identity source for keys* helps. I'd expect at most a small effect; it's cheap to try if you want it.

**Gather-based per-expert slices** (the fair version of batch 104):

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 110: expert specialization study, phase 1 (top-1 of 8, characterization)** (tooling at `f676087c74`)

**Tooling:**
- `--routing-dump-steps 0,250,1000,2817` runs a forward-only pass over 8 fixed held-out batches (round-robin from every validation set, including Paloma) and writes `routing_step{N}.npz` with per-layer counts `[layer, token, expert]`, by current token, by previous token (within a document), and combine-weighted.
- `analyze_routing.py` reports:
  - per layer: I(token; expert), its noise floor, load, and per-token routing entropy;
  - per expert: top tokens by lift, decoded, and a token-class breakdown;
  - across seeds: Hungarian-matched similarity;
  - over time: evolution across steps.
- Seeding flags are also in: `router_embed_tie=L:E:V` (router column = α · `token_embed[V]`, the same parameter, from step 1) and `router_bias_seed=L:E:V:b`.

**A trap at top-1:** every *renormalized* combine (sigmoid-renorm, softmax-renorm, candidate 9's sqrt-softplus) turns the single combine weight into the constant `routing_renorm_sum`. The router would then get **zero** gradient from the LM loss, and only the QB bias would move routing. So the study model uses `router_combine=sigmoid_raw`, which matches at init and keeps the router trainable.

**Runs:** candidate 9 with top-1 of 8 routed experts, each 3072 wide (same active routed compute), `sigmoid_raw` combine, 2 seeds:
- [lc1-b110-t1e8-r](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b110-t1e8-r)
- [lc1-b110-t1e8-r-s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b110-t1e8-r-s1)

(The first attempt crashed at the step-0 dump: the held-out sequences came through the dataset's per-example CPU jit while the GPU context mesh was active. They are now fetched on a worker thread, where the mesh context doesn't apply (`5db0fdf63a`), and the runs are relaunched as `-r`.)

Next: the characterization report (what each expert takes, whether seeds agree, when it emerges), then scale-up to top-1 of 32, and the seeding runs (ties chosen from what the experts turn out to specialize in, plus an arbitrary-token control).

2. **It spreads to the token's *embedding* neighborhood, not to a hand-defined class:**
   - `1` → expert 3 becomes the digit expert (all digits 0.94–0.95 at L0, above the baseline's natural digit expert at 0.30–0.43). In layer 5 it becomes a **number-word** expert: ` six`, ` eight`, ` twenty`, ` hundred`, `-five`. That's semantic spread beyond digits.
   - `\n` → expert 3 takes **every newline-containing token** (class 1.00 at L0, 0.96–1.00 through the layers on seed 0): `"\n`, `}.\n`, `;\n\n`, ` }\n`, … A whitespace / structure expert.
   - `mathbf` → expert 3 takes `mathbf` itself (1.00 at L0) but **none of the LaTeX class** (0.01). It becomes a generic plural-noun expert instead (` millions`, ` indicators`, ` companies`). `mathbf`'s embedding evidently doesn't sit in a LaTeX cluster.
   - ` table` → a broad common-noun expert (` relationships`, ` matrix`, ` schedule`, ` layers`).
   - So the specialization that forms is whatever lies near the tied direction in embedding space. Digits and newline tokens are tight embedding clusters, so they spread cleanly.
3. **It locks in immediately:** at step 250, P(3 | token) is already 1.00 and P(3 | class) is 0.97 for digits and 1.00 for newlines.
4. **A hard +4 logit bias on the token is a weak seed:** P(3 | `1`) is only 0.25 / 0.76 at L0 and falls over training (0.40 at step 1000 on seed 0), and it doesn't spread to the class. QB balancing and the learned router override a fixed per-token bias. The tie works because it moves the whole router direction.
5. **Loss:** the ties cost loss vs the untied baseline: digits +0.0285 / +0.0222, newline −0.0013 / +0.0218, LaTeX +0.0050 / +0.0106, table +0.0100 / +0.0131. The bias prior is neutral (−0.0012 / −0.0003). Forcing one expert in *every* layer onto a fixed direction is a real constraint. Deeper layers want a different partition, and the fading at L5 is the model working around the tie. The learned tie scale α grew from its matched init to ≈ 3.5–9.4, so the router leans *harder* on the tied direction over training.

**Follow-ons, as you suggested:**
- **tie only in layer 0** (where it's clean), not in every layer: does the class specialization persist without the deep-layer cost?
- **tie to a class centroid** (mean embedding of all digit tokens, or all LaTeX tokens) to seed a class whose members aren't embedding neighbors;
- **tie then release** after 250 steps: does the seeded partition persist on its own?
- **several ties at once** (digits, newline, a script like Cyrillic) to seed a larger part of the partition;
- the **scale-up** of the characterization to top-1 of 32 and top-2 of 64.

| rung | non-table params | routed-expert params | bigram rows used so far | table params | table / non-table |

Two ways to make it a function of the model:

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 115: why candidate 9 OOMs at d1024 — the bigram table is all-gathered and all-reduced at full size every step**

**The failure:** all three d1024 runs died on the same `cuMemAllocAsync` of **48.04 GiB** inside `jit_train_step`: at step 435 (remat, 0.75), at step 7 (remat + 0.9), and at step 4348 (no remat + 0.9, a coordination shutdown after another rank failed). That is XLA's single temp buffer for the whole train step, not one tensor. It sits on top of ≈ 21.5 GiB of resident params, optimizer state and EMA copy (21.5 + 48 = the 69.5 GiB peak W&B reported), and the remat + 0.9 runs failed below the 71 GiB limit because the allocator couldn't find one contiguous 48 GiB block.

**Attribution probes** (candidate 9 at d1024, attention remat, 0.9 fraction, 20 steps, no eval / EMA; memory in GiB):

| probe | in use | peak | Δ peak |
|---|---|---|---|
| A, unchanged | 17.9 | 65.0 | — |
| B, no value embeds | 17.9 | 65.1 | +0.1 |
| **C, no bigram table** | **13.9** | **55.2** | **−9.8** |
| D, shared expert 1024 | 17.8 | 64.6 | −0.4 |
| F, 256 experts | 12.2 | 59.2 | −5.8 (all resident expert state) |

The bigram table is the outlier.
- Its ≈ 4 GiB resident share is expected: 2M × 1024 in fp32 plus two Adam moments, row-sharded over 8 GPUs.
- It also adds **≈ 6 GiB of temporaries**. With `embed2_fsdp=true` the model does `reshard(token_embed2, P(None, None))`, so every step:
  - the forward **all-gathers the whole table** (≈ 4.3 GB bf16 at d1024);
  - `_embedding_gather`'s backward builds a **dense full-size fp32 gradient** (8.6 GB) on every GPU and **all-reduces** it, although each GPU keeps only its 1/8 of the rows.
- That is also ≈ 8.6 GB of all-reduce traffic per step. At d512 it is ≈ 1 GB per step, which is likely a good part of the table's known step-time cost.

**Fix being implemented:** a row-sharded lookup that moves ids and activations instead of the table.
- Forward: all-gather the batch's hashed ids (a few MB); each GPU looks up only rows it owns; a reduce-scatter hands each GPU its own tokens' embeddings.
- Backward: all-gather the per-token cotangents; each GPU scatter-adds into its own shard only, with **no all-reduce and no full-size accumulator**.
- The token axis is chunked to cap the temporaries at ≈ 0.5 GB.
- Same math (fp32 gradient accumulation), checked against the current path on a multi-device CPU mesh.
- Expected at d1024: ≈ 6+ GiB less peak, and the table's comm drops from ≈ 8.6 GB all-reduce to ≈ 2 × 2 GB gathers per step. At d512 it should recover some of the table's speed cost.

Candidate 9's d1024 run relaunches on the fix.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Embedding ideas from the new modded-nanogpt record** ([#360, ANVIL2](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/360), merged today: 39.9 s from 73.9 s), per your comment.

Its biggest non-CE change is one **84.6M-row hashed bigram + trigram table** (× 768, row-sharded 1/8 per GPU), worth **35.8 millinats / 7 s** of the gain at only **+1.2 s** of wall time. Their row-count grid: 377k → 21M → 84.6M rows gives 3.315 → 3.284 → 3.279 val loss for +0.5 s total, because nothing in the step scales with table size. How:

1. **Sign trick** (from [#299](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/299)): each n-gram's row is multiplied by a ±1 vector chosen by an *independent* hash from a pool of 8192 sign rows, so n-grams colliding on a row roughly cancel (count-sketch). ≈ −0.5 s in #299. **We don't have it.** It's free and composes with our `embed2_norm`.
2. **Sparse row exchange:** only the unique rows a step touches are fetched from their owners (all-to-all of ids, then rows), and gradients go back the same way. No dense gradient, no all-reduce, no all-gather of the table.
3. **Row-sparse Adam:** β1 = 0 and one fp32 second moment *per row*, so a row with no gradient has an exactly zero update. The update can therefore be gathered, applied and scattered for only the touched rows, and optimizer state is 4 bytes per row. Plus a period-4 update cadence.
4. The **same sparse treatment for value embeddings** (−1.1 s).

**What maps onto us:**
- The row-sharded gather already being built for the d1024 OOM (batch 115) is step toward (2).
- **(3) is the gate for everything else.** Our table uses Adam with momentum and AdEMAMix, which keeps every row moving and so forbids a sparse update.
- **Being implemented now as flags,** for 2-seed d512 tests on candidate 9:
  - the **sign trick**;
  - **row-sparse-compatible Adam on the table** (β1 = 0, per-row v, no AdEMAMix), run *densely* first to check it is loss-neutral here, with an LR bracket.
- If both hold, a sparse update path makes **much larger tables** cheap. Our 524k → 1M test was −0.003 to −0.005 at equal steps and was rejected only on speed (batches 50 / 55). It would also let us **revisit trigrams at tens of millions of rows**: our trigram tests used 262k–524k rows, where collisions swamp them.

**One tension to flag:** rule A fixes the table at 0.41 × the other params, and the record's result is that much bigger tables keep paying when they cost ≈ nothing. If the sparse path works, we may want to revisit rule A for the hashed table, e.g. by counting it separately since it is a memory, not compute.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 119: host stalls. The numpy batch path is in, and a second stall source turned up and is fixed.** (candidate 9, d512, 2817 steps)

**Change 1: build batches in numpy** ([`0cb19d3559`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/0cb19d3559)).
- levanter's `CausalLmDataset` / `PrebuiltLmDataset` ran a per-example CPU `eqx.filter_jit` on the loader threads. Those threads compete with the train loop for the GIL.
- They now build each example with numpy, producing the same leaves and dtypes. A parity test checks this against `GrugLmExample.causal` in 8 configurations.

**Change 2: give single-process tasks their own XLA autotune cache directory** ([`4885d481ae`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4885d481ae), in iris `jax_init`).
- With the loader gone from the stall stacks, every stall showed the `finestore-directory-sync` thread in `stat()`. Each 0.5–2.5 s stall also got only one sample from the stall sampler, a sign that the GIL was held.
- Cause: a single-process task pointed its autotune cache at the shared node-local parent directory. That directory also holds every earlier multi-GPU job's `process-N/` subdirectories.
- The uploader walks its directory recursively every sync, so each walk covered the node's whole cache history. It also queued those other jobs' files for upload.
- Multi-GPU tasks already used a subdirectory per process. Single-process tasks now use their own `single-process/` subdirectory.

| run (step time after step 100) | median | mean | p99 | time above 1.3× median | loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| single-process, old loader (b97) | 191.4 ms | 204.3 ms | 308 ms | 3.70% | 2.9786 |
| single-process, numpy loader only | 193.8 ms | 246.7 ms | 1772 ms | 18.2% | 2.9768 |
| **single-process, numpy loader + own cache dir** | 195.1 ms | 199.8 ms | 250 ms | **0.16%** | 2.9781 |
| same, seed 1 | 194.4 ms | 198.4 ms | 250 ms | **0.12%** | 2.9810 |
| one process per GPU (default), numpy loader | 184.9 ms | 201.7 ms | 400 ms | 6.6% | 2.9740 |
| same, seed 1 | 186.7 ms | 202.0 ms | 594 ms | 5.6% | 2.9825 |

- **Single-process stalls are effectively gone:** mean step time is within 2.5% of the median.
- **Loss is unchanged:** 2.9740 / 2.9825 vs candidate 9's 2.9750 / 2.9791, within noise. That's expected, since the data is identical.
- **The default one-process-per-GPU runs still lose about 8%** of mean step time to stalls above the median. That's worth a fixed-time win if it can be removed, so it's the next profiling target. The cache fix doesn't reach these runs: each rank already has its own directory, although that directory also grows across jobs on a node.
- **The iris fix affects every single-process GPU job, not just ours.** I can open it as a separate PR against main if you want.

comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5889072443)):

> In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:
>
> A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
> or
> B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt
>
> Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
> Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

<!-- belay-intake:5889072443 -->

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 123: semi-orthogonal LatentMoE projections, frozen or updated on the Stiefel manifold** (intake suggestion from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791; [`583d97d120`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/583d97d120))

**The idea:** `w_latent_down` / `w_latent_up` are small and shared by every expert in a layer, so they may work as information-preserving maps rather than doing computation. If so, keeping them semi-orthogonal should cost nothing. Freezing them (option B) should then be about as good as updating them with an orthogonality-preserving optimizer (option A).

**Implementation:**
- **Init** (`latent_orthogonal_init`): a Haar-random semi-orthogonal matrix, with orthonormal columns for down and orthonormal rows for up. Every singular value is `std · √d`, which gives the same Frobenius norm as the current normal init, so only the spectrum changes.
- **Option B** (`latent_proj_update=frozen`): both projections stay at their init.
- **Option A** (`latent_proj_update=stiefel`): Skewon from [arXiv 2608.06218](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218), Muon on the Stiefel manifold.
  - With Nesterov momentum M (MuonH's 0.95) and normalized weight Xn, take `N = skew(M Xnᵀ)` and step along `B = −msign(N) Xn`. That's the exact closed-form solution of Muon's subproblem restricted to the tangent space.
  - Then retract with `Xn ← polar(Xn + ηB)`, using cubic Newton-Schulz.
  - `‖ηB‖_F = lr · ‖Xn‖_F`: the same relative step as MuonH's hyperball, at the MuonH LR, so there's no new hyperparameter.
  - CPU tests check three things. The singular values stay at the init value to 1e-4 over 300 steps. On `max ⟨T, X⟩` it reaches 99.96% of the optimum `c‖T‖_*`. Tall and wide matrices both work.
- The paper's own experiments are synthetic (solver accuracy and speed), so this is its first test inside a network.

| arm | what it isolates |
|---|---|
| `ortho` | orthogonal init only, still trained by MuonH |
| `orthofrz` | option B: orthogonal init, both projections frozen |
| `skewon` | option A: orthogonal init, updated with Skewon |

**How to read it:**
- If `orthofrz` ≈ `skewon` ≈ baseline, the projections really are just information-preserving maps.
- If `skewon` beats `orthofrz`, rotating the subspace matters but reshaping its spectrum doesn't.
- If both lose to the baseline, the trained projections do more than preserve information. I'll check that directly against their spectra in the gradient-capture diagnostics, which record the weights of layers 0 and 5.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 123 results: the LatentMoE projections do real computation. Freezing them costs 0.012; keeping them orthogonal costs 0.005.** (intake suggestion from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs 2.9750 / 2.9791)

| arm | Δ s0 / s1 | mean | ex/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ortho`: semi-orthogonal init, still trained by MuonH | −0.0006 / +0.0023 | +0.0009 (neutral) | 674 / 654 |
| `orthofrz`: option B, orthogonal init, both projections frozen | +0.0116 / +0.0131 | **+0.0123** | 672 / 664 |
| `skewon`: option A, orthogonal init, Skewon (Muon on the Stiefel manifold) | +0.0052 / +0.0049 | **+0.0051** | 659 / 665 |

**Reading, per the plan in the batch 123 comment:**
- **The init doesn't matter.** Starting semi-orthogonal and then training normally is neutral.
- **Frozen is clearly worse than Skewon, and both are worse than training normally.** So the "information-preserving map" hypothesis doesn't hold at d512. Rotating the subspace is worth about 0.007 (frozen → Skewon). Shaping its spectrum is worth about another 0.005 (Skewon → MuonH).
- **The captured weights say the same.** A semi-orthogonal 512 × 256 map has all singular values equal (stable rank 256). The candidate 9 projections, from the batch 120 gradient-capture run, end at stable rank 48–171 (effective-rank fraction 0.81–0.97). The down-projection in layer 5 concentrates over training, from stable rank 114 at step 100 to 48 at step 2760. The model builds a few dominant directions in exactly the map the idea wanted to keep flat.

Closed at d512. The option A / B contrast is informative, though. If a future change makes these maps bigger (a wider latent, more experts), freezing or constraining them would be worth rechecking, since that's where the idea's rationale is strongest. Thanks for the suggestion.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **OKLS deep dive, part 1: what the optimizer assumes, measured on candidate 9's real gradients** (per [your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5885091228))

**Setup.** Batch 120 captured every step's raw gradient and applied update for 46 matrices over four 48-step windows (starting at steps 100, 700, 1700 and 2760). That covers every family: KDA and MLA projections, the shared expert, the LatentMoE projections, the router, and 4 routed experts in layers 0 and 5.
- Two runs: candidate 9 under MuonH (2.9777), and with OKLS on attention (2.9780, 7% slower). So OKLS gives no gain at equal steps on candidate 9, down from −0.0057 on the old base.
- The analysis ran next to the data ([`analyze_grad_capture.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ladderclimb_v1_batch14/experiments/grug/fast_track/analyze_grad_capture.py)). Charts and a data table are on a separate page (private until shared): https://claude.ai/artifact/BSgehVG6J8rfvFegH6ewra

| OKLS assumption | measurement | result |
|---|---|---|
| The Kronecker factors are anisotropic, so whitening changes the step | effective rank and condition number of the row (input-side) factor A and the column (output-side) factor B | **Holds, strongly, on the input side.** A's effective rank is 0.8–17% of the dimension at step 100. Condition numbers (top 90% of eigenvalues) reach 10³–10⁷. B is much flatter (19–81%). |
| The covariance is close to Kronecker | fit A, B on even steps, whiten the odd steps, compare the leftover anisotropy with a Gaussian that has exactly that covariance | **Holds late.** Whitening removes 2–5 decades. At step 2760 the residual is 0.28–0.50 (log₁₀ max/median) against a 0.17 floor. Earlier windows keep 0.5–1.5. Shampoo's factors are within 0.11 of the KL factors. |
| The preconditioner must be fresh | overlap of A's top-10% eigenspace within a window and between windows | **Mixed.** It's stable within 48 steps (0.72–0.94). Between windows it turns over early (0.30–0.58, step 100 → 700) and settles late (0.80–0.92). |
| High-variance directions are mostly noise | signal-to-noise of the window-mean gradient, by A's eigen-rank | **Holds, weakly.** The largest-variance directions have the lowest SNR (log₁₀ −0.7 to −0.15 at step 100). Nothing rises much above batch noise, though. |
| A better-conditioned step makes more progress | overshoot of each applied update along its own line, and each direction's stable rank | **Not here.** See the next point. |

**New finding: every dense step overshoots.**
- For each applied update I measure r = ⟨g_{t+1}, U_t⟩ / ⟨g_t, U_t⟩. On a quadratic, r = 0 means the step landed on the line minimum and r = −1 means it went twice that far.
- Under MuonH, **100% of dense-matrix steps through step 1700 overshoot**. The median r is −0.2 to −0.6 at step 100, meaning steps go 1.2–1.6× past the line optimum. That's the edge-of-stability pattern, and it matches lag-1 gradient autocorrelations of −0.25 to −0.86 at step 100.
- **OKLS on attention cuts the overshoot about in half** (−0.13 to −0.39), but loss is no better.
- By step 2760, with the LR decayed, r is ≈ 0.
- Routed experts sit near 0 throughout. Their per-step gradients are noise-dominated.

**Why OKLS stopped paying on candidate 9, as far as this shows:**
- The inputs to our matrices are dominated by a few directions: effective rank 2–12% for the value, output, KV-latent and shared-down projections at step 2760. So whitening does most of its work boosting weak input directions by orders of magnitude.
- The resulting direction keeps only **14–33% of Muon's stable rank**, and the step overshoots less.
- Muon's flat-spectrum step ignores the input covariance and makes the same progress per step, more cheaply.
- Weight stable rank under OKLS rises for queries and keys (MLA `w_uk` 70 → 106) and falls for output and down-projections (KDA `w_o` 93 → 70). The blog's "higher stable rank" claim holds only for some of our families.

**One correction to my own method.** My first pass also scored each candidate direction (Muon, OKLS, Shampoo, one-sided, SGD) by its first-order gain on the next batches. That's confounded: those gradients come after the run already stepped along roughly the Muon direction. Every gain came out negative, which is how the overshoot showed up. Those scores aren't reported, and the overshoot ratio replaces them.

**What would make OKLS worth another look.** Each item comes from a measurement above:
1. **Output-side-only whitening.** B is well-conditioned, and whitening only that side avoids amplifying near-dead input directions.
2. **A damped input factor** (A + λ·tr(A)/m·I), sweeping λ rather than LR.
3. **Targeting overshoot directly.** Overshoot is uniform across families early on, so a per-matrix step cap during the first third of training is a cheaper test than any preconditioner.

I'd run 3 first. Want any of these queued, or more diagnostics first?

| run | mean vs median step | time lost to stalls > 300 ms | stalls > 300 ms | loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|

**What was stalling:**
- Each GPU node keeps an XLA autotune cache that accumulates every job's files. Process 0 mirrors it to object storage from a background thread (`finestore-directory-sync`), every 120 s.
- The remote copy is keyed by the code's tree hash. So on every new commit, the uploader re-read and re-uploaded the node's whole history. It also walked the whole directory on each sync.
- Both happen in Python on that thread. Process 0 stalled, and every other rank waited on it at the next collective.
- The stall sampler's stacks put `stat` / `read_bytes` in `fileset.flush` at almost every stall over 300 ms.

**Fix 1** (`FineStoreDirectory` counts files present at open as already known) removed the uploads but not the walks. The run landed on a node with a bigger directory and got worse.

**Fix 2** is what matters. The cache fills while XLA compiles, so syncing every 2 minutes during training buys nothing. It now syncs every 30 minutes, and the exit sync publishes what the job added. d512 runs now walk the directory only at start and exit.

- **For the objective:** about 4–5% of step time comes back in every default-mode run. That's worth roughly **−0.007 to −0.009 at fixed time**, on top of PGLE's ≈ −0.0036.
- **Beyond this issue:** both fixes are in shared code (`lib/finestore`, `lib/iris` `jax_init`), along with batch 119's single-process autotune-directory fix. They affect every GPU job on the cluster. I'd like to open them as one small PR to main. Say if you want it.

comments.body:
🤖 **Plan for your router comment ([5905815824](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5905815824)): two arms, implementing now**

**A. A tiny-MLP router, as a residual on the linear one:** `logits = x W_r + W_b · silu(W_a x)`, with 32 hidden neurons and `W_b` zero-initialized.
- It starts exactly as candidate 9, so the MLP only has to learn what a linear router can't express.
- This differs from the low-rank routers that lost earlier: those *replaced* the linear router with a rank-r bottleneck.

**B. Removing the router-aligned component before the expert sees the token.**
- Every token routed to expert e has a large component along the router column r_e. Removing it lets the expert's neurons spend their capacity on how the arriving tokens differ.
- **Handling the LatentMoE:** the router and the latent projection read the same normed input x, and the expert reads `latent = RMSNorm(x W_down)`. The router direction's image in latent space is `u_e = r_e W_down`. RMS scaling doesn't change direction, so projecting `û_e` out of the latent input removes exactly the router-aligned part.
- **As a weight transform:** that projection equals constraining expert e's up-projection to ignore `û_e`: `W_up,e ← (I − û_e û_eᵀ) W_up,e`. It's applied each forward on the weights (E × 256 × 384 multiply-adds, negligible), so the dispatch and expert kernels don't change.
- **Decoupling:** with a stop-gradient on `û_e`, growing the router's alignment no longer raises that expert's neuron activations for the token, which is the separation you describe. The combine weight still carries the router's contribution to the output.

Both get 2 seeds on candidate 9 at d512 with PGLE, paired against 2.9750 / 2.9791.

It removes a **learned** per-expert fraction α_e of the direction: `(I − α_e û_e û_eᵀ) W_e`, with α_e zero-initialized, so the model starts at candidate 9 and chooses how much each expert should ignore. If the α's stay near 0, the idea is closed; if some experts pull theirs up, those are worth a look.

**Tiny-MLP router:** a nonlinear residual on the linear router makes routing slightly worse. Together with HERO-MoE (+0.0126) and the earlier low-rank routers, that says the linear router plus candidate 9's combine is hard to beat at this scale. Closed.

comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5910532511)):

> Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.
>
> Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.
>
> But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:
>
> 1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
> 2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting
>
> And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.
>
> The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Lets do a deepdive on how Muon is behaving. Train for half the duration. Then lets take one step and compute the gradient. For each matrix, make a plot showing the singular values of the gradient, and then after applying NS. 

The opinionated part of Muon is choosing to upweight the low singular values. We want to see where this decision is accurate. We can view each singular value as being connected to a direction in the input space which activates it, which produces a direction in the output space. Boosting a singular value means we really care about strengthing that relationship. More in input X produces more in output Y. 

There are two ways to evaluate if that signal is accurate: 
-does the gradient hold up locally when we sample new data. We can measure SNR via mean(behavior)/square(behavior)
-is the gradient useful beyond nonzero step-size (something can accurately estimate the global gradient, but its not stable for a real step-size change in weights)

Taking an actual step may be too computationally heavy. What we can do to estimate 2 is to repeat the process for n steps in the same local neighborhood. If a gradient aligns across those points, it indicates the direction is consistently downhill in that whole neighborhood, and is likely robust to a step-size update.

Think through this carefully before executing, using clean math and awareness of how much compute it will cost.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 136: Muon direction probe. Results first, plan below.** (d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, probe at step 1408 of 2817, 46 matrices; [lc1-b136-muonprobe](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/lc1-b136-muonprobe) trained normally to the end)

**📊 Plots for all 46 matrices (spectra before and after Newton-Schulz, per-direction consistency on held-out data and along the trajectory) and a per-family table: [Muon Direction Probe](https://claude.ai/artifact/Wmpv9jBGJ8wqP1XwPtPY6N)**

**Results:**
1. **On new data, a direction's reliability falls steadily with its singular value.**
   - Attention and router matrices: held-out consistency (mean / RMS of `s_i = u_iᵀ G_b v_i` over 64 unseen batches) is ≈ 0.95 in the top quarter of directions and ≈ 0.2 in the bottom quarter. The last eighth is essentially noise (0.07–0.12).
   - **Exceptions:** the LatentMoE and shared-expert matrices stay reliable deep into the spectrum (0.40–0.67 even in the last eighth). Routed experts are weak throughout: 0.5 at the top, 0.06 at the bottom.
2. **Newton-Schulz already soft-truncates the noisy tail.**
   - Five quintic steps can't lift singular values below ≈ 10⁻³ of the top one. So for the attention, router and value matrices, Muon's output falls off over the last 20–50% of directions, which is where reliability is lowest.
   - What Muon boosts 10–100× is the **middle** of the spectrum, which is still reliable on data (0.5–0.8). **On the question you asked:** boosting the mid-σ directions is accurate, and the truly unreliable tail mostly isn't boosted.
3. **The expected payoff scales with σ, but that's consistent with Muon's choice.**
   - `E[s_i]` tracks σ_i closely (cosine 0.83–1.00, vs 0.09–0.31 for a flat profile).
   - But Muon is steepest descent under a **spectral-norm** budget, which gives *every* direction with positive expected payoff full weight. 86–100% of directions have `E[s_i] > 0`.
   - The cost is spending equal budget on directions whose payoff is mostly noise.
4. **Along real steps, even the top directions don't hold.**
   - On fixed data at the next 32 positions, consistency drops to 0.2–0.55 even for the top directions, and a direction's sign holds only 50–80% of the time.
   - For MLA `w_q` / `w_uk`, the top ≈ 200 directions go **negative** along the trajectory: the sharpest directions are overshot and flip within a few steps. Mid-spectrum directions often persist better than the top.
   - This matches the edge-of-stability overshoot from the OKLS deep dive.
5. **Routed experts:** in the momentum basis (the directions MuonH actually steps along), held-out consistency is **≈ 0.04**. Each expert sees about 1/64 of the tokens, so its per-step update is nearly pure noise with respect to fresh data. Dense matrices are 0.5–0.8 there, the router ≈ 0.17.

**What this suggests trying** (each tied to a finding):
- **NS steps 5 → 3.** A shallower Newton-Schulz leaves more of the low-σ tail un-boosted (finding 2). It's also faster.
- **Routed experts: a noise-aware step.** Their updates carry almost no fresh-data signal (finding 5). Earlier batches found both momentum directions worse, so the next thing is a smaller expert step or, in the same spirit, SGD-like (σ-weighted) updates for experts only.
- **Probe early and late** (step ≈ 300 and ≈ 2600), about 40 s of GPU time each, to see whether the picture moves through training.

---

**Plan (as posted before the run):**


**The question.**
- Write a matrix's gradient as `G = U Σ Vᵀ = Σ σ_i u_i v_iᵀ`. Direction i is "more of input v_i produces more of output u_i".
- Muon steps along `−η O` with `O ≈ Σ u_i v_iᵀ`: every direction gets the same weight. SGD would weight direction i by σ_i. Relative to SGD, Muon boosts the small-σ directions.
- **Per-direction payoff:** to first order, the step changes a batch b's loss by `−η Σ_i s_i(b)`, with `s_i(b) = u_iᵀ G_b v_i`. So `s_i(b) > 0` means direction i of Muon's step lowers batch b's loss. Boosting direction i pays exactly when `s_i` is reliably positive on data and positions the step will actually meet.

**Design:** one probe inside a normal candidate 9 run at d512, at half duration (step 1408).

- **Matrices:** the 46 captured by the batch 120 gradient capture, covering every family (KDA and MLA projections, shared expert, LatentMoE projections, router, 4 routed experts each in layers 0 and 5).

1. **Basis and spectra.** At θ₀, average the gradient over 8 batches (set A): `G_A = U Σ Vᵀ`. For each matrix, plot σ_i of `G_A` and the singular values after Muon's own Newton-Schulz (quintic, 5 steps).
   - That shows how much each direction is actually boosted: NS gives ≈ 0.7–1.2, not exactly 1.
   - The basis is fixed from set A. It is never scored on its own batches, since there `s_i = σ_i > 0` by construction.
2. **Does it hold up on new data?**
   - **Measure:** on 64 held-out batches (set B), compute `s_i(b)` for every direction.
   - **Report:** the consistency `c_i = mean_b s_i / RMS_b s_i` (1 = the same helpful sign and size on every batch, 0 = pure noise, negative = the reference batch was misleading), against σ-rank.
   - **Also report** `E[s_i]` itself, the expected per-direction payoff.
   - **Muon vs SGD:** compare how well Muon's flat weighting and SGD's σ-weighting line up with that payoff profile, as cosines against `E[s]`.
3. **Does it hold over a real step?** This is your neighborhood test.
   - **Measure:** the run keeps training normally for 32 steps. At each point θ_k on that trajectory, compute `s_i(θ_k)` on a **fixed** set of 4 evaluation batches, with the same θ₀ basis.
   - Fixing the data removes data noise, so the only change is from the parameters moving. And the neighborhood is exactly where training goes.
   - **Report:** the across-position consistency `c_i^pos = mean_k s_i / RMS_k s_i`, and how many steps each direction's sign survives, binned by σ-rank.
   - If a small-σ direction flips sign within a step or two, its boost is consumed or overshot by the step itself. That would tie back to the edge-of-stability overshoot measured in the OKLS deep dive.

**Compute.**
- 8 + 64 + 32 × 4 ≈ **200 extra forward/backward passes**, about 1 train step each (≈ 0.19 s), so **≈ 40 s of GPU time** plus one compile.
- The SVDs of 46 matrices up to 768 × 512 are negligible on GPU.
- The 32 trajectory steps are the run's own training steps, so training isn't disturbed and the run finishes as a normal candidate 9 run.
- Outputs are about 9 MB: per matrix the spectra, `s_i` for 64 batches, and `s_i` at 33 positions.
- Plots go on the diagnostics artifact next to the OKLS page.

**Caveats:**
- The analysis uses the gradient's SVD. MuonH actually orthogonalizes Nesterov momentum after pre-norm and a hyperball step, so I'll also report the basis from the momentum buffer at θ₀ as a check.
- It is one checkpoint in one run. If it's informative, repeating at step 300 and step 2600 gives the early and late picture for another ~40 s each.

**Background:**

| `lc1-b138-probe-el` | 5 (candidate 9) | 300, 2600 | early and late, to compare with the step-1408 probe in batch 136 |

- **Same measurements as batch 136:**

  - the momentum-basis check.

  The probe's own NS spectra now use the run's iteration count, so the 10-iteration run shows the 10-iteration output.

With 10 iterations the tail gets boosted too. The loss says whether that noisy tail is worth boosting, and the spectra show how far 10 iterations actually flatten it.
- The probes are about 40 s of GPU time each and leave training unchanged. Results will be edited into this comment.


---

### Results: early and late probes (5 NS iterations; `probe-el` final 2.9771 vs 2.9750, within noise, as expected for a probe that doesn't change training)

**How to read the table.** Each value is the mean over a family's captured matrices of a per-matrix median.
- **ho:** held-out consistency, mean/RMS of s_i = u_iᵀ G_b v_i over 64 unseen batches, in the gradient's singular basis. Split into the top, middle and last eighth of directions by σ.
- **upd top:** the same measure in the basis of the update applied at the previous step.
- **traj top:** consistency along the next 32 steps on 4 fixed batches.
- **NS tail/top:** Newton-Schulz output σ, last eighth relative to top eighth. 1 means fully flattened.

| family | ho top 300 / 1408 / 2600 | ho tail 300 / 1408 / 2600 | upd top 300 / 1408 / 2600 | traj top 300 / 1408 / 2600 | NS tail/top 300 / 1408 / 2600 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KDA attention | 0.98 / 0.95 / 0.86 | 0.19 / 0.10 / 0.08 | 0.92 / 0.68 / **0.00** | 0.05 / 0.27 / 0.96 | 0.14 / 0.21 / 0.22 |
| MLA attention | 0.99 / 0.97 / 0.85 | 0.16 / 0.10 / 0.05 | 0.93 / 0.68 / **0.05** | 0.10 / 0.18 / 0.95 | 0.04 / 0.06 / 0.10 |
| LatentMoE proj | 0.99 / 0.98 / 0.93 | 0.83 / 0.64 / 0.39 | 0.97 / 0.77 / **−0.02** | 0.09 / 0.40 / 0.91 | 0.82 / 0.93 / 0.95 |
| shared expert | 0.99 / 0.98 / 0.94 | 0.71 / 0.44 / 0.28 | 0.96 / 0.60 / **0.14** | 0.04 / 0.27 / 0.90 | 0.33 / 0.45 / 0.39 |
| routed experts | 0.70 / 0.55 / 0.37 | 0.13 / 0.08 / 0.06 | 0.20 / 0.08 / **−0.05** | 0.33 / 0.61 / 0.84 | 0.79 / 0.86 / 0.90 |
| router | 0.98 / 0.93 / 0.80 | 0.22 / 0.12 / 0.05 | 0.64 / 0.52 / **0.13** | 0.26 / 0.71 / 0.93 | 0.50 / 0.58 / 0.60 |

- **Held-out reliability falls steadily through training in every family.** The gradient's own top directions stay reliable (0.8–0.94 at step 2600), but the tail loses nearly all its signal. Routed experts are the weakest at every step: even their *top* eighth drops to 0.37 by step 2600.
- **Late in the run, the previous update's directions carry no fresh-data signal.** At step 300, the update's top directions predict a descent on unseen batches (0.9+ outside the experts). At step 2600 they sit at about 0: along the directions the optimizer is moving, fresh-data gradients no longer agree on a sign.
  - This fits the overshoot equilibrium from batch 128: along the update's own directions the model sits at the bottom of the valley, and the gradient flips sign from batch to batch. The cosine LR is small by then, so these late steps mostly average noise rather than doing damage.
- **Consistency along the trajectory rises late only because the step size shrinks.** At step 2600 the cosine LR is near zero, so the parameters barely move over 32 steps, and a fixed-batch projection stays the same by construction. Early (step 300) it is 0.04–0.10 for the dense families: the gradient's top directions rotate within a few dozen steps, so the basis changes much faster than momentum (β=0.95, ≈20 steps) integrates.
- **NS behaviour is a property of each family's gradient spectrum, stable over training.**
  - MLA and KDA leave the tail un-boosted: 0.04–0.22 of the top σ.
  - LatentMoE projections and routed experts come out nearly flat (0.8–0.95), because their gradient spectra are already flat and noise-like.
  - So for routed experts, Muon gives every direction almost the same step, including the 87% of directions whose held-out consistency is below 0.2. Batch 140 targets exactly this.
- **Share of directions with a positive held-out payoff (E[s]>0):** 91–100% at step 300, 81–100% at step 2600. Routed experts are the lowest at 0.81. Almost every direction still points downhill on average, but late in the run the average is small next to the noise.

*The 10-iteration NS probes (steps 300 / 1408 / 2600) and the NS10 loss comparison will be added when `ns10-probe` finishes. Seed 1 so far: 2.9804 vs 2.9791, +0.0013.*


---

### Results: 10 Newton-Schulz iterations (all three probes done)

The first `ns10-probe` run died on node CUDA faults. Its rerun `ns10-probe2` wrote steps 300 and 1408. Step 2600 came from a separate single-probe run, `ns10-p2600` (cw-rno2a).

| family | NS tail/top, 5 iters (300 / 1408 / 2600) | NS tail/top, 10 iters | update-basis held-out consistency at 2600, 5 → 10 iters |
|---|---|---|---|
| KDA | 0.14 / 0.21 / 0.22 | 0.95 / 0.95 / 0.95 | 0.00 → −0.03 |
| MLA | 0.04 / 0.06 / 0.10 | 0.90 / 0.91 / 0.91 | 0.05 → 0.16 |
| LatentMoE | 0.82 / 0.93 / 0.95 | 0.95 / 0.96 / 0.96 | −0.02 → 0.03 |
| shared | 0.33 / 0.45 / 0.39 | 0.95 / 0.95 / 0.95 | 0.14 → **0.49** |
| routed experts | 0.79 / 0.86 / 0.90 | 0.95 / 0.95 / 0.96 | −0.05 → −0.04 |

- **10 iterations flatten every family's NS output, as intended.** The weakest directions go to 0.90–0.96 of the top σ, including MLA and KDA, which 5 iterations leave at 0.04–0.22.
- **The gradient's own held-out consistency is unchanged** (same basis), but **the update's directions keep more fresh-data signal late in the run**, most of all for the shared expert (0.14 → 0.49) and MLA (0.05 → 0.16). This is the property ANVIL III measures as its advantage. Trajectory consistency also rises at steps 300 and 1408 (for example KDA 0.05 → 0.22 at step 300).
- **Loss: neutral.** Seed 0: 2.9769 vs 2.9768 (cw-rno2a candidate 9), +0.0001. Seed 1: 2.9804 vs 2.9791 (cw-us-east-02a), +0.0013.
- **Closed:** flattening the spectrum fully, which also boosts MLA and KDA's weak directions, changes how the updates line up with fresh data but not the loss. This agrees with batch 143: the bottom 20% of directions can be dropped or kept with no effect.
