comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 163: Motif 3's techniques** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934643844); [Motif 3 technical report, arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119); d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`a4ab5b17c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a4ab5b17c8))

Every technique in the report, and what this batch does with it:

| Motif 3 technique | what it is | here |
|---|---|---|
| **Grouped differential latent attention (GDLA)** | MLA plus grouped differential attention: `n/(g+1)` noise heads, each shared by `g` signal heads (g = 4), `D = H_S − λ_t ⊙ H_N` with a per-token, per-head `λ_t = σ(x W_λ)`, then an elementwise query-dependent output gate `σ(G) ⊙ D`. Reported to reach MLA's loss with 9.2% fewer tokens. | **testing** (`mla_grouped_diff`) |
| **Expert-specific PolyNorm** | expert activation `Σₙ₌₁³ aₙ zⁿ / RMS(zⁿ) + b`, per-token RMS, coefficients learned per expert | **testing** with fixed equal coefficients (see below) |
| **Multi-token prediction** | DeepSeek-V3 depth-1 MTP, loss weight 0.2 | **testing** (`mtp_mode=deepseek`) |
| Modified manifold-constrained hyper-connections | 4 residual streams with Sinkhorn-projected mixing and a post-scale annealed 2 → 1 | not yet: it replaces the residual path, which Block AttnRes already owns here; a real port is a larger project (next batch if you want it) |
| Decaying Gaussian router noise | cosine-decayed logit noise; the report shows only faster load balancing | skipped: our Gumbel sampling was neutral or worse ([batch 30](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5852213638)), and QB already balances from step 1 |
| FFN magnitude penalty | `ReLU(|y| − 128)²` on layer outputs | skipped: a stability guard for activations far above anything at d512 |
| QK-Clip | caps pre-softmax logits | already covered: QK RMSNorm with a learnable `qk_mult` |
| Sequence-wise aux loss + loss-free bias | load balancing | already covered: QB routing |
| 1 full : 3 sliding-window (128) layers | local attention | already covered: KDA local layers; a local softmax branch was neutral ([batch 156](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927535181)) |
| WSD schedule | warmup-stable-decay | tested: PowerCool lost ([batch 154](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5927409237)) |
| MXFP8 experts, parallel Muon, state offload | systems | MXFP8 needs Blackwell; FP8 on H100 stays on the throughput list |

**Grouped differential attention** (`mla_grouped_diff=g`, MLA layers 3 and 5, 4 heads at d512):
- `g` = 4 gives one noise map shared by all 4 heads, and `g` = 2 gives two maps.
- Each noise map has its own query and key up-projection; its columns are repeated for its `g` signal heads, so the q/k transforms apply unchanged. It reads the same values.
- `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per head and token, with `W_λ` zero-init (λ starts at 0.5, Adam). The sigmoid keeps it a subtraction: batch 77's unconstrained DIFF λ went negative and turned the difference into a sum.
- Motif's elementwise output gate is our existing `attn_gate_elementwise`.

**PolyNorm** (`moe_ungated_activation=polynorm`, ungated routed experts): `(1/3) Σₙ₌₁³ uⁿ / RMS(uⁿ)` per token over the expert's hidden units. The expert activation is a static function inside the EP backends, so learned per-expert coefficients need a backend API change. This first tests the function form; the learned version comes next if it helps. The dropless eval's tied-gate backends use the exact rewrite `polynorm(u)/u`.

| run | change | seeds |
|---|---|---|
| `gda4` | grouped diff, g = 4, + elementwise output gate (Motif's GDLA) | 2 |
| `gda2` | g = 2, + elementwise gate | 2 |
| `gda4-hg` | g = 4 with the per-head gate (isolates the gate) | 1 |
| `egate` | elementwise gate alone (control) | 1 |
| `poly` | PolyNorm routed experts | 2 |
| `polysh` | PolyNorm routed + shared | 1 |
| `mtp02` | DeepSeek MTP, weight 0.2 | 2 |
| `mtp02q` | the same, MTP loss on a random 25% of positions (cheaper) | 1 |

Step time will be reported for each: grouped diff doubles the global-layer attention, PolyNorm is a few extra reductions per expert, and MTP adds a block and an lm_head pass.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gda4 (+ elementwise gate)` | 2.9739 (-0.0029) | 2.9785 (-0.0037) | 183.0 (+6.6%) |
| `gda2 (+ elementwise gate)` | 2.9746 (-0.0022) | 2.9785 (-0.0037) | 183.1 / 185.9† |
| `gda4-hg (per-head gate)` | 2.9760 (-0.0008) | — | 181.3 |
| `egate (elementwise gate alone)†` | 2.9758 (-0.0010) | — | 174.7 |
| `poly (PolyNorm routed)` | 2.9885 (+0.0117) | 2.9942 (+0.0120) | 183.1† / 179.1 |
| `polysh (PolyNorm routed + shared)†` | 2.9908 (+0.0140) | — | 185.0 |
| `mtp02 (MTP, weight 0.2)` | 2.9860 (+0.0092) | 2.9939 (+0.0117) | 188.4 (+10%) |
| `mtp02q (MTP on 25% of positions)†` | 2.9989 (+0.0221) | — | 179.1 |

† launched without PGLE (see below), so its step time is about 3% higher than a PGLE run's; losses are comparable.

**Takeaway.**
- **Grouped differential attention:** −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps, but it runs the global layers' attention twice (+6–7% step time ≈ +0.011 at fixed time), so it loses. The elementwise gate is most of its gain, and alone it's neutral (−0.001).
- **PolyNorm** experts lose clearly (+0.012 routed, +0.014 routed + shared). ReLU² suits these experts better than an RMS-normalized polynomial, at least with fixed coefficients.
- **MTP** loses at weight 0.2 too (+0.009 / +0.012, +10% step), matching batch 18. Applying it to 25% of positions is cheaper but worse (+0.022).
- None of Motif 3's techniques transfers to this rung.

**Crashes:** several runs here restarted with `CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_FAILED` / `ILLEGAL_ADDRESS`. All of them had PGLE on, and every run relaunched without PGLE completed (details in the [batch 157/160 comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 164: token-embedding AttnRes queries** ([intake suggestion](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934727837) from RavnaBergsndot; d512 candidate 9 + PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`a4ab5b17c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/a4ab5b17c8))

**Change** (`attn_res_token_query`). Each AttnRes gate's logit for source `n` becomes

`(q_g + q_e[token]) · RMSNorm(source_n)` instead of `q_g · RMSNorm(source_n)`

with `q_e` a zero-initialized `[vocab, d]` table, so the run is exactly candidate 9 at init. This sits between the paper's data-independent query and its input-dependent `d × d` projection, which it ablated as better but more expensive (Table 4, [arXiv 2603.15031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031)).

| run | table | parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `tqs` | one table shared by all 13 gates | 8.4M |
| `tqg` | one table per gate, as each gate has its own static query | 109M |

**Implementation:**
- The table rows are looked up with the replicated-table gather the value embeddings use (fp32 backward scatter), once per gate.
- Each source's normed key is dotted with the token's row, which adds one read of each source per gate.
- It trains with the AttnRes query group (Adam).

**Tests:** a no-op at init; only the rows of tokens in the batch get a gradient; moving the table changes the output.

**Also, on dropping the NaN check** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934742747)): the device-side check is already gone ([`17dd004ca0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/17dd004ca0)). The loss is copied to the host once per step for logging, and the check runs on that number, so it costs nothing. The pipelining crash ([batch 157/160](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)) started only after the device-side check was removed: that check made each step wait on the next, so the earlier loop never truly overlapped steps.

**Results** (final Paloma macro loss; Δ vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; step = median `throughput/duration`, candidate 9 ≈ 171.6 ms on the flat step)

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tqs (shared table)` | 2.9843 (+0.0075) | — | 175.9 (+2.5%) |
| `tqg (per-gate tables)†` | 2.9983 (+0.0215) | 3.0023 (+0.0201) | 186.3 (+8.6%) |

† without PGLE. `tqs` seed 1 is still running.

**Takeaway.** Token-embedding queries hurt: +0.0075 shared and +0.020 per gate, worse the more parameters. AttnRes routing wants the hidden-state view of the token, not a per-token constant. The table overrides the content-based mixing, and with 109M zero-init parameters at the AttnRes query LR it moves fast. A version at a much lower LR is the only follow-up that might be neutral; I don't plan to run it.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 167: a nonlinearity in the bigram content gate, and a 0.1 logit scale** (your request; d512 candidate 9 without PGLE, equal steps, 2 seeds, paired vs candidate 9 on cw-rno2a, 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`23d846a1be`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/23d846a1be))

Candidate 9's gate is `g = σ((e ⊙ b) A B + c)`:
- `e` and `b` are the RMS-normed token embedding and bigram row.
- `A` is [512, 16], random; `B` is [16, 512], zero-init; `c` = +2.

So each channel's logit is a rank-16 bilinear form in (e, b). Unlike GatedNorm, it has no middle nonlinearity.

| run | gate |
|---|---|
| `gsilu` | `σ(SiLU((e ⊙ b) A) B + c)`, as in GatedNorm |
| `ggelu` | `σ(GELU((e ⊙ b) A) B + c)` |
| `gs01` | `σ(0.1 · (e ⊙ b) A B + c)` |

**Notes:**
- **Same start for every arm:** with `B` zero-init, each one starts at `σ(2) ≈ 0.88` exactly like candidate 9. The 0.1 scale is on the learned logits only, so the bias, and with it the initial gate, is unchanged.
- **What the scale does under Adam:** it makes the gate's logits move about 10× more slowly, and the gate stays smoother. Candidate 9's gate went nearly bimodal per token by step 350 (std 0.34, [batch 69](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5859182603)).
- **Diagnostics:** the gate's mean and std are logged (`train/attn_res/attn_res_bigram_gate_*`), so each arm's learned selectivity can be compared.
- **No PGLE:** launched without it (see the [crash notes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5934720837)); the loss comparison is unaffected.
- **Tests:** every variant starts at `σ(c)`, and the activation and scale enter the logits exactly as written.

**Results**

Several runs were preempted repeatedly on cw-rno2a and moved to cw-us-east-02a (`-ue`). Each is compared against its own cluster's candidate 9: rno2a 2.9768 / 2.9822; 02a 2.9791 / 2.9831 (`lc1-b169-c9-ue`, same code, no PGLE).

| gate | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gsilu`, SiLU | 2.9775 (−0.0016, 02a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | 174.1 ms (0%) |
| `ggelu`, GELU | 2.9768 (−0.0023, 02a) | 2.9830 (+0.0008, rno2a) | 174 ms (0%) |
| `gs01`, 0.1 logit scale | 2.9777 (+0.0009, rno2a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | 173 ms (0%) |

**Takeaway.**
- None clears the noise. SiLU is the most consistent, at −0.0017 on both seeds and no step cost. It could ride along in a bundle, but it isn't a win on its own.
- Slowing the gate's logits 10× changes nothing, so the gate's sharp per-token selection isn't a problem that the scale fixes.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 168: token-embedding AttnRes queries at low LR, with the learned tables dumped for analysis** ([your comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5937972246); d512 candidate 9 without PGLE, equal steps, paired vs 2.9768 / 2.9822; [`1629eb97eb`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1629eb97eb))

[Batch 164](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5935144206) trained the zero-init table with the AttnRes query group (Adam at 0.1 × the Adam LR, 6e-5). That lost +0.0075 (shared) and +0.020 (per gate). The table's rows are dotted with RMS-normed 512-wide sources, so at that LR a row can add logits of several units within a few hundred steps, swamping the static queries. A new `attn_res_token_query_lr_mult` scales the table's LR on top of the query group's.

| run | table | LR | seeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tqs-lr01` | shared | ×0.1 (6e-6) | 2 |
| `tqs-lr001` | shared | ×0.01 (6e-7) | 2 |
| `tqg-lr001` | per gate (13 tables) | ×0.01 | 1 |

**Visualization.** New `--final-param-dump REGEX` writes matching params to `final_params.npz` after training. Each run dumps the token-query table, the 13 static AttnRes queries `q_g` and the token embedding. Planned plots:
1. **Size:** how much the token term moves each gate's query, the distribution over tokens of `‖q_e[v]‖ / ‖q_g‖`.
2. **Direction:** `cos(q_e[v], q_g)` per gate. Does the token term mostly rescale the static query (cos ≈ ±1) or rotate it toward other sources?
3. **What the table encodes:**
   - the table's principal components, with token frequency and token class (punctuation, whitespace, subword pieces, digits);
   - the tokens at each end of the top components.
4. **Relation to the token embedding:**
   - a linear map `q_e ≈ E W` (R² of a ridge fit);
   - nearest-neighbour agreement between the two tables.

   This shows whether the table learns new token structure or re-expresses the embedding.

**Results**

Several runs were preempted repeatedly on cw-rno2a and moved to cw-us-east-02a (`-ue`). Each is compared against its own cluster's candidate 9: rno2a 2.9768 / 2.9822; 02a 2.9791 / 2.9831 (`lc1-b169-c9-ue`, same code, no PGLE).

| run | seed 0 | seed 1 | step |
|---|---|---|---|
| shared, LR ×0.1 | 2.9763 (−0.0028, 02a) | 2.9819 (−0.0012, 02a) | 180.5 ms (+3.6%) |
| shared, LR ×0.01 | 2.9758 (−0.0010, rno2a) | 2.9814 (−0.0017, 02a) | +3% |
| per gate, LR ×0.01 | 2.9763 (−0.0005, rno2a) | — | +6.5% |

**What the tables learned.** Page: [Token-Embedding AttnRes Queries](https://claude.ai/artifact/1dXBT9bmxTFfHNwvk1JGp3).
- **Size:** at ×0.01 the token term stays at 3–4% of each gate's static query, a near no-op. At ×0.1 it reaches about 25%.
- **Direction:** it is nearly orthogonal to the static queries (mean |cos| ≈ 0.1). It rotates each gate's query toward other sources rather than rescaling it.
- **Structure:** weak; the top principal component holds 4–5% of the variance. That component is the same at both LRs:
  - one end is word-continuation fragments and byte pieces (`ud`, `ol`, `qu`, `"><`);
  - the other is whole words with a leading space (` offers`, ` programs`, ` processes`);
  - so tokens shift their AttnRes mixing by whether they start a word.
- **Relation to the token embedding:** a linear map from the embedding explains about 11% of the table. Top-10 nearest neighbours agree 7–12% of the time, against 0.5% for random rows.
- **Per-gate tables:** each gate learns its own small pattern. Mean cross-gate cosine is 0–0.1, up to 0.26 for adjacent early gates.

**Closed.** It is neutral at every LR where it doesn't hurt, and it costs 3–9% step time.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Lets try a radical idea: MLP compression. The intuition is, if we want to fit as many clothes in the closet, it makes sense to spend some effort sorting them. The gradient pushes us to just keep throwing clothes in, but maybe an auxillary loss that encourages sorting will be helpful. Without this, we either run out of space, or have to remove old clothes to fit new ones.

The first thought is that highly sparse routed experts can act as the sponge to absorb new data. However this data wont get absorbed in the most compressed state. Lets combine the 2 shared experts into 1 to simplify. Then we should have some mechanism that takes the knowledge learned by the routed experts and compresses it into the 1 shared expert. One possibility is an aux loss that pulls the shared output towards the routed output. The goal here is that once the shared expert compresses and absorbs what the routed experts are doing, then it frees up space in the routed experts to learn fresh info without worrying about overwriting what they already know.

Think through the design space here carefully, and challenge and rework the initial spec I gave as makes sense. We may need to test in overtrained regime to see benefit here.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 178: MLP compression — move what the shared expert can express out of the routed experts** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`3f0a1199c8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/3f0a1199c8))

**Idea** (from the comment above): routed experts absorb new data, but not in a compressed form. If the shared expert takes over what it can express, the routed experts are freer to learn new things without overwriting old ones.

**Changes to the initial spec:**
- **Already one shared expert** (`num_shared_experts=1`, width 768), so no merge is needed.
- **The shared expert is the small side.** Per layer it has ~0.8M parameters against ~100M routed (~150M in the full-write layers 4–5). Only the common, low-rank part of the routed output can move into it, not facts. Growing it would densify d512, so it stays at 768.
- **"Pull shared toward routed" (`‖s − sg(r)‖²`) settles at `s = r`.** Both paths then hold the same function and nothing is freed. This batch tests two forms that do free the routed side (`y = s + r`, `sg` = stop-gradient):
  - **Transfer:** `λ‖s − sg(s + r)‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Its gradient moves only the shared expert, along the routed output. The shared expert is evaluated a second time on a stop-gradient input, so no gradient reaches the layers below. The LM loss then sheds the overshoot from the routed side. It stops when the routed output has nothing left the shared expert can express.
  - **Routed penalty:** `λ‖r‖² / sg(‖y‖²)`. Routed output is costly, so the LM gradient moves onto the shared expert whatever it can express. The penalty also reaches the layers below, but only in direction, because the routed input is RMS-normalized.
- **Measured first:** a detached width-768 shadow MLP per layer learns `sg(x) → sg(r)` with no effect on training. Its R² is how much of the routed output a shared-sized expert could absorb.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `shadow` | shadow probe only (all runs carry it) |
| `xfer01` | transfer, λ = 0.01 per layer |
| `xfer04` | transfer, λ = 0.04 per layer |
| `rpen01` | routed penalty, λ = 0.01 per layer |

**Early read** (`shadow`, step 572):

| layer | shadow R² | routed share ‖r‖²/‖y‖² | cos(s, r) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.69 | 0.49 | +0.33 |
| 1 | 0.52 | 0.74 | +0.27 |
| 2 | 0.44 | 0.71 | +0.22 |
| 3 | 0.55 | 0.60 | +0.27 |
| 4 | 0.35 | 0.71 | +0.23 |
| 5 | 0.43 | 0.67 | +0.20 |

- A shared-sized MLP reproduces 35–69% of the routed output, so there's plenty to compress.
- The routed side carries most of the MLP output.
- The two paths already partly duplicate each other: cos(s, r) is positive in every layer.

**Reads:** Paloma macro vs the candidate 11 equal-steps controls (2.9621 / 2.9669, rerun 2.9625; noise 0.0056); cos(s, r), routed share and shadow R² over training. Anything that clears noise gets seed 1, early-fact retention from the fact probe, and an overtrained check.

**Ops:**
- **Lost gradient fixed:** the AttnRes recompute backward dropped every gradient from per-layer stats, so a loss added there was silently ignored. It now passes the compress term's gradient through.
- **Sharded-autotuning deadlock:** new fusions deadlocked sharded XLA autotuning in the train step, because the per-process autotune caches disagree. Turning sharded autotuning off instead hung the first step, likely from mismatched collective order. `--fresh-autotune-cache` starts every process empty, so all miss alike.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; control = the two shadow-only runs, 2.9633 / 2.9631, mean 2.9632; candidate 11 controls 2.9621 / 2.9625)

| run | loss | Δ | routed share, late | cos(s, r), late |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `shadow` (control) | 2.9632 | — | 0.52–0.62 | +0.17 to +0.29 |
| transfer λ = 0.01 | 2.9634 | +0.0002 | 0.23–0.32 | +0.18 to +0.29 |
| transfer λ = 0.04 | 2.9700 | +0.0068 | 0.21–0.38 | +0.16 to +0.32 |
| transfer λ = 0.16 | 2.9745 | +0.0113 | 0.39–0.56 | +0.32 to +0.40 |
| gap `‖s − sg(r)‖²` λ = 0.04 | 2.9679 | +0.0047 | 0.47–0.58 | +0.47 to +0.63 |
| gap λ = 0.16 | 2.9711 | +0.0079 | 0.46–0.59 | +0.49 to +0.66 |
| routed penalty λ = 0.01 | 3.0078 | +0.0446 | 0.01–0.31 | 0.00 to +0.14 |
| routed penalty λ = 0.04 | 3.0070 | +0.0438 | 0.03–0.12 | +0.03 to +0.07 |

- **Closed at d512.** Moving routed work onto the shared expert never helps. Every form strong enough to change behavior costs loss.
- **The shadow probe does nothing to training** (2.9632 vs 2.9621 / 2.9625).
- **Transfer works mechanically but buys nothing.**
  - At λ = 0.01 the routed share halves and the shadow's R² drops ~45%, so the routed side keeps mostly what a shared-sized expert can't express. Loss is unchanged.
  - Stronger weights don't move more. They spend the shared expert's fixed-size MuonH updates chasing the routed output, and loss rises with λ.
- **The gap loss duplicates, as predicted.** cos(s, r) roughly doubles while the routed share barely moves, and loss rises.
- **The routed penalty is destructive even at λ = 0.01.** It shrinks the routed path in every layer, almost entirely in layer 4 (share 0.01). The routed bank does work the shared expert can't take over.
- **Reading:** in the 8-minute regime the routed bank isn't short of space, and the shared expert is already fully used. The capacity argument could still hold when overtrained, but nothing here points to a gain to carry over.
- **Ops: the sharded-autotuning deadlock is unsolved.** Programs with new fusions deadlock in compile about half the time on 8 processes. Every rank waits on the key-value exchange for results no rank publishes. Neither an empty per-process cache nor `xla_gpu_autotune_level=0` fixes it; level 0 instead hangs the first step, inside the lazy custom-kernel load. Resubmitting works, since runs that compile train normally.

comments.author: marin-belay-bot
comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5968183668)):

> Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):
>
> 1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
> 2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
> 3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
> 4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.
>
> Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:
>
> 1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
> 2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.
>
> These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

<!-- belay-intake:5968183668 -->

comments.author: marin-belay-bot
comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-5980816116)):

> Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).
>
> Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
> where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".
>
> Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
> where y = s + r
>
> Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.
>
> Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

<!-- belay-intake:5980816116 -->

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 180: scale-free MLP compression, plus new training diagnostics** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`4207f522d8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4207f522d8))

**Why:** RavnaBergsndot's intake comment (above) explains a likely flaw in batch 178's transfer loss.
- **The flaw:** the gradient of `‖s − sg(s + r)‖²` on the shared output is `−2r` however long `s` already is, so the loss rewards stretching `s` without bound.
- **It fits batch 179:** `ot100-xfer04` read 0.00 routed share in 5 of 6 layers at baseline loss, which looks like `s` growing large rather than `r` going silent.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `tn01` | `transfer_normed` (choice 2): `λ‖s/‖s‖ − sg(y/‖y‖)‖²` per token, λ = 0.01 |
| `tn04` | the same, λ = 0.04 |
| `xn2` | transfer λ = 0.04 + counter force `λ₁ (‖s‖² / sg‖y‖²)^{n/2}` (choice 1), λ₁ = 0.01, n = 2 |
| `xn4` | the same with n = 4, a softer cap |

**Comparison:** the shadow-only control from batch 178 (2.9632) and the plain transfer arms (λ = 0.01: 2.9634; λ = 0.04: 2.9700).

**Reads:**
- Paloma.
- Routed share and cos(s, r).
- New: the absolute per-token RMS of `s` and `r`, which separates a growing `s` from a silent `r`.

**New diagnostics** (the other intake suggestion):
- **Weights** (`--weight-diagnostics N`): every N steps, for every projection matrix, the stable rank `‖W‖_F²/‖W‖_2²` (mean and min over stacked or expert matrices) and the max/mean output-channel norm. Also each RMSNorm gain's distance from 1.
- **Layer outputs** (`--model-set layer_output_stats=true`): each layer's attention and MLP output max |x| vs RMS.
- **This batch:** the four runs log the output stats. The weight hook is in an 8-GPU smoke test after two sharding fixes for expert banks. Once it passes, a candidate 11 control with both diagnostics on follows.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; control: shadow-only runs from batch 178, 2.9632; noise ~0.0056)

| run | loss | Δ | routed share, late | cos(s, r), late | per-token RMS, s / r |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tn01` normalized, λ = 0.01 | 2.9648 | +0.0016 | 0.36–0.52 | +0.32 to +0.49 | 1.9–3.6 / 2.3–4.0 |
| `tn04` normalized, λ = 0.04 | 2.9679 | +0.0047 | 0.43–0.67 | +0.41 to +0.59 | 1.2–2.7 / 2.4–4.5 |
| `xn2` transfer + counter force, n = 2 | 2.9688 | +0.0056 | 0.29–0.43 | +0.32 to +0.47 | 2.7–6.2 / 2.7–6.7 |
| `xn4` transfer + counter force, n = 4 | 2.9697 | +0.0065 | 0.29–0.42 | +0.33 to +0.47 | 2.8–6.3 / 2.9–6.6 |
| plain transfer λ = 0.04 (batch 178) | 2.9700 | +0.0068 | 0.21–0.38 | +0.16 to +0.32 | not logged |

- **Both fixes work mechanically.** `s` no longer runs away: it stays the same size as `r` or smaller.
- **Neither helps the loss.** Both forms land within noise or worse.
- **With a bounded `s`, every form duplicates.** cos(s, r) rises to about +0.4 to +0.6, the same thing the gap loss did. The stretching flaw was real, but it isn't why compression loses at 1×.
- **Closing the direction at d512.** ClassicLarry's read above stands: no signs of life yet. A cleaner place to look for them is a toy task with a known answer.
  - In a side experiment on grokking `(a + b) mod 113` with a ReLU MLP, the generalizing circuit is already present at step 300, right after memorization. Keeping only each neuron's top-2 frequencies and refitting the output layer groks up to 16× sooner (step 800 vs 13,100).
  - Low-rank SVD truncation and norm-based pruning don't help there. Compression that works has to find the solution's own basis.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 181: learned output scalars and RMSNorm gain parameterizations** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`4b2fb2b8d6`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/4b2fb2b8d6))

**Diagnosis first.** Every run logs, every 100 steps, each RMSNorm gain's distance from 1 and each projection matrix's stable rank and max/mean output-channel norm. It also logs each layer's output max |x| vs RMS, and dumps every norm gain and output scalar at the end. The control dump shows what the default gains learn per module, which says which gain function fits.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `ctrl` | none (diagnostics only) |
| `ss_lin` | learned scalar on every attention and MLP output (`sublayer_scales`), linear, init 1 |
| `ss_sig2` | the same scalar as `2·sigmoid(w)`, init `w = 0`, so it modulates in (0, 2) |
| `g_exp` | every RMSNorm gain as `e^w`, init 0 |
| `g_sp` | `softplus(w)`, init `log(e − 1)`; gain LR ×1.6 |
| `g_sig2` | `2·sigmoid(w)`, init 0; gain LR ×2 |

**Why the functions could matter:**
- **Scale of an output.** AttnRes scores sources on RMS-normed copies but mixes the raw sources, so an output scalar sets that branch's weight in the mix, and the next RMSNorm removes only the overall scale. Batch 01 found learned output scalars neutral (MoE outputs grew to 1.2–2.1×), but that was a much earlier recipe.
- **Positivity and relative steps.** A linear gain moves additively and can cross 0. `e^w` keeps it positive and makes Adam's steps relative (the same fraction at any size), which suits gains spanning orders of magnitude. `softplus` is linear above about 1 and exponential near 0. `2·sigmoid` bounds it in (0, 2), and that bound is the test of whether large gains are needed.
- **Plain `sigmoid`:** I used `2·sigmoid` rather than a plain sigmoid, which can't start at 1 and can only shrink activations. If the control's gains never exceed 1, plain sigmoid becomes worth a run.

**LR.** Gains train with Adam, so a step moves the raw parameter by about lr, and the gain by `f'(w)` times that. At init `f'` is 1 for `exp`, 0.63 for `softplus` and 0.5 for `2·sigmoid`, so the gain LR multipliers (×1.6, ×2) give every arm the same initial step as linear. A ×0.5 / ×2 sweep follows on whichever helps.

**Ops:** the weight-diagnostics hook needed three fixes to run on 8 GPUs (expert-bank sharding twice, then gathering global scalars). Batch 181 waits on a 150-step smoke test that confirms the metrics land in wandb.


**What the default gains learn** (`ctrl`, Paloma 2.9644, within noise of the candidate 11 controls; [per-module plots](https://claude.ai/artifact/KcoMDyEcULNMFebyS5eTRQ))

| module | final gain | trend |
|---|---|---|
| `final_norm` | 1.2–7.6, mean 5.8 | still rising at the end (mean \|g − 1\| 2.1 / 3.5 / 4.5 / 4.8 at steps 500 / 1k / 2k / 2817) |
| MoE `latent_norm` | 1.5–2.1 in most layers (layer 5: 0.16–1.3) | still rising |
| `rms_attn`, `rms_mlp` pre-norms | 0.4–2.8 | mean \|g − 1\| 0.1–0.4, mostly settled |
| `o_norm`, `kv_latent_norm` | 0.44–1.6 | small moves |
| `embed_norm` / `embed2_norm` | 0.16–1.2 (mean 0.62) / 0.01–0.45 (mean 0.30) | shrink |

- **No gain goes negative.** A positive parameterization gives up nothing the model uses.
- **The scale is per module.** Gains span about 700× across modules but cluster tightly inside each one, so each norm acts mostly as one scale plus small per-channel adjustments.
- **The biggest gains were still moving at the end.** Under additive Adam steps a gain climbs about lr per step; `e^w` moves by the same fraction at any size. That makes `g_exp` the best-motivated arm.
- **`2·sigmoid` caps every gain at 2.** It clamps `final_norm` (which reaches about 6) and pins the MoE latent norms, so I expect `g_sig2` to lose. A plain sigmoid (cap 1) would be worse; only the embedding norms stay below 1.
- **`final_norm` likely works as a logit temperature** in front of the `lm_head` (soft cap 10). A learned output scalar there may be the cleaner lever.


**Results** (Paloma macro, seed 0; noise ~0.0056)

| run | loss | Δ vs `ctrl` | `final_norm` gain | MLA L3 latent gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ctrl` (linear gains) | 2.9644 | — | 1.17–7.56 | 1.81–2.11 |
| `ss_lin` (linear output scalars) | 2.9641 | −0.0003 | 1.25–7.64 | 1.49–1.87 |
| `ss_sig2` (`2·sigmoid` output scalars) | 2.9629 | −0.0015 | 1.40–7.65 | 1.53–1.98 |
| `g_exp` (`e^w` gains) | **2.9618** | **−0.0026** | 0.56–**15.0** | 1.87–2.39 |
| `g_sp` (softplus gains, LR ×1.6) | 2.9636 | −0.0008 | 0.86–9.12 | 1.67–2.25 |
| `g_sig2` (`2·sigmoid` gains, LR ×2) | **3.0793** | **+0.1149** | pinned at 1.99 | 1.73–1.92 |

- **The cap prediction holds.** `2·sigmoid` gains pin `final_norm` at the cap and cost 0.115, the largest change in the batch. The output norm needs a gain well above 2.
- **`e^w` gains come out best**, but within noise. The mechanism checks out: with relative steps `final_norm` climbs to 15 rather than about 7.6, and the MoE latent gains grow further.
- **Softplus is in between.** It is linear above about 1, so large gains climb only a little faster.
- **Output scalars are neutral** either way, matching batch 01. MLP outputs scale up (linear: 1.0–1.95×); `2·sigmoid` holds them lower (0.94–1.52×) and lands slightly ahead.
- **Next:**
  - `g_exp` seed 1;
  - the planned gain LR sweep on `g_exp` (×0.5 / ×2);
  - a targeted test of whether the gain is just a faster-growing output temperature: `e^w` on `final_norm` only, or a learned logit-temperature scalar on the head.
- **Ops:** 3 of the 6 runs deadlocked in sharded XLA autotuning on their first compile; resubmitting fixed each.

🤖 **Batch 182: sigmoid gains on the embedding norms; router on the latent** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`83560499bf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/83560499bf))

| run | change | loss | Δ vs batch 181 `ctrl` (2.9644) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sg_embed` | `sigmoid(w)` gains on `embed_norm` and `embed2_norm` (`sigmoid_gain_norms=embed,embed2`); init `w = 0`, a gain of 0.5 | 2.9634 | −0.0010 |
| `rol` | the router reads the RMS-normed MoE latent (`latent_dim` = 256) instead of the full MLP input (512) (`router_on_latent`); router weight `[256, E]` | 2.9651 | +0.0007 |
| `roe` | every router reads only the RMS-normed token embedding (`router_on_embed`): routing by learned token identity, one router per layer; a token picks the same experts in any context | **3.0063** | **+0.0419** |

- **`sg_embed` is neutral.** Linear `embed_norm` gains rarely pass 1 (1% of channels), so the cap barely binds. The sigmoid gains also moved slowly from their 0.5 start (0.25× step at init): `embed_norm` ended at a mean of about 0.43, below the control's 0.62. A 4× gain LR on these two norms would match linear's initial speed.
- **`rol` barely loses: +0.0007, within noise.** Routing on the 256-wide normed latent costs essentially nothing against the full 512-wide input at d512 (single seed). Step time is unchanged (179.2 vs 178.1 ms).
- **`roe` is the extreme:** context-free routing. Batch 30 found a fixed token-id hash neutral at layer 0 only.
- **Next, sigmoid on the embedding norms plus KDA `o_norm` and `kv_latent_norm`.** KDA layers 0–2 share one module, so a "KDA layer 0 only" version needs per-layer gain functions.

**A finding from the batch 181 control.** Layer 5's MoE latent has one channel acting as a hidden per-token gate.
- **The evidence:** that channel's column in `W_latent_down` grows to 2.37× the mean column norm between steps 400 and 800. Meanwhile its `latent_norm` gain falls from 0.87 to 0.13, while the other 255 rise to about 1.24. Layer 4 shows the same pattern, weaker (1.65×, gain 0.61). The latent-only layers stay at 1.05–1.09×.
- **The reading (inference):** a large `z_j*` inflates the latent's RMS and scales down the other channels for that token. With relu² experts, the MoE output shrinks quadratically. The near-zero gain resizes the outlier back to an ordinary input. Layers 4–5 write full width into the AttnRes history, and the router's renormalized combine can't set per-token output size, so this is the only lever. It is the pattern the GatedNorm paper describes, and what RavnaBergsndot's diagnostics comment asked us to look for.
- **The check:** an explicit per-token MoE output gate (`moe_out_gate`). If the outlier stops forming and loss holds, the reading is right.




**`roe` result:** routing on the token embedding alone costs +0.042, while routing on the 256-wide latent costs +0.0007. The router needs the token's context, not just its identity; given the context, a narrow input is enough.

**Why:** the combine weights are renormalized to a fixed per-token sum (2.5), so the router can't make the MoE output louder or quieter per token. One channel's `W_latent_down` column grows to 2.37× the mean, and its `latent_norm` gain falls to 0.16, so it inflates the RMS denominator (see the batch 182 comment).

- **Drop renorm:** `moe_drop_renorm` stays on. It rescales relative to each token's own pre-drop total, so it still works without a fixed sum.

| `ctrl` (sqrt-softplus, renorm to 2.5) | 2.9644 | — | 0.163 | 2.37 |
| `csr` (sqrt-softplus, no renorm) | 2.9646 | +0.0002 | **0.984** | **1.11** |
| `srw` (sigmoid, no renorm) | 2.9656 | +0.0012 | **0.94** | **1.13** |
| `mog` (renorm + per-token MoE output gate) | 2.9640 | −0.0004 | 0.234 | 2.07 |
| `lsum` (renorm, learnable per-layer sum) | 2.9644 | 0.0000 | 0.169 | 2.31 |

- **Without the renorm, the layer-5 outlier never forms.** Gains stay near 1 and no `W_latent_down` column stands out. The outlier was a workaround for the fixed per-token sum: the model built its own per-token output scale through the latent norm's denominator. A raw combine gives it that scale directly.
- **Loss doesn't move.** The workaround already delivered the same function, so this explains a mechanism rather than giving a win.
- **The explicit output gate only shrinks the outlier** (2.07×). It reads a fixed 12-channel slice of the input and also scales the shared expert, so it is a coarser stand-in.
- **Learned sums all rise above 2.5,** to 3.3–3.6 in layers 0–3 and 2.95 / 2.69 in layers 4 / 5. The MoE output wants to be louder overall, as the learned output scalars found. One scalar per layer can't provide a per-token scale, so the outlier stays.
- **Next:** with the outlier explained, `csr` is the cleaner design at equal loss. It frees the latent norm and `W_latent_down` from building a gate. A seed-1 pair (`csr` vs `ctrl`) would confirm the loss is the same before adopting it. A raw combine with a learnable scale (`csr` + `lsum`) would test whether a louder MoE output helps once the scale is per token.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batch 184: two weight sets for the MLA attention (previous step + current)** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`2ebb73734a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2ebb73734a))

**Idea** (ClassicLarry): keep the previous step's weights for a parameter group, and run half of each batch on them.
- **Implementation** (`dual_attn_prev`): each MLA attention module gets a frozen copy of the previous step's weights, refreshed after every update.
- **Batch split:** in training, odd batch rows run attention at those old weights and even rows at the current ones.
- **Gradient:** the old rows read `sg(θ_old) + (θ − sg(θ))`, so their gradient reaches the current weights. Each update then averages the gradient at both ends of the last step, about its midpoint.
- **Expected effect:** that damps directions that flip sign every step (period-2 bounce) and lags drifting directions by about half a step.
- **Evals** use the current weights only.

| run | loss | Δ vs batch 181 `ctrl` (2.9644) | step time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dual` | 2.9630 | −0.0014 | 193.0 ms (+8% vs 178.1) |

- **Neutral at equal steps** (within ~0.0056 noise).
- **A loss at fixed time.** The extra attention pass in the two MLA layers costs 8% step time, about +0.014.
- **Not pursued further** unless a seed-1 pair shows the equal-steps gain is real and the second pass can be made much cheaper.

comments.body:
🤖 **Speed track: PR #9708, FP8, and a fresh profile of candidate 11** (d512, 8×H100, steps 300–305; profiled step 233 ms vs 178 ms unprofiled)

**Where the step goes** (GPU 0, ms per profiled step):

| | ms/step | share |
|---|---|---|
| compute stream busy | 152 | 65% |
| compute stream idle | **81** | 35% |
| NCCL, on its own stream (SendRecv 29, AllGather 5, ReduceScatter 3) | 41 | overlapped or exposed |
| GEMMs (excluding FA4) | ~42 | |
| memory-bound XLA fusions (reduce 17, select 9, scatter 5, convert 6, add 7, ...) | ~45 | |
| KDA kernels | ~15 | |
| short conv | ~3 | |

- **Exposed communication is the largest lever.** Net of profiler overhead, roughly 26 ms of a real 178 ms step has no compute running, mostly waiting on the expert-parallel SendRecv all-to-all. At about 0.0017 per 1% of step time, hiding it all is worth up to about −0.02 at fixed time.
- **Memory-bound fusions cost as much as every GEMM together.** Many are probably MoE dispatch/combine; attributing them to source ops comes next.

**PR #9708** (hero MFU 28.2% → 31.1%): most of its gains are in ragged-transport code (transport buffers, token-major scatter, expert-side routing-weight gradient, dispatch overlap). fast_track runs `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all`, so those don't apply.
- **What does apply:** the streaming Triton short convolution. fast_track's KDA calls `short_conv`. I added `sconv_impl=triton_gpu` on a test branch with the PR's kernel ([`5100adbf80`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5100adbf80)).
- **Expected size:** about 3 ms of short-conv kernels, so 1–2 ms at best. A same-code A/B (`lc1-pr-pallas` vs `lc1-pr-triton`, 2817 steps with Paloma) is running.
- **Router top-k:** the PR's Triton top-k (+0.53% on hero) would need wiring into fast_track's own router top-k; it's a later step.

**FP8:** only FP8 dispatch has been tried here (batch 79: no time saved; the quantize/dequantize ate the gain). FP8 GEMMs never have been.
- **The modded-nanogpt scheme:** static scales throughout, so no per-step amax. The input scale comes from the RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)`. e4m3 forward and e5m2 gradients with a static grad scale; weights quantized once per optimizer step into both layouts. It covers the `lm_head`, both MLP GEMMs and the QKV projection.
- **Our GEMMs are about 42 ms per profiled step,** so FP8 on most of them is worth an estimated 10–15 ms, −0.010 to −0.015 at fixed time. The static-scale design matters here because our GEMMs are small (hidden 512).
- **Plan:** attention and shared-expert projections plus the `lm_head` first, then per-expert scales for the routed GEMMs.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 188–189: ragged baseline, and an FP8 protocol that holds as width grows** ([`d34ed93f76`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d34ed93f76), [`274839618f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/274839618f))

**Batch 188: current ragged path on candidate 11** (d512, 2817 equal steps, one-shot ragged transport, drop renorm off)

| run | loss | step ms | Δ loss vs `ctrl` 2.9644 | step time vs pooled wave (176.5 ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rag105` (capacity 1.05) | 2.9633 | 193.6 | −0.0011 | +9.7% |
| `rag115` (capacity 1.15) | 2.9620 | 203.1 | −0.0024 | +15% |

- Ragged still costs about 10% at d512, which is about +0.017 at fixed time, against −0.001 to −0.002 per step.
- The #9708 ragged commits are being ported onto lc1, keeping ungated ReLU², the fused relu² kernel and FP8 dispatch. Two of three are done. A ported-ragged vs pooled-wave A/B comes next.

**FP8: microbenchmarks on one GB200** (16k tokens, fwd+bwd of one linear `[16k, d] × [d, n]`)

| d (FFN up, n = 4d) | bf16 GEMMs | per-tensor FP8 GEMMs | MXFP8 GEMMs | JAX MXFP8 linear, end to end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512–1024 | launch-bound | no gain | no gain | 0.4–0.6× bf16 |
| 2048 | 2.1 PF | 4.2 PF | 2.7 PF | 0.78× |
| 4096 | 2.3 PF | 4.5 PF | 3.1 PF | 1.02× |
| 6144 | 2.3 PF | 4.6 PF | 3.0 PF | 1.20× |

- **In the training layouts, block-scaled MXFP8 runs as fast as per-tensor FP8.** In the d=6144 profile, cuBLAS's 1×32 block-scaled kernels (`Avec32UE8M0_Bvec32UE8M0`) take 1.44–1.49 ms per GEMM, against 1.43 ms for per-tensor FP8 and 2.7 ms for bf16. Fine-grained scaling itself costs nothing.
- **The overhead is all in quantization.** `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` re-quantizes both operands for every GEMM. That is six bf16 reads, separate amax / convert / transpose fusions, about 2.1 ms at d=6144 against 4.4 ms of GEMMs. A fused cast kernel would read x, w and g once and write row- and column-wise e4m3 plus e8m0 scales. By bandwidth that is about 0.4 ms, so about 1.9× bf16 at d=6144.
- **Below d≈2048 FP8 can't pay.** The GEMMs are too small to be tensor-core bound. On the d512 H100 rung, FP8 is a numerics question, not a speed lever.
- **Width dependence of the error:** relative error is 3.8% for MXFP8 (e4m3 everywhere) and 5.9% for per-tensor with e5m2 gradients. It is flat from d=512 to 6144 on Gaussian inputs, and four 100× outlier channels don't change it.

**Protocol chosen: MXFP8, just-in-time scales.** Each 32-element block along each GEMM's contraction axis gets a power-of-two (e8m0) scale from its own amax. e4m3 is used everywhere, gradients included. The router, embeddings, lm head, norms, attention core and optimizer stay high precision.
- **Why not modded-nanogpt-style fixed scales:** they are tuned to one width and one activation distribution. The RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)` grows with d, and the gradient scale drifts with depth, LR and training phase.
- **Why not per-tensor current scaling:** a single outlier channel sets the scale for the whole tensor. Massive activations grow with width and training.
- **With 1×32 blocks, an outlier only coarsens its own block,** and no scale state depends on width, step or calibration. It is also the native Blackwell format (same GEMM speed, as above).

**Batch 189: does MXFP8 hold as width grows?** Simulated MXFP8 (`fp8_recipe=mxfp8_sim`) rounds every operand of every forward, dgrad and wgrad GEMM to exact e4m3 with the recipe's block scales; the GEMMs still run in bf16, so this measures numerics only. It covers the attention/KDA projections, the fused latent/shared projection (router columns excluded), the latent up-projection, the shared expert and the routed experts. Candidate 11 is scaled to each width; steps are the baseline counts.

| run | width | steps | loss | Δ vs bf16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mx512` / `mx512-s1` | d512 | 2817 | ⏳ | vs `ctrl` 2.9644 / 2.9667 |
| `bf768` / `mx768` | d768 | 6929 | ⏳ | ⏳ |
| `bf1024` / `mx1024` | d1024 | 9268 | ⏳ | ⏳ |

- **Pass criterion:** Δ within seed noise (0.0056) at every width, and not growing with d.
- If it passes, next is the real kernel path on GB200: a fused MXFP8 cast plus a `custom_vjp` linear over `jax.nn.scaled_matmul`, starting with the hero-width projections and experts.

| probe | step ms |

- **AttnRes backward pads:** each gate read of a block's precomputed `[G, B, S]` logits, and of its softmax weights, became a pad back to full size in the backward, 290 of them in the HLO.

**More, narrower KDA heads; d768; a free KDA kernel speedup** ([`acec39b84f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/acec39b84f))

| candidate 12, `block_v` 32 | 190.9 |
| candidate 12, `block_v` 64 | 190.7 |
| 4 × (64 × 256), `block_v` 64 | **190.1 (no cost)** |
| 8 × (64 × 128), `block_v` 64 | 195.2 (+2.3%) |
| 16 × (64 × 64), `block_v` 64 | 207.4 (+8.6%) |

- **The 4 × (64 × 256) shape is now free.** Its −0.0067 per-step gain should hold at fixed time. Two seeds at 2817 steps with `block_v=64` and a same-run control are running to confirm.
  - 8 heads is now about −0.006 at fixed time and is running at its fixed-time step count (2755).
  - 16 heads is still held back by the intra-chunk prep kernels (4.1 vs 2.2 ms), whose per-program work shrinks with the head width. Packing several heads per prep program is the next kernel lever, worth up to about −0.015 per step if it reached 4-head speed.

---

**df14–df17 results** (cw-us-east-02a; controls 2.9543 / 2.9584 at 2817 steps, about 190 ms)

| run | change | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hgate` | MLA H-gate, rank 32 | 2817 | 2.9511 | 2.9563 | −0.0027 | 191.5 |
| `kdahg` | the same content gate on the KDA output gate ([`393d68cfa8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/393d68cfa8)) | 2817 | 2.9515 | 2.9551 | −0.0031 | 192.2 |
| `kv-hg` | KDA 64 × 256 + MLA H-gate | 2817 | 2.9466 | 2.9480 | −0.0090 | 195.9 |
| `h8` | **8 KDA heads × (64 × 128)** | 2817 | **2.9439** | **2.9485** | **−0.0102** | 198.0 |
| `h8-ft` | the same at fixed time | 2704 | 2.9527 | 2.9540 | −0.0030 | 198.8 |
| `kv-ft` | 4 KDA heads × (64 × 256) at fixed time | 2766 | 2.9519 | 2.9532 | −0.0038 | 194.4 |

- **Content-conditioned output gates replicate in both mixers.**
  - The gate logits gain a rank-32 term read from what the head retrieved: −0.0027 on MLA and −0.0031 on KDA, both seeds negative.
  - Each costs about 1% step time, so each nets about −0.001 at fixed time.
- **8 KDA heads × (64 × 128) is the best per-step result:** −0.0102 on two seeds.
  - It has the same total state and the same q/k and v/o widths as 4 × (64 × 256). The extra gain comes from more independent states, each with its own β and decays.
  - Its kernel cost (+4.4%) leaves it tied with 4 × (64 × 256) at fixed time (−0.0030 vs −0.0038). If the 8-head kernel ran at the 4-head cost, it would be the better shape.
- **Running:**
  - All three stacked (64 × 256 + MLA and KDA content gates), two seeds.
  - 16 KDA heads × (64 × 64).
  - The d768 pair for 64 × 256.

---

**Why 32 × 512 is slow, and HyGA gates** (cw-us-east-02a)

KDA fused forward+backward on one H100, at the per-GPU d512 shape (B = 16, S = 4096, 4 heads; erase gate, Pallas state grads):

| state | chunk 32 | chunk 16 |
|---|---|---|
| 128 × 128 (candidate 12) | 4.5 ms | — |
| 64 × 256 | 4.7 ms | 5.5 ms |
| 32 × 256 | 6.0 ms | — |
| 64 × 512 | 12.1 ms | 9.5 ms |
| 32 × 512 | 31.9 ms | 7.8 ms |

- **The forward is fine at every shape:** 2.2 ms at 32 × 512 vs 1.6 ms at 64 × 256.
- **The backward degrades** as values widen past 256 (about 2.6×) and as keys narrow to 32 (about 1.3×), and the two compound.
  - The prep backward holds whole `C × d_v` fp32 value tiles per chunk, which very likely spills at `d_v` = 512.
  - Chunk 16 halves those tiles and recovers most of the loss.
- **Even so, 32 × 512 costs about +3 ms per KDA layer over 64 × 256** (+8% step), which outweighs its extra −0.004 per step at fixed time.
  - A fully tuned kernel would at best tie 64 × 256 at fixed time, so I'm not spending kernel work on it.
  - **64 × 256 at chunk 32 is the shape to keep.**

**HyGA gates on MLA** ([arXiv 2608.11805](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11805), [`2629cbe0d4`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2629cbe0d4); seed 0, control 2.9543)

| run | gate | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df12-hgate` | H-gate: `SiLU(H_i W_d) W_u` (rank 32) added to the output gate's logits, read from the head's own attention output | 2.9511 | −0.0032 | 191.8 |
| `df12-cgate` | C-gate: per-head `2σ((H W_c)_i)` from all heads' outputs | 2.9540 | −0.0003 | 192.5 |
| `df12-hyga` | both | 2.9534 | −0.0009 | 191.6 |

- Our existing output gates read `x`. HyGA's **H-gate reads the attention output itself** (what the head retrieved), which no earlier gate variant did.
- −0.0032 is within one-seed noise. Seed 1 is running, along with the stack on `k64v256` (two seeds).
- **Also running:** 8 KDA heads × (64 × 128). It has the same total state and the same q/k and v/o widths as 4 × (64 × 256), so it separates head count from per-head value width. The d768 pair (candidate 12 vs `k64v256`, 6929 steps) is on cw-rno2a.

---

**df9 / df10 results: the KDA state shape** (cw-us-east-02a; controls 2.9543 / 2.9584 at 2817 steps, about 190 ms)

| run | state (key × value) | steps | seed 0 | seed 1 | mean Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k64v256`, equal steps | 64 × 256 | 2817 | 2.9500 | 2.9493 | −0.0067 | 193.3 |
| **`k64v256`, fixed time** | 64 × 256 | 2766 | **2.9519** | **2.9532** | **−0.0038** | 194.4 |
| `k32v512`, equal steps | 32 × 512 | 2817 | 2.9446 | 2.9467 | **−0.0107** | 270 (+42%) |
| `k128v256` (2× state, diagnostic) | 128 × 256 | 2817 | 2.9473 | — | −0.0070 | 206.4 (+8.7%) |

- **`k64v256` wins at fixed time on both seeds: −0.0024 / −0.0052.**
  - It changes only the KDA layers' key/value widths (`--model-set kda_key_dim=64 --model-set kda_value_dim=256`).
  - The state size is unchanged. The q/k projections halve and the v/o projections double.
- **Value width is what pays.** Narrowing the keys further to widen the values (32 × 512) gains −0.0107 per step, on both seeds. Doubling the state at 256-wide values (`k128v256`) gains less than 32 × 512 does at the original state size.
- **32 × 512 is held back only by speed.** The fused KDA kernels run +42% slower at that shape. A kernel microbenchmark across shapes is running to find which pass is slow; if it's a tiling problem, 32 × 512 could be worth about −0.008 at fixed time.

**Kalman write strength: parked.**
- Every attempt hit a NaN loss between steps 4 and 31, on both seeds and with either optimizer for the projection.
- A debug run shows why: at step 10 the gradient norm of KDA layer 2's `kalman_b` was **5e18**, with every other gradient below 0.4. Its square overflows fp32 in the global-norm clip, and the loss turns NaN a few steps later.
- The scan itself is not the source. On CPU at 4096 tokens its forward and gradients are finite and O(1) for decays 0.5–0.999 and extreme `ω`/`r`.
- So the blow-up arrives through the kernel's `β` cotangent, on tokens where the Kalman β departs from the sigmoid's narrow range. Finding them needs kernel-level instrumentation; I'm not chasing that further now.

---

**df6–df8 results** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps; controls 2.9543 (seed 0) / 2.9584 (seed 1), about 190 ms)

| run | change | seed 0 | seed 1 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df6-fts` | per-token logit temperature `2σ(ĥ·w)` on the lm_head input | 2.9554 (+0.0011) | 2.9577 (−0.0007) | 192.5 |
| `k64v256` (df5 / df7) | KDA state 64 × 256, 4 heads | **2.9500 (−0.0043)** | **2.9493 (−0.0091)** | 193.3 (+1.7%) |
| `df7-k32v512` | KDA state 32 × 512 | 2.9446 (−0.0097) | — | 268.7 (+41%) |
| `df8-h2k128v256` | 2 KDA heads × (128 × 256), same total state | 2.9640 (+0.0097) | — | 187.7 |
| `df8-h2k64v512` | 2 KDA heads × (64 × 512), half the state | 2.9593 (+0.0050) | — | 194.3 |

- **KDA keys 64 × values 256 replicates: −0.0067 mean over two seeds at equal steps.** At +1.7% step time that nets about −0.004 at fixed time.
  - **Wider still (32 × 512) keeps gaining** (−0.0097), but the KDA kernels run far slower at `d_k` = 32. A kernel tile tuned for 32-wide keys might recover this.
  - **The heads matter too:** 2 wider heads at the same total state lose (+0.010 / +0.005).
  - The best shape so far is 4 heads, each with a narrow key address and a wide value.
- **The per-token output temperature is neutral** (mean +0.0002), as the removed final GatedNorm was in batch 10. Closed.
- **df9 (running):**
  - `k64v256` at fixed time: 2766 steps = 2817 × 189.8 / 193.3, two seeds.
  - `k128v256`: values 256 with keys left at 128. This doubles the state; it's a diagnostic of state size vs value width, not a candidate.
  - **Kalman write strength** (`kda_kalman_beta`, [arXiv 2609.07816](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07816), [`9ac96e5826`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9ac96e5826)), two seeds.
    - Each KDA head tracks a scalar memory uncertainty, `b̂ₜ = aₜ bₜ₋₁ + ωₜ` with `bₜ = rₜ b̂ₜ / (rₜ + b̂ₜ)`, and writes with `βₜ = b̂ₜ / (rₜ + b̂ₜ)` in place of `σ(x W_β)`.
    - So a head writes hard while its memory is uncertain and softly once it has absorbed evidence.
    - `ω` and `r` are per-token softplus projections. The recursion is a Möbius map, run as one associative scan of 2 × 2 matrices before the KDA kernel.

---

**df5 results: KDA state shape at fixed size** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps; controls `df1-ctrl` 2.9543 (seed 0, 189.8 ms) and `df4-ctrl-s1` 2.9584 (seed 1, 190.4 ms))

| run | per-head state (key × value) | Paloma | Δ vs seed 0 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k64v256` | 64 × 256 | **2.9500** | **−0.0043** | 193.1 (+1.7%) |
| `k256v64` | 256 × 64 | 2.9645 | +0.0102 | 227.9 (+20%) |

- **Wider values with narrower keys help, and the reverse hurts.**
  - This matches batch 203's MLA finding, where loss tracked value capacity.
  - The KDA state reads back 256-wide values per head from 64-dim key addresses, with the state size unchanged.
- **Cost:** the v/o projections double (n·256 wide) while q/k halve, so +1.7% step time. That nets about −0.0014 at fixed time, inside noise for one seed.
- **Running (df7):**
  - `k64v256` seed 1.
  - `k32v512`: the same state with even wider values.
  - `k96v192`: a milder reshape (state +12%).

---

**df2 / df3 results** (cw-rno2a, 2817 steps, seed 0; control `df2-ctrl` 2.9542 at 189.7 ms)

| run | change | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `df2-g12n6l01` | GDLA 6 × (1 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9543 | +0.0001 | 207.1 |
| `df2-g9n3l01` | GDLA 3 × (2 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9539 | −0.0003 | 199.1 |
| `df2-g8n2l01` | GDLA 2 × (3 + 1), λ starts at 0.1 | 2.9603 | +0.0061 | 194.9 |
| `df3-h12x64` | MLA 12 heads × 64 | 2.9557 | +0.0015 | 302.1 |
| `df3-h12x64q` | 12 × 64, `qk_mult` × √2 | 2.9547 | +0.0005 | 302.8 |
| `df3-h8x96` | 8 × 96 | 2.9540 | −0.0002 | 257.6 |

- **The low λ start removes batch 203's small penalty** (`g9n3`: +0.0019 → −0.0003), but there's still no gain. With 2 value heads (`g8n2`) it still loses.
- **Differential attention is closed on this model.** Every variant lands between neutral and worse:
  - Motif's GDLA inside the head budget, plus three larger head counts.
  - DIFF-style pairs.
  - A free mean-value noise map.
  - Two λ starts.
- **Likely reason:** the MLA layers already have the tools DIFF supplies.
  - The ×2-sigmoid output gate can switch a head's read off per token, which is the gated-attention fix for attention sinks.
  - XSA removes the self-value component, and q/k norms with a learned temperature keep maps sharp.
  - λ always collapses early, i.e. at first the model pushes the subtraction out of the way.
- **More, narrower heads at equal FLOPs don't help at equal steps either,** and FA4 runs 64- and 96-dim heads far slower here (+59% / +36% step).
  - So the 4 → 6 head gain was capacity, not head count.
  - Closed.

---

**Follow-ups running** (d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0)

- **df2 (rno2a, own control `df2-ctrl`): GDLA with λ starting at 0.1** (`mla_diff_lambda_init=0.1`, a learned per-head bias) on `g12n6`, `g9n3` and `g8n2`. λ dropped from 0.5 to about 0.1 early in every batch 203 and df1 run.
- **df3 (rno2a): more, narrower MLA heads at equal attention FLOPs** (`mla_head_dim`, [`911452ce68`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/911452ce68)).
  - *Source:* batch 203 shows the global layers' loss tracking their number of value heads, and 4 → 6 heads gave −0.007 (batch 192).
  - The arms trade head width for head count at the same q/k/v/o parameters and attention FLOPs:
    - `h12x64`: 12 × 64 instead of 6 × 128.
    - `h12x64q`: the same with `qk_mult` × √2. Halving the head dim shrinks the normalized q·k/√d logits by √2.
    - `h8x96`: 8 × 96.
  - The KV latent stays at 512.
- **df5 (cw-us-east-02a; controls `df1-ctrl` and `df4-ctrl-s1`): the KDA state's shape at fixed size** (`kda_key_dim` / `kda_value_dim`, [`9abaa83612`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/9abaa83612)).
  - Each KDA head's 128 × 128 delta-rule state is reshaped to 64 × 256 (wider values, as Gated DeltaNet's `expand_v`) or 256 × 64 (wider keys).
  - State size per head is unchanged. The q/k vs v/o projections trade width.

---

**Batch df1 results** (cw-us-east-02a, 2817 steps, seed 0; control `df1-ctrl` 2.9543 at 189.8 ms)

| run | noise map | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mu` | uniform prefix mean | 2.9554 | +0.0011 | 194.3 |
| `md16` | decayed mean, half-life 16 at init | 2.9565 | +0.0022 | 195.3 |
| `md64` | half-life 64 | 2.9564 | +0.0021 | 194.7 |
| `md256` | half-life 256 | 2.9554 | +0.0011 | 195.0 |

- **No gain anywhere, and the scan costs about 2.5% of step time.**
- **λ follows the GDLA pattern:** it drops from 0.5 to 0.03–0.16 in the first fifth of training, then settles at about 0.21 (layer 3) and 0.15 (layer 5).
- **The learned decays split by head:**
  - Some heads go to a half-life of about 2.5 tokens, i.e. subtracting the last couple of values.
  - Others go to thousands of tokens, i.e. the uniform mean.
  - The model uses a small common-mode subtraction, but it buys no loss.
- **Closed.** The λ-init question is tested on GDLA in df2.

---

**Batch 203 results** (Paloma macro loss, 2817 steps, seed 0, cw-rno2a. Candidate 12 controls on rno2a: 2.9529 (`b201-binit1`) / 2.9539 (`b202-ctrl`), mean 2.9534, about 194 ms per step with hyperball logging on.)

| run | signal + noise heads | value heads | Paloma | Δ vs 2.9534 | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `g6n1eg` | 5 + 1 | 1 | 2.9697 | **+0.0163** | 190.6 |
| `g6n2eg` | 2 × (2 + 1) | 2 | 2.9625 | +0.0091 | 189.1 |
| `g8n2eg` | 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | 2.9577 | +0.0043 | 196.9 |
| `g8n2` (per-head gate) | 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | 2.9590 | +0.0056 | 193.0 |
| `g9n3eg` | 3 × (2 + 1) | 3 | 2.9553 | +0.0019 | 199.3 |
| `g12n6eg` | 6 × (1 + 1) | 6 | 2.9527 | −0.0007 | 207.1 (+7%) |
| `eg` (elementwise gate, no differential) | 6 | 6 | 2.9545 | +0.0011 | 192.0 |

**Reading.**
- **The loss tracks the number of value heads, not the subtraction.** 1 value head: +0.016. 2: +0.004 to +0.009. 3: +0.002. 6: 0.
  - Inside the head budget, GDLA costs the global layers their value capacity. That costs far more than the noise cancellation returns.
  - With values intact (`g12n6eg`, DIFF-style pairs), the subtraction is neutral (−0.0007) and the extra heads cost +7% step time.
- **The elementwise output gate alone is neutral** (+0.0011), as in batch 163.
- **What λ learned** (mean over tokens and heads, at 0 / 20 / 40 / 60 / 80 / 100% of training):

  | run | layer 3 | layer 5 |
  |---|---|---|
  | `g12n6eg` | 0.50 → 0.09 → 0.35 → 0.40 → 0.44 → 0.45 | 0.50 → 0.12 → 0.12 → 0.17 → 0.21 → 0.24 |
  | `g9n3eg` | 0.50 → 0.15 → 0.28 → 0.33 → 0.37 → 0.39 | 0.50 → 0.12 → 0.14 → 0.17 → 0.21 → 0.25 |
  | `g6n1eg` | 0.50 → 0.22 → 0.31 → 0.37 → 0.40 → 0.41 | 0.50 → 0.26 → 0.19 → 0.21 → 0.25 → 0.28 |

  - The noise read is as large as the signal read: RMS ratio 0.93 at layer 3 and 1.00 at layer 5 in `g12n6eg`.
  - So the model does use the subtraction late in training. But it first throws λ down from 0.5 to about 0.1: the start is too strong.
- **Next (df2):** a learned λ bias starting at 0.1 (`mla_diff_lambda_init=0.1`) on `g12n6`, `g9n3` and `g8n2`, against a fresh control.
- To pay at fixed time, `g12n6` needs about −0.012 at equal steps (+7% step time).

---


Note: another agent is also running a batch 203 (`badam*`). My differential-attention batches from here on use the `lc1-df<N>-` prefix.

**Why the batch 163 version lost.**
- Batch 163 got −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps but cost +6.6% step time.
- It added its noise maps on top of the signal heads, as a second full attention call.
- It also tiled each shared noise map out to all `g` heads of its group, so each map was computed `g` times.
- Motif 3's GDLA ([arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119)) does neither:
  - The noise heads come out of the head budget: 80 query heads = 64 signal + 16 noise.
  - Each group's signal and noise heads share one KV head, and only the query differs.
  - Its attention kernel therefore runs no extra heads.

**Batch 203: GDLA inside the head budget** (`mla_gdla_noise_heads=m`, MLA layers 3 and 5)
- The `N` query heads form `m` groups of `g` signal heads plus 1 noise head, and run in one kernel call.
- Each group shares one value head, so `w_uv` and the value embeds have `m` heads. Keys stay per head, since MLA up-projections are cheap.
- The output is `D = H_signal − λ·H_noise(group)`, with `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per signal head and token (zero-init, so 0.5).
- Only the signal heads reach `w_o`.

| run | heads (signal + noise) | value heads | output gate | attention cost vs candidate 12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `g6n2eg` | 6 = 2 × (2 + 1) | 2 | elementwise (Motif) | same |
| `g6n1eg` | 6 = 5 + 1 | 1 | elementwise | same |
| `g8n2eg` | 8 = 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | elementwise | +2 heads |
| `g9n3eg` | 9 = 3 × (2 + 1) | 3 | elementwise | +3 heads |
| `g12n6eg` | 12 = 6 × (1 + 1), i.e. DIFF pairs | 6 (no value loss) | elementwise | ×2 |
| `g8n2` | 8 = 2 × (3 + 1) | 2 | per head (ours) | +2 heads |
| `eg` | 6, no differential | 6 | elementwise | control for the gate |

The `g6` arms test whether the noise subtraction is worth giving up signal heads and value heads at no extra cost. `g12n6eg` tests whether it helps when nothing else is taken away.

**Batch df1: differential attention with a free noise map** (original idea; on cw-us-east-02a with its own control)
- *Source:* DIFF's noise map is meant to cancel common-mode attention, the broad mass a softmax spreads over irrelevant context. The cheapest estimate of that common mode is a fixed average of the values, so no second softmax map is needed.
- *Mechanism:* `D = softmax(qkᵀ)v − λ·mean_{j≤t}(v_j)` per head, within documents, with the same token-dependent sigmoid `λ`. Cost is one segment-reset scan, with no extra kernel call.
- *Variants:*
  - `uniform`: the plain prefix mean.
  - `decay`: an exponentially decayed mean with a learned per-head decay, half-life 16 / 64 / 256 at init. This makes the noise map a local/recent baseline.
- *Logged:* `knob_mean_noise_lambda_mean` and the learned half-lives per layer.

| run | noise map |
|---|---|
| `df1-ctrl` | none (cw-us-east-02a control) |
| `df1-mu` | uniform prefix mean |
| `df1-md16` / `md64` / `md256` | decayed mean, initial half-life 16 / 64 / 256 |

Results will be edited in here.

comments.body:
🤖 **Batches 202–205: hyperball step size, `w_beta` on Adam, Adam warmup, cheap MTP** (d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0, cw-rno2a; [`587e7e2cbe`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/587e7e2cbe), [`1df62e45f0`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/1df62e45f0), [`ac5560b321`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/ac5560b321), [`d642ff8db7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d642ff8db7))

**Base changes**
- **`w_beta` init back to ×1** (`init_std_mult_beta=1`): batch 201 gave −0.0010 (noise), and ×1 is simpler. `w_g` stays at ×2. → `base14`.
- **`w_beta` on plain Adam at 1× the Adam LR** (`kda_beta_group=adam`): 2.9540, against base14's 2.9529 / 2.9539. → **`base15`** (control `lc1-b205-ctrl`: 2.9521).
  - Adam LR sweep on `w_beta`: 0.1× 2.9538, 0.3× 2.9538, 1× 2.9540, 3× 2.9526. It doesn't care about its LR.

**Batch 202/204: hyperball with fixed norms but free step size** (`muonh_step`; base14 + hyperball logging, control 2.9539)

| mode | run | Paloma | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| spectral, Muon's own step size (`lr·α·√max(1, fan_out/fan_in)·d`) | α 0.25 / 0.5 / 1 | 2.9705 / 2.9684 / 3.0080 | +0.017 / +0.015 / +0.054 |
| grad, step ∝ smoothed gradient norm over its early mean | reference over the first 100 / 500 steps | 2.9913 / 2.9607 | +0.037 / +0.0068 |

- **Spectral:** at α 0.5 the relative step per matrix is `w_q` 1.0×, `w_o` 0.85×, `w_g` 0.51× (its ×2 init) and routed experts 1.8×.
- **Grad:** expert gradients grow over training while attention gradients shrink. The step multiplier ends at 2.3× for routed `w_up` and 0.4× for `w_q` and `w_o`.
  - The first grad version keyed on the momentum norm, which drops 10–70× at the Bi-Maxwell rail switch around step 1000, so that version (+0.12) was a bug.
- **MuonH's equal relative step for every matrix beats both alternatives.** Closed.

**Batch 203: longer Adam warmup with a higher Adam peak** (base14; today's Adam warmup is 1% = 28 steps at peak 0.00495, which averages 2.9534)

| Adam warmup | peak ×1 | ×1.5 | ×2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.5% | 2.9568 | 2.9527 | 2.9569 |
| 10% | 2.9586 | 2.9575 | 2.9613 |

A longer warmup hurts at the same peak, and a higher peak only wins back what it costs. Nothing to adopt.

**Batch 205: cheap MTP** (`future_aux`; base15, control 2.9521 at 190.9 ms)

| head | weight | Paloma | Δ | step ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16k-bucket hash of t+2 | 0.05 | 2.9557 | +0.0036 | 205.9 |
| hash of the (t+1, t+2) bigram | 0.05 | 2.9595 | +0.0074 | 204.6 |
| hash of the (t+1…t+3) trigram | 0.05 | 2.9561 | +0.0040 | 203.2 |
| t+2 hash through a 128-wide bottleneck | 0.05 | 2.9539 | +0.0018 | 198.0 |
| cosine regression on the mean embedding of t+2, t+3 | 0.05 | 2.9532 | +0.0011 | 190.2 |
| bigram hash, decaying to 0 at mid-run | 0.1 | 2.9546 | +0.0025 | 203.7 |
| bigram hash, decaying to 0 at the end | 0.05 | 2.9528 | +0.0007 | 203.6 |

- **Every future-prediction objective costs main-loss quality at d512, at 1× tokens.** The more of the future it targets, the more it costs. Decaying the weight to 0 gets back to neutral, but it doesn't turn positive.
- **The 16k-bucket hash heads aren't cheap:** +7% step time from the fused CE and AdamH on a 512×16k head. The embedding regression is free.
- **This matches both full-MTP attempts (batches 18, 163).** At this scale and token count, MTP takes capacity rather than adding signal. Closed at d512. It would only be worth retrying where the model has spare capacity: at larger rungs, or in the overtrained regime.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Partial key offset study: what the shifted half of the MLA heads learns** (d512 current best / candidate 12, EMA weights of `lc1-b234-attn-distance`, 2.9528)

With `mla_key_offset`, each MLA head's first 64 key channels come from the previous token (j−1); channels 64–127 come from the current token. I looked at what that split learns: the query/key directions of each head, then a probe of where the heads attend.

**Method**
- **Directions in the attention input x:** the query direction is the `W_q` column. The key direction is backed out through the latent: `W_dkv · diag(latent norm gain) · W_uk`, with the latent RMSNorm linearized.
- **The 128 per-channel pairs aren't unique:** any rotation of a head's channels gives the same scores. So each head is also analyzed through the SVD of its query–key product `B = W_q W_kᵀ`, which gives canonical (query direction, key direction, strength) pairs. The raw-channel and canonical numbers agree closely.

**1. The shifted half is an induction lookup, built into the weights**

Mean query/key cosine on the shifted half (channels 0–63), per head:

| head | layer 3 | layer 5 |
|---|---|---|
| H0 | 0.61 | 0.90 |
| H1 | 0.87 | 0.70 |
| H2 | 0.41 | 0.85 |
| H3 | 0.80 | 0.85 |
| H4 | 0.85 | 0.45 |
| H5 | 0.89 | 0.88 |

- **Query and key point the same way in all 12 heads.** By pair strength, 92–100% sits on positively matched pairs, and no head has negatively matched pairs. So a query scores keys whose *previous* token resembles its own token: "find where I appeared before and read what came next."
- **The current-token half matches only weakly** (+0.14 to +0.40), except L3 H2 (+0.87), a copy head.
- **The attention probe agrees.** Queries at fixed in-document positions (x = 20…4,000), with each query's full softmax row kept rather than averaged:
  - at x = 4,000, 30–49% of the top long-range keys of the sharp layer-3 heads (H1, H4, H5) are induction targets;
  - half of those heads' long-range mass sits on 6–36 keys;
  - L3 H2 picks earlier copies of the query token (33% of its top keys).
- **Layer-5 heads are induction-shaped in the weights too (0.85–0.93), but diffuse in behavior.** Half their long-range mass needs 93–172 keys. They likely match on broader features, so many keys qualify.

**2. The 64 shifted dims are not redundant in weight space**

| per head, shifted half | range |
|---|---|
| directions for 50% / 90% of B's strength | 11–19 / 40–48 |
| effective rank (of 64) | 41–55 |
| stable rank | 12–28 |
| average \|cos\| between different key channels | 0.04–0.07 |
| top 8 channels' share of strength (uniform = 0.125) | 0.14–0.15 |

The channels are near-orthogonal and none dominates. A dozen or so stronger directions plus a long real tail. This is weight space only: whether the data uses all 64 needs an activation-side rank or an ablation, which isn't run yet.

**3. Tying the query to the key on the shifted half costs nothing**

`mla_tie_prev_qk` (`b759695d8f`): the query's shifted half *is* the token's own un-shifted key half, so those channels score `k_prev(x_i) · k_prev(x_{j−1})`, a symmetric similarity. It needs no query projection for those 64 channels.

| run | Paloma | step ms |
|---|---|---|
| current best (`lc1-b217-ctrl`) | 2.9521 | 190.2 |
| **tied shifted half (`lc1-b236-tie-prev-qk`)** | **2.9517** | 190.3 |

Neutral: the free query directions were re-learning the key. That makes it a free simplification, and it drops 64 query columns per head in both MLA layers.

**4. For sparse attention**

The shifted half is close to a symmetric positive form, a learned similarity between the query token and each key's previous token. A low-rank index over previous-token states (around 16–32 dims) could pre-select long-range candidates for the retrieval heads. The diffuse layer-5 heads look better suited to pooled chunk summaries than to top-k selection.

**Next:**
- an activation-side effective rank of the shifted half;
- shifting 16 or 32 channels instead of 64;
- the Inkling relative-position bias by distance. That probe run (`lc1-b235-relpos-probe`) just finished.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Config change: KDA write and erase gates dropped** (Gated DeltaNet-2 gates, adopted in batch 88)

They were worth −0.0024 at d512 (batch 88, two seeds) for about +1% step time. At the hero shape, d6144 / 48 layers on one GB200 rack, they cost far more: each is a full 6144×6144 projection in all 36 KDA layers.

| GB200 1-rack, late steps | step time | MFU | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| with write + erase gates | 19.42 s | 25.7% | 216k |
| without (`lc1-gb200-nogate30`) | **17.95 s** | **27.6%** | **232k** |

Kimi K3's KDA has neither gate: it keeps a full-rank output gate, a low-rank decay gate and a per-head β ([arXiv 2607.24653](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1)). The base config is now `base16` (base15 without `kda_write_gate`, `kda_erase_gate`, `kda_onchip_erase_gate`), and new d512 pairs run against it.

comments.author: marin-belay-bot
comments.body:
📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-6079384012)):

> Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.
>
> Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.
>
> Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.
