- [`generate_report.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d25821/scripts/ops/storage/generate_report.py) — existing Iris compute and CI publication pattern

# Proposed Fix

1. Reuse the catalog pin and segment metadata from `rw/cross-region-catalog`. Process selected segments one at a time in a temporary directory: filter `epoch_ms`, `key`, and `data` with DuckDB, consume matching rows in batches, merge counters and bounded samples, then delete the segment before the next download. Preserve the existing report counts and sample ordering. Record selected bytes and fail if a segment exceeds the configured local disk budget.
2. Move that scan and the controller-checkpoint join into an Iris CPU job pinned with `region_constraint(["us-central2"])`. Write only the JSON, Markdown, and CSV outputs to a `us-central2` staging prefix. Let the GitHub workflow submit and wait for the job, fetch those small outputs, create the gist, and post to Discord, following the storage report's orchestration pattern.
3. Add a dedicated report channel and webhook, pass it through `egress_report.py --channel`, and restore the daily schedule only after the channel is configured. Keep manual dispatch for dry runs.
4. Test catalog cutoff and delayed segments, and compare one-segment versus multi-segment reports on a fixture with duplicate log lines and cross-region paths. Run a current-catalog dry run on a `us-central2` worker; require recent segments, nonempty in-window input, bounded peak disk use, and a successfully fetched report before enabling the schedule. A day with zero cross-region mentions remains a valid report if input coverage is healthy.

The branch is a starting point, not a merge candidate: its bulk download path must be replaced before the schedule returns.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
Since 2026-10-18 05:49 UTC, every mini-swe-agent trial on Harbor main fails before its first model call, and SWE-bench Verified scores read 0. Marin main pins Harbor `18e71265`, so any SWE eval launched from marin main today is affected. Harbor `38742b0f` on `benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-runtime` has the fix, but Harbor main does not.

Harbor installs the agent inside each sandbox with `uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0` ([`mini_swe_agent.py` L456 on main](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/18e712655917ee1c5f82624809339daff3a26a9e/src/harbor/agents/installed/mini_swe_agent.py#L456)). mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 requires only `litellm>=1.75.5`. litellm 1.106.0, released at 05:49 UTC, raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` on the first query.

Symptom: the vLLM server logs `/tokenize` requests but no `/v1/chat/completions`. Each trajectory has 2 steps and 0 prompt/completion tokens. The orchestrator log does not show the import error, because the captured agent stdout is cut off before it. The shootout's plain-arm SWE r100 screen read 0/99: 98 trials ended in `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`, 1 in `VerifierRuntimeError`, 1 in `AgentTimeoutError`.

Local repro, against any OpenAI-compatible server set in `HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE`:

```python
# uv run --no-project --with mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with litellm==1.106.0 repro.py
from minisweagent.models.litellm_model import LitellmModel
LitellmModel(model_name="hosted_vllm/m", model_kwargs={"api_key": "EMPTY"}).query(
    [{"role": "system", "content": "s"}, {"role": "user", "content": "u"}]
)
```

It raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` and sends no request. With `litellm==1.103.5` the request goes through. With Harbor 38742b0f's install (`uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with mcp==2.3.0`) it also goes through: litellm 1.106.0 + mcp 2.3.0.

Who is affected: every mini-swe-agent eval and SWE-smith generation trial whose sandbox installed after 05:49 UTC on 2026-10-18, on Harbor `016dd78b` (the September campaign pin) or `18e71265` (marin main). Terminus-2 (TBLite, TB2), Evalchemy and BFCL do not install mini-swe-agent and are unaffected. The task204 LR-sweep SWE screens finished before 05:49 UTC and are valid.

Fix options:
1. Recommended: port 38742b0f's install change (`--with mcp==2.3.0` plus the setup-time import check) to Harbor main, then advance marin's Harbor pin. The setup check turns this kind of dependency drift into a setup failure, not a 0 score. Runs on the fix use litellm 1.106.0 instead of the earlier < 1.106 client, so comparisons should rerun their baseline under the same install.
2. Add `--exclude-newer 2026-10-18T05:00:00Z` to the install. This reproduces the pre-incident dependency set exactly, but the date must be bumped by hand later.
3. Pin `litellm<1.106` in the install. This is narrower, but leaves the other mini-swe-agent dependencies unpinned.

The shootout reruns its SWE screens (three arms plus v0) on 38742b0f. Shootout: #10213. Eval policy: #10197.


Incident note: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/789

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
The [public Snowball model family tree](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/d3b5517a-c119-4fd9-999d-362183422bf3/v/6/) has been on main since commit 55dd5cc892 ([#9737](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9737), 2026-10-19). Its source is `infra/marina/applets/snowball_family_tree/`. [The documentation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/references/snowball-family-tree.md) describes adding models to `graph-data.json` by PR. Make that the only route, with main as the tree's single source of truth.

Every model addition or edge change should be a reviewed PR to `graph-data.json` on main. Each node should carry its `source` and `evidence` links, and inferred lineage should remain marked `inferred`. Changes should not be sent as files outside the repo.

Releases should come only from main. Run `marina release ... --base-version CURRENT_VERSION` from a clean checkout at the current remote main, as the documentation describes. The release records the git commit. If the live version differs from main, record the difference and its reason in this issue or in the PR that will close the gap. Each tree PR should state whether it needs a release; merging alone does not publish.

As checked on 2026-10-23, live v6's embedded graph data matches main's `graph-data.json`: 130 nodes, 138 edges, snapshot 2026-10-19. Its `app.js` and `style.css` match #9737's second-to-last commit, d33f3101a9. Main includes the final refactor, b41de53442 ("Unify lineage edge markup and remove overridden styles"), which adds an `edgePath()` helper and removes overridden `.edge` CSS rules. That refactor should not change what the tree shows. `index.html` matches once the data is substituted as `build.py` does it.

Earlier versions contain these snapshots: v2/v3, 2026-10-04 with 118 nodes; v4/v5, 2026-10-12 with 126 nodes; and v6, 2026-10-19. Their frontend files match commits on the #9737 branch. There is no data drift to fix today. The proposed process would keep the data aligned as more models arrive.

About 25 SFT-shootout runs trained from Snowball v0 and v0.1 are coming soon, most without published weights. They would be added in one reviewed PR with `model: null` where no public weights exist.

@penfever, does this match your intent for the tree? Should outside contributors' additions also come as PRs, from a fork or opened on their behalf, instead of being folded into a release by hand? Should releases follow every merged tree PR or happen in batches?

issues.author: ryan-williams
issues.body:
We want to answer some high-level questions about how Marin uses our compute resources today. This likely involves a combination of querying our existing deployments (Iris, Finelog), and building more subjective analyses on top of that. Where necessary, we may need to extend our existing telemetry to capture more information (if we aren't adequately capturing the runtime of tasks or whatever).

- How effective is OA/Marin at using its compute resources?
  - For reserved quotas (GPU compute), how good are we at keeping these resources active at all times?
  - For dynamic quotas (preemptible TPUs), how much do we observe fluctuations in compute over time and region?
- Of the work we're doing, *where* are we spending our time (perhaps broken across CPU & GPU)? Some example categories we might break things into:
  - Data processing
  - Data generation
  - Pre-training
  - Post-training experiments
  - Evaluations
  - External collaborations

Internally, we might also want to know how we can use compute *better*. Are there areas where we are idling large amounts of compute?

- Jobs requesting large CPU/memory quotas but only using a fraction
- Jobs holding GPU resources that are mostly idle - maybe an opportunity for refactoring and making it easier for users to write shared services across multiple jobs

Related ideas: Iris already collects periodic CPU and thread profiles for every job. Extending that to accelerator profiles (xprof on TPUs, nsys on GPUs) for a sample of jobs would give fleet-wide accelerator utilization without profiling everything. #8247 is one known case of stranded GPUs.

(Adapted from writeups by @rjpower)

# Proposed Fix

1. Build a 30-day hourly inventory by cluster and region. Confirm time-varying reserved GPU capacity from the capacity owner; separately report ready inventory, allocated GPU-hours, and device-active GPU-hours. For preemptible TPUs, plot held chip-hours, running-task chip-hours, queue depth, and provisioning stockouts by zone; do not treat held capacity as cloud quota.
2. Join Iris jobs and attempts to task measurements and GPU node telemetry. Assign each root job to the issue's work categories with a reviewed mapping and an explicit unknown bucket. Report accelerator-hours, CPU core-hours, requested-versus-used CPU and memory, and telemetry coverage for each category.
3. Rank the largest gaps in accelerator-hours and request-versus-use ratios, then inspect representative jobs. Separate unallocated capacity, allocated but low-activity devices, placement blockage, and missing telemetry. Track the known placement cases in #8247 and #8925 without duplicating their fixes.
4. Publish a reproducible report with queries, time window, capacity sources, category mapping, missing-data rates, and the highest-impact opportunities. Open focused telemetry or scheduling issues only where the measured gaps prevent an answer or identify a specific fix.

issues.title: Audit how Marin uses its compute resources

issues.author: ryan-williams
issues.body:
Most storage written by Iris jobs has no recorded owner, so nobody can tell who is responsible for cleaning it up. Iris does not choose output paths. Marin prefixes `users/<username>/` onto a few outputs ([#6787], [#6790]), only in these cases:

- `train_lm` and a handful of experiment entry points, when the step's version is mutable (`dev` or `*-dev`), through `user_namespaced_name` (`lib/marin/src/marin/experiment/namespacing.py`).
- About eight post-training launchers that call `user_owned_name` themselves.
- Datasets and fixed (calendar-versioned) checkpoints stay shared by design.

On 2026-10-22, `gs://marin-us-central2/users/` held 10.4 TB. In a 6h sample of task log lines naming `gs://` write paths, one user's jobs wrote under `users/`. Everyone else wrote to shared top-level prefixes such as `checkpoints/` and `grug/`, or to personal top-level directories (one holds about 100 TB), mostly from launchers that never call `train_lm`. The [disk-usage dashboard][gcs.oa.dev] can attribute only the `users/<seg>/` prefixes, manual assignments, and a few signals. That leaves several hundred TB of non-dataset storage with no owner.

A job's writer is identified in three places, and none of them is authoritative:

- `Provenance.built_by` in `MARIN_PROVENANCE` is the submitting machine's OS login (`lib/rigging/src/rigging/provenance.py`). `username_segment()` derives the `users/` segment from it (#7470), and every executor step writes it into `.artifact.json`.
- The `/<user>/` segment of the Iris job ID comes from `--user`, `IRIS_USER`, or the OS login (`resolve_job_user`, `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/job_info.py`). It is chosen by the client.
- The controller's `submitting_user` is the authenticated principal, such as an IAP email (`submitting_user_for_root`, `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/jobs.py`). It is the only verified identity, but nothing in a task or an artifact record exposes it.

Writes outside the executor (scripts writing straight to `gs://` paths, launchers in other repositories) leave no record at all. #7205 (move storage usage onto the per-user scheme and update docs and defaults to match) closed as stale on 2026-10-15 with only a docs branch done.

Done when:

1. Tasks can read their verified submitting user, and `.artifact.json` provenance records it together with the Iris job ID. `username_segment()` prefers it over the OS login.
2. Every executor step with a mutable version namespaces its output under `users/<username>/` by default, not just `train_lm` and the opt-in launchers. Shared datasets and fixed versions are unchanged.
3. The launchers that wrote the most unowned data in a recent log sample either write under `users/` or write an artifact record naming their owner. The log-sample query is checked in so the audit can be rerun.
4. The docs say where scratch outputs go, who owns them, and how they are cleaned up, which completes #7205.

Open question: whether `users/` should also get a retention policy (for example a lifecycle rule or an age-based report to each owner), or whether recording owners is enough for now.

[#6787]: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6787
[#6790]: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/6790
[gcs.oa.dev]: https://gcs.oa.dev

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Iris persists the authenticated `submitting_user` on each job and inherits it for child jobs, but `RunTaskRequest` does not carry it into a task. Marin resolves artifact paths before execution, while lazy and plain executor steps write records through different paths; changing only `username_segment()` would leave paths or records unattributed. `local_admin` is an anonymous machine principal, so it cannot establish a human owner.

**Relevant code**
- [`ops/job.py#L175-L211`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/ops/job.py#L175-L211) — verified submitter and child inheritance.
- [`job.proto#L646-L687`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/job.proto#L646-L687) — task dispatch lacks that field.
- [`runtime/env.py#L163-L230`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/runtime/env.py#L163-L230) — shared task environment builder.
- [`lazy.py#L225-L241`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/lazy.py#L225-L241) and [`lazy.py#L297-L379`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/lazy.py#L297-L379) — path calculation and lazy record write.
- [`artifact.py#L350-L376`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/artifact.py#L350-L376) — plain step record write.

# Proposed Fix

This spans Iris, rigging, Marin, launchers, and docs; implement it in three reviewable PRs.

1. **Carry trusted task identity.** Add `submitting_user` to `RunTaskRequest` from the persisted job row in both dispatch paths. Set `IRIS_SUBMITTING_USER` after merging user environment variables in both the worker and Kubernetes paths, and expose it through `JobInfo`; derive the job ID from the existing task ID. Test root and child jobs, both backends, and attempts to override the system value. Keep `local_admin` distinguishable from an authenticated person.
2. **Record the writer.** Add optional `submitting_user` and `iris_job_id` fields to `Provenance`, retaining `built_by` as the launcher OS login. Merge the current task identity at the actual `.artifact.json` write in both lazy and plain step paths, so a launcher-side capture cannot erase the writer's identity. Make `username_segment()` prefer a verified person, then the existing launch identity for local or anonymous runs. Use a stable segment mapping that distinguishes email domains; do not attribute `local_admin` to a human.
3. **Apply one mutable-path rule.** Resolve canonical `dev` and `*-dev` output paths under `users/<segment>/` at the executor boundary, so `ArtifactStep.path()`, lowered `StepSpec` output paths, dependency paths, and cache reads agree. Remove the `user_namespaced_name()` calls that would double-prefix paths. Preserve explicit adopted/pinned paths and fixed calendar-versioned artifacts; audit any direct `StepSpec` caller that encodes a mutable version outside `ArtifactStep`. Tests should cover two users building the same mutable name, dependency resolution, fixed-version sharing, and explicit paths.
4. **Audit the remaining writers.** Check in the bounded six-hour task-log query with its time range and grouping by job and destination prefix. Use it to rank the largest non-dataset writers, then update each in-scope launcher to use the executor path rule or write an owner-bearing artifact record. Re-run the query and compare owner coverage. Document scratch paths, ownership, and cleanup in `docs/explanations/marin-prefix.md` and the storage guide. Leave existing objects in place; report aged `users/` prefixes before proposing an automatic retention rule, since some contain checkpoints worth keeping.

The first PR should establish the Iris identity contract; the next should change provenance and paths with regression coverage; the last should address the measured launcher list and docs.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
When a served model's Iris task is preempted and replaced, the native capability proxy answers requests that arrive during the replacement with HTTP 502 `upstream transport error: client error (Connect)`. Clients see a hard failure for a gap Iris is already recovering from.

Impact: on 2026-10-18 an Evalchemy GSM8K screen on H100 lost 112 of 1,319 rows. Kueue preempted the serve task at 00:14:07 UTC; Iris rescheduled it and the replacement was initializing from 00:14:55. At 00:19 the proxy returned 502 to the queued requests, the client exhausted its retries, and the rows were recorded as `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` (`model_transport`). Recovery needed a manual selective rerun of the 112 doc ids and a cached regrade before the record could be merged (1,215/1,319 after recovery).

A second instance on 2026-10-19 lost 960 of 1,319 GSM8K rows. Kueue preempted the serve task at 03:42:04 UTC. Requests in flight at that moment got 502 `client error (SendRequest)` (15 responses at 03:42). Requests sent afterwards got 502 `client error (Connect)` (985 responses from 03:42 to 03:47) until the client gave up, and the rows were recorded as `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR`. The same serve task was preempted six more times over the next 11 hours (attempts 1 to 6) at interactive priority. That record needed a full GSM8K rerun.

The 502 comes from the native proxy's upstream error path ([`lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs` L1243-L1246](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L1243-L1246)), which maps any connect failure to `BAD_GATEWAY`. [`lib/iris/docs/federation.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/iris/docs/federation.md) documents this message as "cannot connect to its upstream".

Reproduce:
1. Serve a model through a capability URL (for example the eval launcher with Harbor or a capability-routed Evalchemy run).
2. Send a steady stream of requests through the capability URL.
3. Preempt or cancel the serving task and let Iris start a replacement under the same endpoint name.
4. Requests sent before the replacement registers return 502 with the message above.

Expected: while the endpoint's job is still live and a replacement task is pending or initializing, the proxy holds the request until the endpoint registers again (bounded by the request timeout), or returns 503 with `Retry-After`. Clients retry connect errors and 503s with backoff for at least the documented serve replacement time. A replacement can take much longer than a request timeout: in the second instance the serve stayed unavailable for the rest of the GSM8K client's retry budget. Holding requests therefore covers short gaps only. Long gaps need the 503 signal so that the client can pause instead of recording failures.

Done when: a serve-replacement test through the capability proxy completes requests sent during the gap, or receives 503 with `Retry-After`, and no 502 is returned while the job is live.

Related: #10237 covers the direct-route client (`remote_inference`) keeping a stale address after rescheduling.

Evidence (Iris task events and the Evalchemy client log, URLs omitted):

```
2026-10-18T00:14:07.473Z attempt 0  k8s/kueue        WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted  Preempted to accommodate a workload (UID: 3fc9af02-…)
2026-10-18T00:14:50.525Z attempt 0  iris/controller  TaskRetryScheduled             Backend reported PREEMPTED; controller returned the task to PENDING.
2026-10-18T00:14:55.578Z attempt 1  k8s/container    PodInitializing
[00:19:08] eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0 | API request failed! Status code: 502, Response text: {"error":"upstream transport error: client error (Connect)"}. Retrying...
[00:19:09] eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0 | API request failed! Status code: 502, Response text: {"error":"upstream transport error: client error (Connect)"}. Retrying...
```

Second instance: serve task `/karan/eval-20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-04d5/inference-177d09d0c73a4f048310e082db087746/0` (Kueue `WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted` at 03:42:04, 05:19:02, 07:12:39, 10:56:25, 11:04:59, 14:19:01 and 14:24:54 UTC), evaluator task `/karan/eval-20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-04d5/eval-gsm8k-0shot-4ac3cd86/0`, record `20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-gsm8k-0shot-6554` (`infra_failed`, 359/1,319 scored).

First instance: serve task `/karan/eval-20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-1b9b/inference-a54b7942d3b34ffba92e5f0d4192aa69/0`. Evaluator task: `/karan/eval-20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-1b9b/eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0`. Record: `20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-gsm8k-0shot-77c1`.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Iris keeps a serving endpoint's last address until its lease expires (at most 10 minutes). The native proxy can therefore route a request to a preempted task; its upstream transport error path returns 502. Once the lease expires, the registry omits the endpoint and the same live job can instead return 404. The registry has no replacement state, so changing 502 to 503 alone would leave that later gap unresolved. [PR #10033](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10033) handles Evalchemy's direct-route relay and does not change this capability path.

**Relevant code**
- [`endpoint_service.py#L40-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/endpoint_service.py#L40-L49) — ten-minute registration lease.
- [`endpoint_service.py#L165-L177`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/endpoint_service.py#L165-L177) — live mappings enter the proxy snapshot.
- [`lib.rs#L230-L264`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L230-L264) — expired mappings are skipped.
- [`lib.rs#L1190-L1240`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L1190-L1240) — transport failures become 502.
- [`client.py#L79-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L79-L93) — Evalchemy allows eight request retries.

# Proposed Fix

The failure chain is task preemption → old endpoint address remains routable → connect/send fails → proxy returns 502; after lease expiry, lookup returns 404. This needs a controller/proxy availability contract and a capability-client retry budget, so it is larger than a local status-code patch.

1. Preserve an authenticated endpoint name while its owning task is being retried. Publish `ready` versus `replacing` in the controller's proxy snapshot/deltas; preemption and lease expiry make the old address unavailable, replacement registration restores `ready`, and terminal job/task state removes the route. Reconstruct the same state after controller restart.
2. Return 503 with `Retry-After` for `replacing` and for connect/send failures to task-owned endpoints, including a race before the registry update. Keep ordinary 404 for unknown names and 502 for unrelated upstream/protocol failures. Do not replay an in-flight POST inside the proxy.
3. Verify the pinned Evalchemy and Harbor capability clients retry 503 according to `Retry-After` with a time budget tied to the evaluation deadline and stop on terminal serve state. Extend their policy where needed; leave the direct-route relay in #10033 alone.
4. Add a real HTTP capability-proxy test that sends requests before preemption, during replacement, after the old lease expires, and after a new address registers. Assert no 502/404 during the recoverable gap, 503 plus `Retry-After` until recovery, successful forwarding afterwards, and terminal/unknown routes ending promptly. Cover an in-flight send failure and the federated capability relay as separate cases.

Open decision: the repository documents a 10-minute endpoint lease but no upper bound on serve replacement. Use the evaluation's overall deadline as the retry cap unless a shorter serve-replacement contract is established; eight immediate request retries are insufficient for the observed multi-minute gaps.

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
On a Kubernetes cluster, submitting a running job again with `EXISTING_JOB_POLICY_RECREATE` starts the new attempt and leaves the old attempt's pod running. Iris stops listing the old attempt, so nothing stops that pod. Each redeploy of a job this way adds one more running copy: on 2026-10-26, four copies of one controller job ran at once on cw-us-east-02a, and the stale copies kept submitting jobs.

Reproduce (cw-us-east-02a, submitted through the hub, default profile and egress):
1. Submit a job whose PID 1 does not exit on SIGTERM, for example `python3 -c "import time; time.sleep(3600)"`. Python as PID 1 has no SIGTERM handler, so the kernel drops the signal.
2. When it runs, submit the same job name again with `existing_job_policy=EXISTING_JOB_POLICY_RECREATE`. The submit returns within seconds.
3. `kubectl -n iris get pods | grep <job>` shows two Running pods. Both have the same `iris.job_id`, `iris.task_id` and `iris.attempt_id: "0"` labels, and neither has a `deletionTimestamp`. `iris task describe <job>/0` lists one attempt.

Expected: RECREATE stops the old pod before it drops the old attempt, by deleting the pod so that Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after the grace period.

The drain wait does not cover this on Kubernetes. After the cancel, the RECREATE path waits up to 120 s for `has_unfinished_worker_attempts` to become false, then removes the old job ([jobs.py#L731-L757](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/jobs.py#L731-L757)). That check counts only attempts with a `worker_id` ([reads.py#L717-L733](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L717-L733)). Kubernetes attempts have none (`iris task describe` shows WORKER `-`), so the check is false at once. Pods whose PID 1 exits on SIGTERM did not stay behind, so the old attempt probably gets a SIGTERM but no pod delete. We have not confirmed this in the controller logs.

A later `iris job cancel <job>` deletes every pod with the job's labels, including the stale ones.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

`LaunchJob(RECREATE)` cancels the old job, but its drain predicate counts only attempts with a worker ID. Kubernetes attempts have no worker ID, so the service removes their rows and admits the replacement before pod deletion is confirmed. The Kubernetes sync also identifies unwanted pods by `(task_hash, attempt_id)`; a replacement reuses that pair, so the old running pod appears desired even after the new attempt starts. Coscheduled replacements reuse the same Kueue pod-group name, which makes deleting the old Workload unsafe once the new pods exist.

**Relevant code**
- [`service.py#L1665-L1709`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/service.py#L1665-L1709) — cancel, drain, remove, resubmit
- [`reads.py#L704-L727`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/reads.py#L704-L727) — worker-only drain predicate
- [`tasks.py#L2479-L2486`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2479-L2486) — desired pod keys
- [`tasks.py#L2768-L2811`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L2768-L2811) — stray deletion
- [`tasks.py#L293-L302`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L293-L302) — reused gang identity

# Proposed Fix

1. Retain cancelled Kubernetes attempts as stop targets in the controller's reconcile snapshot, carrying `attempt_uid`. Have the Kubernetes backend delete each exact old pod and report completion only after the pod has disappeared; do not force-delete its API object. Finalize the old attempt on that observation.
2. Make every job replacement path treat unfinished Kubernetes attempts as undrained. For RECREATE, wait for stop completion before removing the old job and admitting a new one. If deletion cannot be confirmed within the deadline, return an error and keep the old attempt record so reconciliation can continue; never start another copy on timeout.
3. Match desired pods by incarnation-specific identity, and give a resubmitted coscheduled gang a distinct Kueue pod-group identity. Old pod and Workload cleanup must not delete the replacement's resources.
4. Add a fake-Kubernetes regression that resubmits a running attempt with the same task ID and attempt number, including a delayed deletion and a deletion failure. Assert that only one pod can run before submission succeeds; cover the coscheduled Workload case separately.

The prior pod-name change in [#7518](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7518) avoids adopting a stale *terminal* pod, but does not stop a stale running one. No open PR found for #10712. The implementation PR should use `Fixes #10712`.

comments.body: 🤖 Recorded the incident response and diagnostic discriminator in [Echo](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/874). Until the lifecycle fix lands, cancel the old Kubernetes job and verify its pods have disappeared before submitting the replacement; a returned RECREATE call or one listed attempt does not confirm pod deletion.

issues.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
issues.body:
The October 26 Tier 2 Datakit canary hit its 14,400-second Actions wait limit at 18:01:33 UTC while Iris still reported the ferry running. In the ferry's first Iris task attempt, a fuzzy-cluster worker waited about 110 minutes without receiving an attempt. Iris then retried the parent task after its worker failed. Fuzzy-cluster verification was still running at the CI deadline. This is an infra/scheduling timeout; the reason the child was not placed and the cause of the worker's cancelled RPCs are unknown.

Reproduce:
1. Open the [failed Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/40335620738) and its `Wait for datakit tier2 ferry` step.
2. Under the [Iris job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Frunner%2Firis-run-job-20261026-140103), inspect child job `zephyr-fuzzy-large-clusters-a0997992-coordinator-06c0e778-workers` and its sole task. It has no attempt or run duration.

Expected: the worker receives an attempt in time for the ferry to finish, or Iris reports why it remains unplaced before the four-hour wait expires.

<details><summary>Evidence</summary>

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
**Try adding CPLM Plus from #10678 to the Belay experiment ladder.** It extends the copy head with predecessor-conditioned keys and normalized case-class emissions, adding only d² + 2d + 1 parameters over ordinary CPLM.

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. At d1024, Plus also improves over Belay (1.021640 → 1.014601 Paloma; 0.772050 → 0.767052 Uncheatable).

These runs approximately match analytical useful FLOPs, not wall time, and use one seed, so I think this is worth testing against the current recipe under Belay's fixed-time evaluation with paired seeds. The PR is stacked on #10260 and includes the implementation and results; throughput for the current PR revision still needs validation.

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
Add three selected public text-only subsets of [LAB-Bench v1](https://openathena.ai/bio-evals/benchmarks/lab-bench) to Marin's vendored Evalchemy and expose each component separately in EvalDash. This prepares LAB-Bench for a proposed in-distribution (ID) development evaluation under the [Marin evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Canonical policy adoption remains a separate decision after validation.

Scope:

| Component | Public questions | Evaluation key |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| ProtocolQA | 108 | `lab-bench-protocolqa` |
| SeqQA | 600 | `lab-bench-seqqa` |
| CloningScenarios | 33 | `lab-bench-cloning` |

Support all 741 public questions from the pinned [dataset revision](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench/tree/5c77cec648430f30611808808861eb86f81d5eaa); routine policy selection remains open. The model receives text and generates a multiple-choice answer without browsing, code execution, or other external tools. SeqQA therefore measures unaided sequence reasoning.

Implementation decisions and alternatives considered (2026-10-26):

These choices define the current draft implementation; they do not constitute team approval for canonical evaluation-policy adoption.

| Decision | Alternative considered | Reason for the current choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start with the three public text-only components, without tools. | Add retrieval, vision, or tool-enabled tasks in the same integration. | Establish a bounded no-tools baseline. The omitted components and requirements for revisiting them are listed below. |
| Preserve separate ProtocolQA, SeqQA and CloningScenarios scores, with SeqQA subtask diagnostics. | Publish only one aggregate LAB-Bench score, or hide component scores inside one evaluation record. | Components measure different capabilities and need separately comparable histories. No canonical aggregate or ranking weight has been agreed. |
| Use generated answers with reasoning allowed. | Score answer-letter log probabilities without generation. | Evaluate reasoning followed by an answer, using the existing generation path. Log-probability scoring would define a different protocol. |
| Remove the author harness's added abstention choice; report accuracy, standard error and sample counts. | Retain abstention-aware precision and attempted-answer coverage. | The current goal is forced-choice capability measurement. This deliberately gives up reproduction of the original uncertainty-calibration protocol. |
| Request a final `Answer: X` and reuse the shared MCQ extractor. | Require the original answer tags and maintain a LAB-Bench-specific grader and reducer. | Follow existing Evalchemy conventions and avoid benchmark-specific formatting machinery. Answers the shared grader cannot extract count as incorrect; deviations from the requested format may still be recoverable. API delivery failures remain ungraded. |
| Use deterministic per-item choice shuffling and pin the dataset and scorer. | Reproduce the author harness's exact permutations. | Preserve reproducible Marin runs without claiming exact historical score comparability. |
| Add the benchmark within vendored Evalchemy, with minimal Marin registration. | Add a Harbor adaptation, dedicated launcher suite, dashboard group, and general tutorial changes. | These direct no-tools questions fit Evalchemy. Existing registration and dashboard behavior provide the three component entries. Keep benchmark-specific protocol documentation close to the adapter. |
| Use shared output-budget resolution, allowing explicit run/model overrides. | Hard-code an 8192-token LAB-Bench output cap. | Avoid a benchmark-specific budget constant. The eventual policy budget is still open; the 32768-token GLM diagnostic cap is not a policy default. |
| Retain the dataset's answers and scientific conventions. | Adjudicate or repair possible scientific ambiguities, including ORF conventions. | Scientific benchmark repair is outside the current integration scope. No answer-key changes or scientific exclusions have been made. |
| Reuse shared runtime/grader tests, with focused coverage only where behavior changes. | Add a separate extensive test suite for every benchmark registration. | Test adaptation and shared behavior that can fail without duplicating implementation details or creating a mandatory per-benchmark suite. |

Open decisions for the team before policy adoption:

- **Suitability and protocol:** Are these three components appropriate ID development evaluations, and are the forced-choice and formatting departures acceptable? Implementation choices above remain subject to this policy decision.
- **Full dataset or fixed subset:** The integration supports all 741 public questions. Decide whether routine evaluations should use all of them or a fixed representative subset. SeqQA contains 15 subtasks with 40 questions each; a first-N limit can cover only one subtask. Any subset must pin its selection rule and question IDs, preserve component/subtask coverage, and report uncertainty.
- **Reasoning and output limits:** Choose the reasoning effort, output cap, and treatment of model-specific endpoint limits. The context-derived GLM smoke, 32768-token GLM diagnostic and 128000-token Luna run are exploratory settings, not agreed cross-model policy. A continuation request or higher reasoning effort would be another explicit protocol choice, not an automatic remedy for truncation.
- **Runtime and cost:** Measure evaluator wall-clock time per component, excluding scheduler wait and model-server startup; retain model, reasoning/output limits, concurrency and timeout settings. Report mean and sample standard deviation across the evaluated cohort following the [evaluation policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197). Separate per-request/trial limits from overall job limits and small-smoke timings from full-panel measurements. Decide whether the measured runtime warrants subsetting or tighter generation budgets.
- **Aggregation and ranking weight:** Decide between keeping only component-level reporting and defining an explicit aggregate. Pooling all questions heavily weights SeqQA; including all three dashboard columns also gives the benchmark three ranking entries. No canonical weighting is chosen.
- **Failures and retries:** Answers the shared grader cannot extract and reasoning-only output-budget exhaustion score incorrect under the current grader. API/transport failures remain ungraded. Agree on bounded infrastructure retries, completion requirements, and how retry provenance is reported; do not silently retry wrong or truncated answers. Luna's combined result explicitly identifies two separately generated diagnostic retries.
- **Validation required for adoption:** Direct endpoint runs establish prompt/grader results but do not establish the full native Marin → Evalchemy → EvalDash path. Complete that integration validation before claiming readiness for canonical panels.

Detailed results, the collapsed SeqQA subtask table, and archived launcher code are in the [Luna results record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10575#issuecomment-6423403346).

Deferred scope and rationale:

| Item | Why deferred | Requirements for a follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool-enabled versions of the selected subsets, especially SeqQA | Tools change the measured capability from unaided reasoning to performance with an agent and its tools. Establish the no-tools baseline first. | Define a separately named protocol with fixed tools, agent, network access and execution budgets; validate a Harbor task adaptation and retain tool traces. |
| LitQA2 (199), SuppQA (82), DbQA (520) | These target literature, supplementary-material and database retrieval. A no-tools score is possible, but would not establish retrieval capability. | Specify literature/corpus access, supplement handling and database versions or snapshots, plus tool and network policy. Validate source availability and scoring under that protocol. |
| FigQA (181), TableQA (244) | Both supply images, including TableQA's tables. They require a vision-capable evaluation path and model cohort. | Preserve image inputs and validate the multimodal route. Treat the existing Harbor FigQA agent protocol separately from direct tool-free image answering; it does not cover TableQA. |
| LABBench2 | It is a distinct benchmark with different tasks and grading, requiring its own scope and integration assessment. | Review dataset access, subset selection and native evaluators before proposing a separate addition. |
| Authors' private holdout | It is not part of the public release available for this implementation. | Obtain author-approved access and evaluation terms before considering its use. |

Counts refer to the public [LAB-Bench dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/futurehouse/lab-bench). These deferrals do not assign the omitted subsets an ID or OOD designation.

Implementation and protocol details:

[Draft PR #10582](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10582) implements `marin-labbench-no-tools-v3` with one shared loader/prompt builder, three Evalchemy registrations and three Marin evaluation configurations. Evalchemy's sources are part of the vendored runtime; Harbor's adapter generators are maintained separately, and its existing LAB-Bench adapter covers FigQA only. EvalDash's [measurement layer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/86fc7b67c9/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py#L254) uses one headline measurement per registered evaluation name, motivating the three entries.

The shared `letter_choice` grader uses HLE's deterministic extractor, without an LLM fallback. It prefers provider final-answer content and strips explicit thinking blocks. Normally completed reasoning-only responses remain eligible for extraction; reasoning-only truncations score zero. Within the selected text, it uses the first answer-prefixed letter, then the last isolated letter as a fallback. The final-content correction also affects HLE and GPQA Diamond. Earlier v2 results and separately labeled v3 rescoring are preserved.

Choice shuffling uses the seed, subset and item ID. Shared output-budget resolution honors explicit run/model limits; otherwise it uses remaining context after prompt reserve and margins. The checked-in configuration requests one response per item, temperature 0, seed 42 and thinking enabled. Effective run overrides must be recorded. Earlier tagged-answer/abstention runs are not comparable to this variant.

Current full-panel evidence:

Full Luna high run and diagnostic retries (2026-10-26): all 741 requests were attempted with eight concurrent standard OpenRouter requests. The original run retained 739 graded responses: ProtocolQA 78/108, SeqQA 507/599, CloningScenarios 26/32. One SeqQA completion exhausted its output budget and scored zero. Two outer API responses failed JSON decoding, leaving those questions ungraded; the original run remains marked partial. Runtime was 1h13m50s including setup and reported model cost was $1.64005307, excluding any unreported charges for the failed responses.

The original diagnostic capture was insufficient: it decoded JSON before saving the HTTP body and did not retain headers or the decoder position. The exact cause of those two failures cannot be recovered. A separate diagnostic run repeated only indices 652 (SeqQA restriction-fragment lengths) and 723 (CloningScenarios), using unchanged request bodies at concurrency one, no automatic retries, and raw-body/status/header capture before parsing. Both returned HTTP 200, valid JSON and normal stops. SeqQA was correct; Cloning was incorrect. Diagnostic model cost was $0.004148025. This failed to reproduce the original problem and does not establish a provider or model root cause.

A separately labeled result combining 739 original responses with these two new attempts yields ProtocolQA 78/108 (72.2%), SeqQA 508/600 (84.7%), and CloningScenarios 26/33 (78.8%). Original failures and scores remain unchanged. The diagnostic artifacts and `recovered-summary.json` are under `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/eval-validation/labbench-10575/luna-diagnostic-20261026/`; original run artifacts are under `luna-full-20261026/` at the same parent. issues.title: [eval] Add no-tools LAB-Bench evaluations with separate component scores

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## Goal

Run a weight-merging loop on spare Marin compute: merge Snowball checkpoints on CPU (reserved v4 hosts in us-central2-b), screen the merges cheaply with TPU vLLM on preemptible single-host slices, and promote winners to the H100 policy evaluation. This issue tracks the project end to end.

## Pins

- Marin base `24ce375f06`
- vLLM fork `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d` (head of marin-community/tpu-inference#27, stacked on #29 and #28), applied job-locally
- Evalchemy `3bb8278`, MATH500 full set, harness seed 19311
- S = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` @ `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`

## Status

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| Inventory, feasibility, campaign matrix | done 2026-10-15 |
| Parents S, C, A5, M staged and sha256-verified in `gs://marin-us-central2/scratch/karan/rsi-merge/parents/` | done 2026-10-16 |
| Merge toolkit: allowlisted BF16 to F32 widening for M's router biases (branch `task/197`) | done, no PR yet |
| TPU scoring smoke test | done: TPU scores 6-7 points below H100 |
| Matched H100 control | done 2026-10-17: 0.944 |
| Quantized serving on v5e | blocked: the pinned fork rejects every quant config for GrugMoE |
| Localize the TPU gap | in progress (#10250) |
| Iteration-one merges (3 recipes) | not started, waiting on the scoring path |

## MATH500 scores for S, same model revision, same Evalchemy pin, same effective sampling

| Server | Score |
|---|---|
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-03 record | 0.950 |
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-17 | 0.944 |
| TPU v6e-8 TP8 bf16 (two runs) | 0.878, 0.882 |
| TPU v5p-8 TP4 bf16 | 0.884 |

Per item: 421 right everywhere, 39 right on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU, 12 wrong everywhere. The 39 are long solutions; 22 of them drift onto a different problem mid-solution.

## The TPU gap (#10250)

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 items match the H100 within noise up to token 2047 and diverge from exactly token 2048, which is S's `sliding_window` (`global_every` 4). The gap grows to about 0.14 nat mean absolute logprob difference by 3-4k tokens.

Ruled out: truncation, thinking mode, sampling (Evalchemy strips temperature and seed, both servers run vLLM defaults), batch dependence, sharding degree and chip generation (v5p-8 TP4 scores the same), cross-request contamination, mask off-by-one (training, FA3 and the TPU kernel all keep the last W tokens including self), KV block eviction (the TPU runner keeps one full-attention cache group), per-layer window plumbing (reaches the TPU kernel unchanged; global layers get no window), KV cache dtype (bf16 on both).

Not valid controls at this pin: `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` (never read by the vLLM model), a GPU TP8 run (GPU GrugMoE requires TP=1), the experimental batched RPA kernel (fails to compile: its SMEM schedule is sized from a reported capacity above the compiler's 1 MiB limit).

A standalone probe of the pinned ragged-paged-attention v3 kernel against its dense reference with random inputs passes 22 cases around the window boundary (error flat at bf16 noise). Random inputs spread attention over about 2048 keys, so that probe cannot see an edge or sink effect. Running now: a kernel probe with peaky scores, a BOS-like sink key and position-bucket values, and a TPU serving control with the window disabled.

Consequence for the loop: TPU vLLM cannot rank merges until this is fixed. One H100x8 MATH500 run costs about 14 minutes of box time per candidate.

## Related

- #10250 TPU sliding-window divergence
- #9400 tpu-inference pin bump and hardware checks
- #8323 Snowball TPU serving
- #7555 earlier long-context divergence on TPU
- marin-community/tpu-inference#28 custom router selections, #29 host storage release, #27 TP8 head padding (the stack every TPU run here used)
- Two Evalchemy integration gotchas found on the way: the pinned Evalchemy strips `temperature` and `seed` from requests, so the server's defaults apply; and marin's FineStore result reader expects native results JSON while Evalchemy `3bb8278` writes parquet tables, so the parent eval job reports FAILED although the child succeeded and the score is in `data/evalchemy_results/`.

## Open decisions

1. Score iteration-one merges on H100 now, or wait for the TPU fix.
2. Open a PR for the merge-toolkit change on `task/197`.
3. File the Iris autoscaler tier-blocking issue (a v6e-4 group in backoff blocks v6e-8 demand in the same zone).

The pinned Evalchemy writes parquet tables while Marin's result reader looks only for `results_*.json`, so a successful child can leave the parent failed. comments.body:
## Localization update: the TPU/H100 gap is the sliding window, and the TPU side matches training

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 MATH500 prompts (Snowball S, `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02@50fe2f48`), now in five configurations: H100 and TPU v6e-8 each with the model's 2048 sliding window and each with the window disabled (`--hf-overrides '{"sliding_window": 262144}'`), plus an H100 repeat for run-to-run noise. Mean |Δ logprob| per position bin:

| positions | H100 vs TPU, window off on both | H100 vs TPU, window on | H100: window on vs off | TPU: window on vs off | H100 repeat noise |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0–2047 | 0.014–0.016 | 0.015–0.017 | 0.013–0.015 | 0.000 | 0.013–0.015 |
| 2048–2111 | 0.012 | 0.026 | 0.013 | 0.025 | 0.012 |
| 2112–2303 | 0.012–0.014 | 0.037–0.039 | 0.018–0.024 | 0.038–0.041 | 0.011–0.014 |
| 2304–2431 | 0.011–0.017 | 0.040–0.066 | 0.037–0.084 | 0.058–0.114 | 0.010–0.014 |
| 2432–3071 | 0.014–0.015 | 0.066–0.079 | 0.124–0.186 | 0.143–0.211 | 0.012–0.015 |
| 3072–4095 | 0.021 | 0.142 | 0.703 | 0.700 | 0.013 |
| 4096–8000 | 0.033 | 0.133 | 1.123 | 1.096 | 0.010 |

1. With the window off on both platforms, H100 and TPU agree at every position to within 0.03 nats. The whole divergence is in how the 2048 window is applied.
2. On TPU (tpu-inference `ae387b8`, ragged paged attention v3) the window takes effect at token 2049 on every long item. Three standalone kernel probes (random, peaky/sink, and serving's per-shard head geometry and request classes) put exactly zero attention mass outside the window. This matches levanter's training mask (`splash_attention_mask.LocalMask(window_size=(W-1, None))` AND causal, `lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/splash_attention.py`).
3. On H100 (vLLM fork `01911be`, FlashAttention 3) the window's effect stays at noise until about token 2150, is about half the TPU's around token 2340, and equals the TPU's from about 2460 on. Past 3072 the two effects are the same size, so every local layer is windowed on both platforms; the H100 differs only in the first few hundred tokens past the boundary, i.e. it keeps seeing some early tokens that the exact window drops.
4. Ruled out on the TPU side: the kernel, the batched kernel (does not compile at this pin), KV block eviction (one cache group on TPU), KV dtype, per-layer window plumbing, RoPE, prefill chunk size (knee stays at 2048 with 1536-token chunks).

Open: which code path in the FA3 backend produces the loose boundary (an FA2 run is in flight), and why the looser window scores higher on MATH500 (0.944 H100 vs 0.878–0.884 TPU). Data: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-{h100x8,h100x8-nowindow,h100x8-fa3repeat,v6e8,nowindow-v6e8,chunk1536-v6e8}/`.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
## TPU serving defect localized: global attention layers get the sliding window

Follow-up to the seven-way comparison above. The TPU-side defect is now named and fixed by a config override; the proper fix is in tpu-inference.

**What happens.** tpu-inference registers a vLLM general plugin (`tpu_inference/layers/vllm/__init__.py`, `register_layers` -> `_register_grugmoe`). Whenever the TPU stack is present it sets `_CONFIG_REGISTRY["grug_moe"] = GrugMoeHfConfig`, replacing the vLLM fork's `GrugMoeConfig`. `GrugMoeHfConfig` (`tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py`) is a plain `PretrainedConfig` with name aliases; it never sets `layer_types`. The fork's `GrugMoeConfig` sets `layer_types` from `grug_moe_layer_types(num_layers, global_every)`. Plugins load in `EngineArgs.__post_init__`, before the model config is built, so on TPU `hf_text_config.layer_types` is `None`. vLLM then sets `cache_config.sliding_window = 2048` (arg_utils: "only set CacheConfig.sliding_window if the model is all sliding window"), and the fork's GrugMoE model, which passes `per_layer_sliding_window=None` for its 7 global layers (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25 of 26), gets 2048 for them through the `Attention.__init__` fallback. A static trace of the TPU engine shows all 26 layers at `sliding_window=2048`. On H100 the plugin is absent, the fork config is used, and the engine builds 4 KV cache groups with the global layers unwindowed. The fork model derives its own layer pattern from `global_every`, so nothing crashes; the window is just applied to the wrong layers.

**Verification.** Passing `--hf-overrides '{"layer_types": [...]}'` (the fork's list: `full_attention` at 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25, `sliding_attention` elsewhere) changes the trace to 7 layers at `None` and 19 at 2048, with 4 KV cache groups. Teacher-forced probe (same 10 MATH500 items, 35,801 positions) against the exact-window eager reference, mean |delta logprob|:

| positions | TPU, override | TPU, default | H100 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0-2048 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.015-0.018 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 2048-2304 | 0.013-0.016 | 0.023-0.038 | 0.012-0.014 |
| 2304-3072 | 0.015-0.017 | 0.054-0.080 | 0.014-0.016 |
| 3072+ | 0.012-0.015 | 0.132-0.142 | 0.011-0.014 |

TPU with the override vs H100 directly: 0.011-0.017 at every position. MATH500 with the override (Evalchemy 3bb8278, seed 19311, same settings as the TPU runs above): **0.940** (470/500, 500 generated and scored, 1421 s), against 0.878-0.884 for TPU without it and 0.944 / 0.950 for the two H100 runs. The gap is closed.

**Fix.** Proper fix is in tpu-inference: `GrugMoeHfConfig` should set `layer_types` the same way the fork does, or the plugin should not replace a registry entry the fork already provides. tpu-inference `main` at 340444337772 (2026-10-19) still has the overwrite. Until then, TPU serving of any GrugMoE checkpoint whose `config.json` lacks `layer_types` needs the override above. Pins: vLLM fork fb02daf, tpu-inference ae387b8, Step12 @50fe2f488aee.
